Ad quod tibi necesse est, ut quo ego dignantius et gratiosius egero tecum, eo tu exsistas humilior, gratior atque subjectior, et nequaquam tanquam vacca lasciviens extollaris de donis tuis: quoniam ego sum et lilium convallium, id est humilium, in quorum mentibus velut in vallibus descendunt, colliguntur, multiplicantur, ac fervent gratiarum mearum charismata, sicut in vallibus aquarum abundant fluenta, et radii solis plus inardescunt: et sicut lilium dulcem reddit odorem, ejusque pars adusta medicinalis efficitur; sic ego mentem quam inhabito, dulcem, in se ipsa tranquillam, aliisque benignam efficio. Igne quoque passionis adustus, factus sum animarum medela.
paras.en: The heavenly Bridegroom speaks to the loving soul: [[2:1|I am the flower of the field|Ego flos campi]]. As if to say: Rightly hast thou said, [[Cant 1:15|Our bed is flourishing|Lectulus noster floridus]], since I myself am the flower of the field, that is, of every devout and fervent created intellect; for in it, as in a fair and level field, I stand, abide, rest and flower, and I adorn it and make it flourish: and so thou thyself, O fervent soul, my spouse, art a flowering and comely field. And as a field outdoors is adorned with flowers, shrubs, seeds and fruits, so thou art adorned with grace and infused virtues, with gifts, fruits, merits and the beatitudes of the way [that is, of this present life, the pilgrim's way to the heavenly homeland]. And because thou art sincere and simple, free of the crookedness of injustice and of the thorns and thistles of passions and vices, and stretching thyself out by the breadth of charity to all, even to enemies, thou art level and broad like a field; therefore I gladly walk in thee as in a pleasant and spacious field. Again, as a field is ploughed, sown and tilled by its owner, so thou art prepared for grace, sown and made fruitful by the Holy Ghost. If then thou wilt have me be the flower of thyself, by no means suffer vices to sprout in the field of thy heart, nor useless thoughts and the stirrings of the passions to remain; but keep this field for me, that I may till it, enrich it and make it fruitful, and walk in it as in a paradise. For this it is needful that the more condescendingly and graciously I deal with thee, the humbler, the more grateful and the more submissive thou be, and that thou by no means be puffed up over thy gifts like a wanton heifer: since I am also [[2:1|the lily of the valleys|et lilium convallium]], that is, of the humble, into whose minds, as into valleys, the gifts of my graces come down, are gathered, are multiplied and glow, as streams of water abound in valleys and the rays of the sun burn more hotly there. And as the lily gives a sweet smell, and its part that is burnt becomes medicinal, so I make the mind I dwell in sweet, peaceful in itself and kind to others. Burnt also by the fire of the passion, I have become the medicine of souls.

paras.t: Sicut lilium inter spinas, sic amica mea inter filias: id est, tu, o anima mihi fidelis, contemplationi intenta, et fervens amore, animabus sæcularibus (quæ aculeis passionum suarum pungunt se ipsas, et per iram, impatientiam, detractionem ac consimilia vitia lacerant alios) ita præstantior, pulchrior, suavior amabiliorque consistis, ut lilium spinis: ideo sicut lilium ornat campum, sic tu Ecclesiam. Verumtamen, quoniam omnes qui volunt pie vivere in me, persecutionem patientur; sic oportet et te pati adversa, et irrisionibus, obtrectationibus, injuriis iniquorum quasi spinis transfigi aut tangi: quod totum si æquanimiter tuleris, et bona pro malis reddideris, dulcedinemque mansuetudinis ac pii et caritativi sermonis inter injuriantes effuderis, sicut lilium inter spinas suavem spargit odorem, digna es nomine lilii. Si vero remordes, irasceris, indignaris, et malum pro malo rependis, seu detrahendo repungis, jam desinis esse sponsa mea; nec lilium, sed spinam te judico; nec sequeris me, qui quum maledicerer, non remaledicebam; quum paterer, non comminabar, imo pro crucifixoribus meis orabam. Fac ergo similiter, nec aliorum improbitate vincaris; sed tua potius caritate, mansuetudine, humilitate, beneficentia, aliorum aversionem, iram, elationem injuriationemque vince, et lucrare sic proximos tuos, ac plures mihi sponsas acquire.
paras.en: [[2:2|As the lily among thorns, so is my love among the daughters|Sicut lilium inter spinas, sic amica mea inter filias]]: that is, thou, O soul faithful to me, intent on contemplation and fervent in love, art as much more excellent, fairer, sweeter and more lovable than worldly souls (which prick themselves with the stings of their passions, and tear others by anger, impatience, detraction and like vices) as the lily is than thorns: therefore, as the lily adorns the field, so dost thou the Church. Yet since [[2 Tim 3:12|all that will live godly|omnes qui volunt pie vivere]] in me [[2 Tim 3:12|shall suffer persecution|persecutionem patientur]], so thou too must suffer adversity, and be pierced or touched as by thorns by the mockeries, slanders and injuries of the wicked: and if thou bear all this with an even mind, and render good for evil, and pour out the sweetness of meekness and of kind and charitable speech among those who wrong thee, as the lily among thorns gives forth a sweet smell, thou art worthy of the name of lily. But if thou bitest back, art angry, art indignant, and repayest evil for evil, or prickest back by detraction, thou ceasest at once to be my spouse; I judge thee not a lily but a thorn; and thou followest not me, who, when I was reviled, did not revile again, when I suffered, did not threaten[[1 Pet 2:23||]], nay, prayed for my crucifiers[[Luke 23:34||]]. Do thou likewise, then, and be not overcome by the wickedness of others; but rather overcome their aversion, anger, pride and injuriousness by thy charity, meekness, humility and kindness, and so win thy neighbours, and gain me more spouses.

paras.t: Denique, his anima virtuosa erudita doctrinis, sponsum commendat, dicendo: Sicut malus inter ligna silvarum, sic dilectus meus inter filios: quia speciosus est præ filiis hominum, et tanta excellentia in omni virtute præfulgens, ut ejus comparatione ceteri sint quasi ligna silvestria; estque lignum vitæ omnibus apprehendentibus ipsum. Unde et bajulans sibi crucem, ac foris jam marcidus, comparavit se florido et immarcescibili ligno, dicens: Si in viridi ligno hæc faciunt, in arido quid fiet? Et quoniam ipse incomparabiliter major me est, ideo comparo eum arbori malo, quæ ab eo comparata sum lilio. Ipse enim non solum sua sanctitate ac fama odorat suaviter, sed et pascit salubriter: quod ego facere nequeo, nisi ministerialiter, in quantum id ipsum ab ipso accepero.
paras.en: Then the virtuous soul, taught by these teachings, commends the Bridegroom, saying: [[2:3|As the apple tree among the trees of the woods, so is my beloved among the sons|Sicut malus inter ligna silvarum, sic dilectus meus inter filios]]: for he is [[Ps 44:3|beautiful above the sons of men|speciosus est præ filiis hominum]], and shines with such excellence in every virtue that compared with him the rest are as trees of the woods; and he is [[Prov 3:18|a tree of life to them that lay hold|lignum vitæ omnibus apprehendentibus]] on him. Hence also, carrying his cross, and outwardly already withered, he compared himself to green and unfading wood, saying: [[Luke 23:31|For if in the green wood they do these things, what shall be done in the dry?|Si in viridi ligno hæc faciunt, in arido quid fiet?]] And since he is beyond compare greater than I, therefore I compare him to an apple tree, I who am compared by him to a lily. For he not only smells sweet by his holiness and good name, but also feeds wholesomely: which I cannot do, save as a minister, in so far as I have received this very thing from him.

paras.t: Sub umbra illius quem desiderabam, sedi: id est, cordis evagationes vitavi, nec per plura dispersi me, quum unum sit necessarium: idcirco sub hujus unius umbra quiescere studeo, quoniam umbra ejus a concupiscentiarum fervore, a passionum vitiorumque æstu refrigerat, et cupiditatis ignem exstinguit. Idcirco, o Domine, sub umbra tuæ omnipotentiæ a malignorum potestate spirituum sim semper securus, sub alis pietatis tuæ defende me; pone me juxta te, et cujusvis manus pugnet contra me. Nempe si Deus pro nobis, quis contra nos? Maledictus autem qui confidit in homine, et ponit carnem brachium suum, et a Domino recedit cor ejus. Ideo in te, Domine, etiam si occideris me, sperabo.
paras.en: [[2:3|I sat down under his shadow, whom I desired|Sub umbra illius quem desiderabam, sedi]]: that is, I have shunned the wanderings of the heart, and have not scattered myself over many things, since [[Luke 10:42|one thing is necessary|unum sit necessarium]]: therefore I strive to rest under the shadow of this One alone, since his shadow cools from the heat of concupiscences, from the burning of passions and vices, and quenches the fire of cupidity. Therefore, O Lord, under the shadow of thy almighty power may I be ever safe from the power of evil spirits; defend me under the wings of thy loving-kindness[[Ps 16:8||]]; [[Job 17:3|set me beside thee, and let any man's hand fight against me|pone me juxta te, et cujusvis manus pugnet contra me]]. For indeed: [[Rom 8:31|If God be for us, who is against us?|si Deus pro nobis, quis contra nos?]] But: [[Jer 17:5|Cursed be the man that trusteth in man, and maketh flesh his arm, and whose heart departeth from the Lord|Maledictus autem qui confidit in homine, et ponit carnem brachium suum, et a Domino recedit cor ejus]]. Therefore in thee, O Lord, even though thou slay me, will I hope[[Job 13:15||]].

paras.t: Et fructus ejus dulcis gutturi meo. Etenim fructus arboris hujus, est quidquid virtutis et gratiæ, quidquid consolationis et gaudii spiritualis in nobis exstiterit: et omnia merita nostra sunt ejus dona, sine cujus actuali motione nec aliquid meritorie possumus cogitare. Et sicut fructus ejus in patria, est beatifica illa fruitio, qua replet, reficit, oblectat et plene contentat omnes Beatos, ac cetera gaudia eorumdem: sic fructus ejus in via, est contemplatio illa profunda, pura ac fervida, quæ appellatur mystica theologia in apice intellectivæ consistens, omnisque sinceritas, quies, oblectatio ei annexa, quæ suavissime reficit animam in hac vita: sed et sacra communio, intelligentia Scripturarum, spiritualis profectus, et gustare quam dulcis est Dominus, ac alia multa, sunt fructus sponsi istius; similiter duodecim fructus Spiritus, de quibus ad Galatas scribit Apostolus.
paras.en: And [[2:3|his fruit was sweet to my palate|Et fructus ejus dulcis gutturi meo]]. For the fruit of this tree is whatever of virtue and grace, whatever of consolation and spiritual joy, there is in us: and all our merits are his gifts, without whose actual moving we cannot even think anything meritoriously. And as his fruit in the homeland [that is, in heaven] is that beatific fruition by which he fills, refreshes, delights and fully contents all the Blessed, together with their other joys, so his fruit on the way is that deep, pure and fervent contemplation which is called mystical theology, which rests in the summit of the intellective power, and all the sincerity, quiet and delight joined to it, which most sweetly refresh the soul in this life: but the holy communion too, the understanding of the Scriptures, spiritual progress, and to have [[1 Pet 2:3|tasted that the Lord is sweet|gustare quam dulcis est Dominus]], and many other things, are fruits of this Bridegroom; likewise the twelve fruits of the Spirit, of which the Apostle writes to the Galatians[[Gal 5:22||]][[Gal 5:23||]] [the Vulgate there names twelve: charity, joy, peace, patience, benignity, goodness, longanimity, mildness, faith, modesty, continency, chastity].

paras.t: Itaque Christus vere et excellentissime est arbor, de qua figuraliter legitur in Daniele: Ecce arbor in medio terræ, et altitudo ejus nimia. Magna arbor et fortis, et proceritas ejus contingens cœlum; adspectus illius erat usque ad terminos universæ terræ. Folia ejus pulcherrima, et fructus ejus nimius, et esca universorum in ea. Subter eam habitabant animalia et bestiæ, et in ramis ejus conversabantur volucres cœli, et ex ea vescebatur omnis caro. Ista tamen ad litteram de Nabuchodonosor dicta sunt; sed verba secundum se sumpta, applicari possent ad Christum multo sublimius, quam ad illum.
paras.en: Thus Christ is truly and most excellently the tree of which we read in figure in Daniel: [[Dan 4:7|behold a tree in the midst of the earth, and the height thereof was exceeding great|Ecce arbor in medio terræ, et altitudo ejus nimia]]. [[Dan 4:8|The tree was great and strong, and the height thereof reached unto heaven: the sight thereof was even to the ends of all the earth|Magna arbor et fortis, et proceritas ejus contingens cœlum; adspectus illius erat usque ad terminos universæ terræ]]. [[Dan 4:9|Its leaves were most beautiful, and its fruit exceeding much: and in it was food for all: under it dwelt cattle and beasts, and in the branches thereof the fowls of the air had their abode: and all flesh did eat of it|Folia ejus pulcherrima, et fructus ejus nimius, et esca universorum in ea. Subter eam habitabant animalia et bestiæ, et in ramis ejus conversabantur volucres cœli, et ex ea vescebatur omnis caro]]. These things, indeed, were said literally of Nabuchodonosor; but the words taken in themselves could be applied to Christ far more sublimely than to him.

paras.t: Introduxit me rex in cellam vinariam. Cella vinaria optime saporosa, salubriter inebriativa, est mysticæ visio theoriæ, tam clara et ardens, quod elevat animam sanctam super cuncta creata, et transfert ac rapit eam in increatum illud objectum: ita quod obliviscitur sui ipsius ac ceterorum, et tota in abyssum lucis incircumscriptibilis absorbetur, afficitur, inflammatur, atque ingenti jucunditate perfunditur, ita quod ex sententia dicere valet: Torrente voluptatis suæ potavit me; et rursus, Concaluit cor meum intra me, et in meditatione mea exardescet ignis. Hinc Augustinus loquitur Deo: Introducis me quandoque in quemdam saporem incognitum. Bernardus quoque: Si quis, inquit, orando obtineat mente excedere in divini arcani thesauros, unde mox redeat divino amore vehementissime flagrans, æstuansque justitiæ zelo, et spiritualibus studiis totaliter fervens; iste quum ructare cœperit crapulam vini spiritualis lætitiæ, dicere potest: Introduxit me rex in cellam vinariam.
paras.en: The king [[2:4|brought me into the cellar of wine|Introduxit me rex in cellam vinariam]] [Denis's text has *rex*, "the king", as at 1:3; the Vulgate here has only *Introduxit me*, "He brought me"]. The cellar of wine, of the finest savour, wholesomely inebriating, is the vision of mystical contemplation [*theoria*, the Greek word for contemplation], so clear and burning that it lifts the holy soul above all created things, and carries it over and ravishes it into that uncreated object: so that it forgets itself and all else, and is wholly absorbed, moved and inflamed in the abyss of uncircumscribable light, and flooded with immense gladness, so that it can say with full meaning: He hath made me drink of the torrent of his pleasure[[Ps 35:9||]] [the Psalm has "thou shalt make them drink of the torrent of thy pleasure"]; and again, [[Ps 38:4|My heart grew hot within me: and in my meditation a fire shall flame out|Concaluit cor meum intra me, et in meditatione mea exardescet ignis]]. Hence Augustine says to God: Thou bringest me in at times to a certain savour unknown. Bernard too: If anyone, he says, in praying obtains to go out of his mind into the treasures of the divine secret, and returns thence presently burning most vehemently with divine love, glowing with zeal for justice, and wholly fervent in spiritual pursuits, he, when he begins to belch forth the surfeit of the wine of spiritual gladness, can say: The king [[2:4|brought me into the cellar of wine|Introduxit me rex in cellam vinariam]].

paras.t: Ordinavit in me caritatem, id est, gratiam discretionis largitus est mihi, ne ex spirituali fervore me ipsam inordinate affligerem, aut per intolerabilia mihi exercitia corpus destruerem. Hæc ordinatio est tanto plus necessaria, quanto fuerit caritatis accensio magis intensa. Zelum quoque caritatis oportet esse secundum scientiam, ne fervens zelator suo fervore præcipitet semetipsum ac alios. Itaque quamvis caritas Dei non posset in se ipsa esse nimis intensa, aut major quam decet: imo quo major, eo et melior; tamen ordinata debet consistere in effectibus, qui ex ea procedunt, aut potius putantur procedere. Nam, ut asserit Augustinus, Virtute nullus male utitur: quia videlicet actus ex virtute directe elicitus, nunquam est malus, sed semper bonus. Virtus tamen, præsertim intensa, est sæpe occasio operis excessivi: cujus excessus seu immoderantia non est directe ac elicitive ex virtute, sed potius ex rationis inconsideratione aut indiscretione: quoniam vehementi affectu trahitur ratio, ut minus attendat quod congruit, sicque arbitratur ex virtute procedere, quod partim ex indiscretione et inconsideratione progreditur.
paras.en: [[2:4|he set in order charity in me|Ordinavit in me caritatem]], that is, he has bestowed on me the grace of discretion, so that I should not afflict myself inordinately out of spiritual fervour, or destroy my body by exercises beyond my strength. This ordering is the more needful the more intense the kindling of charity has been. The zeal of charity, too, must be [[Rom 10:2|according to knowledge|secundum scientiam]], lest the fervent zealot hurl himself and others headlong by his fervour. And so, although the charity of God could not in itself be too intense, or greater than is fitting (nay, the greater it is, the better), yet it must be ordered in the effects which proceed from it, or rather are thought to proceed from it. For, as Augustine asserts, No one uses virtue badly: since, that is, an act elicited directly from virtue is never bad but always good. Yet virtue, especially intense virtue, is often the occasion of an excessive work; and the excess or immoderation of that work does not come directly and elicitively from the virtue [that is, it is not an act the virtue itself produces], but rather from reason's want of consideration or of discretion: for reason is drawn along by vehement affection so that it attends less to what is fitting, and so it judges to proceed from virtue what proceeds in part from indiscretion and want of consideration.

paras.t: Fulcite me floribus, stipate me malis, quia amore langueo. Flores sunt actus sapientiæ, et theologicarum virtutum, per quas immediate circa Deum versatur. Mala vero seu poma sic nominata, sunt opera exteriora pia ac virtuosa. Petit igitur anima caritate languescens, floribus fulciri, id est, incremento divinæ cognitionis interius perfici, summæ bonitatis dilectione calidius inflammari, in exspectatione futurorum bonorum per prælibationem suavem exhilarari, in rationibus credendorum illuminationeque fidei crescere: quatenus tantis ac talibus roborata charismatibus, queat diuturnius in sponsi amplexibus demorari, nec more solito, humana fragilitate naturalique instabilitate retrahatur ac labatur deorsum. Siquidem optimum est talibus gratiis stabiliri cor; et plane beatus vir, qui implevit desiderium suum ex ipsis. Hæc igitur postulat anima radiosa, quoniam languet amore, ideo pati non valet separationem a sponso; sed quantum fieri potest, appetit tam incomparabili ac supernobilissimo bono stabiliter atque assidue frui: quæ quum desiderasset a paranymphis atque sodalibus sponsi sibi ministerialiter exhiberi, mox a sponso est exaudita, sicut subjungit.
paras.en: [[2:5|Stay me up with flowers, compass me about with apples: because I languish with love|Fulcite me floribus, stipate me malis, quia amore langueo]]. The flowers are the acts of wisdom and of the theological virtues, by which the soul is occupied immediately about God. The apples, or fruits so named [Denis adds *poma*, "fruits", since *mala* could also be read as "evils"], are pious and virtuous outward works. The soul, then, languishing with charity, asks to be stayed up with flowers: that is, to be perfected inwardly by growth in the knowledge of God, to be more warmly inflamed with love of the highest goodness, to be gladdened in the expectation of the good things to come by a sweet foretaste, and to grow in the reasons for what is to be believed and in the light of faith: so that, strengthened with gifts so great and of such a kind, she may linger longer in the Bridegroom's embraces, and not be drawn back, as usually happens, by human frailty and natural instability, and slip downward. For [[Heb 13:9|it is best that the heart be established|optimum est talibus gratiis stabiliri cor]] with such graces; and indeed, [[Ps 126:5|Blessed is the man that hath filled the desire with them|beatus vir, qui implevit desiderium suum ex ipsis]] [in the Psalm *them* are the arrows of the verse before; Denis applies the word to these graces]. This, then, the radiant soul asks for: since she languishes with love, she cannot bear separation from the Bridegroom, but, as far as may be, longs to enjoy so incomparable and so supremely noble a good steadily and constantly: and when she had desired that these things be ministered to her by the groomsmen and companions of the Bridegroom, she was presently heard by the Bridegroom himself, as she goes on to say.

paras.t: Læva ejus sub capite meo: id est, pia et gratiosa visitatio ac consolatio sponsi, sustentat ac stabilit imbecillitatem ac labilem fluxum mentis meæ, ne pondere corporis aut propria imperfectione ab arce contemplativi intuitus ruat. Et dextera illius amplexabitur me, in patria: sicut expositum est in præcedenti articulo. Felix mens quæ sic in Christi pectore requiescit, atque æterni Verbi amplexibus stringitur. Quis hanc cœlestis superdignissimi sponsi caritatem, dignationem, affluentiam queat exprimere, qui animam in sinu, imo in corde suo sic facit quiescere, in quo mens taliter tranquillatur, quod vere dicere potest, In pace in id ipsum dormiam et requiescam? Animam autem sic sibi conjunctam non vult sponsus importune in exterioribus occupari, vel ante tempus a sua revocari quiete. Ideo subditur:
paras.en: [[2:6|His left hand is under my head|Læva ejus sub capite meo]]: that is, the loving and gracious visitation and consolation of the Bridegroom upholds and steadies the weakness and slipping flow of my mind, lest by the weight of the body or by its own imperfection it fall from the citadel of contemplative gazing. And [[2:6|his right hand shall embrace me|Et dextera illius amplexabitur me]] in the homeland: as was explained in the preceding article. Happy the mind that so rests on the breast of Christ, and is clasped in the embraces of the eternal Word! Who could express this charity, condescension and bounty of the heavenly, most supremely worthy Bridegroom, who makes the soul rest so in his bosom, nay, in his heart, wherein the mind is made so tranquil that it can truly say, [[Ps 4:9|In peace in the self same I will sleep, and I will rest|In pace in id ipsum dormiam et requiescam?]]? Now the Bridegroom does not wish the soul so joined to him to be importunately busied with outward things, or called away from her rest before the time. Therefore it is added:

paras.t: Adjuro vos, filiæ Jerusalem, id est, o animæ pusillæ subditorum ac communitatis, per capreas cervosque camporum (juxta expositionem inductam), ne suscitetis neque evigilare faciatis dilectam, sponsam meam particularem, a suæ contemplationis quiete, quoadusque ipsa velit: quæ utique permittit hoc fieri congruo tempore, propter fraternam salutem, aut vitæ hujus provisionem. Innotescit ex hoc, quam periculosum ac improbum sit, animam contemplationi intentam inquietare. Si enim magnæ esset improbitatis, familiariter loquentem cum rege terreno sine regis consensu avellere, molestare, aut deridere: quanto culpabilius est, hominem omnipotenti universorum Imperatori per contemplationem, raptum, ecstasimve conjunctum, abstrahere, subsannare aut conturbare? Nam etsi hoc vitandum non esset propter hominem, ipsum tamen intuitu Dei, et propter reverentiam ejus esset omnino cavendum. Nec de tali homine expedit temere judicare: quia hoc esset inconvenienti inconveniens addere, ac discrimen augere. Verumtamen subditus exercitium suæ contemplationis non debet obedientiæ anteferre, nec caritati proximi in ejus necessitate: ideo si a superiore suscitetur, aut a proximo indigente rogetur, obtemperet quantum valet.
paras.en: [[2:7|I adjure you, O ye daughters of Jerusalem|Adjuro vos, filiæ Jerusalem]], that is, O little souls of the subjects and of the community, [[2:7|by the roes, and the harts of the field|per capreas cervosque camporum]] (according to the exposition already given), [[2:7|that you stir not up, nor make the beloved to awake|ne suscitetis neque evigilare faciatis dilectam]] my own particular spouse from the rest of her contemplation, [[2:7|till she please|quoadusque ipsa velit]]: and she does allow this to be done at a fitting time, for the salvation of the brethren, or to provide for this life. From this it is plain how perilous and wicked it is to disquiet a soul intent on contemplation. For if it would be great wickedness to drag away, trouble or mock someone speaking familiarly with an earthly king, without the king's consent, how much more blameworthy is it to draw away, scoff at or disturb a man joined by contemplation, rapture or ecstasy to the almighty Emperor of all things? For even if this were not to be avoided for the man's sake, it would still have to be shunned altogether out of regard for God and reverence for him. Nor is it expedient to judge such a man rashly: for that would be to add one unfitting thing to another, and to increase the danger. Yet a subject ought not to put the exercise of his contemplation before obedience, nor before charity to his neighbour in his need: so if he is roused by a superior, or asked by a neighbour in want, let him comply as far as he can.

paras.t: Vox dilecti mei, est commissio quam audivi, qua commisit ne suscitet, eo quod ipse adhuc velit me suis mundissimis applicare amplexibus, præveniendo me gratiose ac præ solito copiose. Nam ecce iste sponsus venit saliens in montibus, transiliens colles: id est, cum tanta celeritate ac festinantia venit ad me, ut salire magis quam pergere videatur; et tam familiariter adjungit se mihi, quasi mihi soli velit uniri, cohærere ac loqui.
paras.en: [[2:8|The voice of my beloved|Vox dilecti mei]] is the charge that I heard, by which he charged that none should rouse me, because he still wishes to draw me into his most pure embraces, going before me with his grace, and more abundantly than usual. For [[2:8|behold he|ecce iste]], the Bridegroom, [[2:8|cometh leaping upon the mountains, skipping over the hills|venit saliens in montibus, transiliens colles]]: that is, he comes to me with such speed and haste that he seems to leap rather than to walk; and he joins himself to me so familiarly, as though he would be united, cleave and speak to me alone.

paras.t: Ideo capreæ hinnuloque cervorum assimilo eum, quia et ipse sic visitans me, reddit me interiori visu acutum, et instar hinnuli ad bona velocem. Verumtamen non se ostendit mihi in propria claritate, sicuti est in se ipso, ideo addo: En ipse stat post parietem nostrum: juxta expositiones prætactas. Quasi dicat: Habet se instar amatoris, qui ad domum veniens suæ dilectæ, non statim ingreditur, sed per fenestras cancellosque prospicit, et aliqualiter se ostendit, quatenus majori sui desiderio accendat amicam: sic et sponsus iste infinitam suæ amœnitatis ac serenitatis amabilitatem, suavitatem ac decorem aliqualiter mihi nunc pandit, intuendamque præbet, ut vehementius incalescam, atque ad clarum ac beatificum ejus intuitum calidius inardescam.
paras.en: Therefore I liken him to [[2:9|a roe, or a young hart|capreæ hinnuloque cervorum]], because he too, visiting me thus, makes me keen of inward sight [the roe was held to be very sharp-sighted], and swift toward good things like a young hart. Yet he does not show himself to me in his own brightness, as he is in himself; therefore I add: [[2:9|Behold he standeth behind our wall|En ipse stat post parietem nostrum]]: according to the expositions touched on before. As if to say: He behaves like a lover who, coming to the house of his beloved, does not go in at once, but looks out through the windows and lattices, and shows himself in some measure, so as to kindle his friend with greater desire of him: so this Bridegroom too now in some measure opens to me, and offers to my gaze, the infinite lovableness, sweetness and beauty of his delightfulness and serenity, so that I may grow hotter, and burn more warmly toward the clear and beatific sight of him.

paras.t: En dilectus meus loquitur mihi, suo occulto divino instinctu, et per inspirationem ac directionem angelicam, per Scripturas et per homines præsidentes et sapientes: Surge a contemplationis sopore, propera, amica mea, id est, cum omni promptitudine et ardore exerce exteriora quæ tibi incumbunt, columba mea, formosa mea, et veni. Ecce quanta est dignitas animæ virtuosæ ac contemplativæ, et quam amabilem Deo faciunt virtutes creaturam rationalem, quæ tot amorosis nominibus invitatur ac nominatur a sponso.
paras.en: [[2:10|Behold my beloved speaketh to me|En dilectus meus loquitur mihi]], by his hidden divine prompting, and through angelic inspiration and guidance, through the Scriptures and through men who preside and are wise: [[2:10|Arise|Surge]] from the sleep of contemplation, [[2:10|make haste, my love|propera, amica mea]], that is, with all readiness and ardour carry out the outward tasks that are laid upon thee, [[2:10|my dove, my beautiful one, and come|columba mea, formosa mea, et veni]]. See how great is the dignity of the virtuous and contemplative soul, and how lovable to God the virtues make the rational creature, which is invited and named by the Bridegroom with so many loving names.

paras.t: Jam enim hiems, id est torpor accediæ, frigus invidiæ, aut sterilitas ultionis, transiit. Imber, id est profluvium perstrepentium cogitationum ac tumultuantium desideriorum carnalium, instar imbris incidentium, abiit. Flores apparuerunt in terra nostra, id est, virtutum ornatus eruperunt in agro cordis tui: qui est terra mea et tua, id est nostra: mea, per creationem, dilectionem et prædestinationem; tua, per concessionem et possessionem. Tempus putationis advenit: id est, hora nunc est, ut omnem culpam quantumlibet parvam, abscidas a te, ne quid inveniatur in te quod meum offendat adspectum, et lucem contemplationis obfuscet. Itaque, sicut sole oriente fugantur caligines, expellunturque tenebræ, et nebulæ dissipantur, clarescit aer ac mundi facies decoratur: sic Sole sapientiæ, sponso cœlesti, veniente atque ingrediente in animam contemplativam, et radiante in ea, omnis torpor accediæ propulsatur, gelu rancoris fugatur, ira sopitur, evagationes cordis et inordinatæ affectiones pelluntur, et serenatur atque exhilaratur anima tota. Ideo sponso adveniente, protinus est surgendum et properandum in ejus occursum, ut cum ingenti reverentia suscipiatur, et quidquid gratiæ dederit, diligentissime conservetur; nec aurea illa suæ visitationis hora est negligenda, ne forsitan indignatus, postea etiam, quamvis rogatus, sic advenire recuset.
paras.en: [[2:11|For winter|Jam enim hiems]], that is, the torpor of acedia [*accedia*: sloth and weariness in spiritual things], the chill of envy, or the barrenness of vengefulness, [[2:11|is now past|transiit]]; [[2:11|the rain|Imber]], that is, the downpour of clamorous thoughts and of tumultuous fleshly desires falling like rain, [[2:11|is over|abiit]]. [[2:12|The flowers have appeared in our land|Flores apparuerunt in terra nostra]], that is, the adornments of the virtues have broken forth in the field of thy heart: which is my land and thine, that is, ours: mine by creation, love and predestination; thine by grant and possession. [[2:12|the time of pruning is come|Tempus putationis advenit]]: that is, now is the hour for thee to cut off from thyself every fault, however small, lest anything be found in thee that offends my sight and darkens the light of contemplation. And so, as at the rising of the sun the mists are put to flight, the darkness is driven out, and the clouds are scattered, the air grows clear and the face of the world is made fair: so when the Sun of wisdom, the heavenly Bridegroom, comes and enters into the contemplative soul and shines in it, all torpor of acedia is driven off, the frost of rancour is put to flight, anger is lulled, the wanderings of the heart and inordinate affections are expelled, and the whole soul is made serene and glad. Therefore, when the Bridegroom comes, one must at once rise and hasten to meet him, that he may be received with immense reverence, and whatever grace he gives may be most carefully kept; nor must that golden hour of his visitation be neglected, lest perhaps, offended, he should afterwards refuse to come so again, even when asked.

paras.t: Vox turturis audita est in terra nostra: id est, oratio pudicæ, castæ ac solitariæ mentis, ad aures pietatis meæ devenit, et mihi accepta est. Hinc ad animam pœnitentem et gementem, et de suis culpis erubescentem, benigne revertor: et ita quasi tempus vernale resplenduit animæ.
paras.en: [[2:12|the voice of the turtle is heard in our land|Vox turturis audita est in terra nostra]] [the turtle-dove]: that is, the prayer of a modest, chaste and solitary mind has come to the ears of my loving-kindness, and is acceptable to me. Hence I turn back kindly to the soul that repents and groans and blushes for her faults: and so a springtime, as it were, has shone upon the soul.

paras.t: Ficus protulit grossos suos. Per arborem fici, significatur hic anima fructuosa, caritatis, pietatis et devotionis suavitate referta: quæ statim ut potuit, cœpit agere aliquid boni ac devotioni insistere, quamvis exercitia ejus essent adhuc imperfecta, immatura, facileque ex vento tentationis seu adversitatis cujusque labentia. Propter quod designantur per grossos, qui sunt fructus primi, immaturi, ac levi vento cadentes.
paras.en: [[2:13|The fig tree hath put forth her green figs|Ficus protulit grossos suos]]. By the fig tree is signified here the fruitful soul, filled with the sweetness of charity, piety and devotion: which, as soon as she could, began to do some good and to apply herself to devotion, though her exercises were still imperfect, unripe, and apt to fall at the wind of any temptation or adversity. Therefore they are signified by the green figs [*grossi*, the first unripe figs], which are the first fruits, unripe, and falling at a light wind.

paras.t: Vineæ florentes dederunt odorem suum. Non solum Ecclesia, sed et quælibet devota anima merito vinea appellatur, quæ in corpore suo quasi in terra plantata, a Spiritu Sancto principaliter et per ejus ministros ministerialiter colitur, a superfluitate sua purgatur, et fructus virtutum jucundos spiritualiter inebriantes producit. Bonæ quoque conversationis redolet fama, et interna suavitate perfunditur, per quam etiam ad proximos habet se dulciter. Hanc vineam, id est animam suam, unusquisque Deo auxiliante, angelo dirigente, Scripturis ac prælatis docentibus, debet excolere, ab æstu concupiscentiæ præservare, devotionis pinguedine impinguare, bonis replere operibus, putare a vitiis, atque ad perseverantiæ maturitatem ac ubertatem perducere. Vineæ ergo florentes, id est animæ virtuosæ bene excultæ, dederunt odorem suum, quo proximos ad meliora traxerunt. Idcirco et tu, o anima quam exhortor, illarum vigilantiam ac virtutes debes sectari, et cavere ne negligens inveniaris ac fœda.
paras.en: [[2:13|the vines in flower yield their sweet smell|Vineæ florentes dederunt odorem suum]]. Not only the Church but any devout soul whatever is rightly called a vine: planted in its body as in soil, it is tilled by the Holy Ghost as its principal husbandman and by his ministers as his servants, it is purged of what is superfluous in it, and it brings forth pleasant fruits of the virtues that spiritually inebriate. It is fragrant too with the good name of a good life, and is steeped in an inward sweetness, by which it bears itself sweetly toward its neighbours as well. This vine, that is, his own soul, each one must cultivate, with God helping, the angel guiding, and the Scriptures and prelates teaching; he must keep it from the heat of concupiscence, enrich it with the fatness of devotion, fill it with good works, prune it of vices, and bring it to the ripeness and abundance of perseverance. [[2:13|the vines in flower|Vineæ ergo florentes]], then, that is, virtuous souls well cultivated, [[2:13|yield their sweet smell|dederunt odorem suum]], by which they have drawn their neighbours to better things. Therefore thou also, O soul whom I exhort, must follow their watchfulness and virtues, and beware lest thou be found negligent and foul.

paras.t: Surge, contemplando superna, amica mea, per amicitiam mutuam, sponsa mea, mihi per fidem, spem et caritatem desponsata, a me fecundata; et veni, ut mihi quotidie vicinius ac perfectius uniaris;
paras.en: [[2:13|Arise|Surge]], by contemplating the things above, [[2:13|my love|amica mea]], by mutual friendship [*amica*, "friend"], my spouse, espoused to me by faith, hope and charity, made fruitful by me [Denis reads *sponsa mea*, "my spouse", where the Vulgate has *speciosa mea*, "my beautiful one"]; [[2:13|and come|et veni]], that thou mayest be united to me more nearly and more perfectly every day;

paras.t: columba mea, id est, columbinis proprietatibus decorata, et mihi dilecta, in foraminibus petræ, in caverna maceriæ. Præter expositiones præcedentis articuli super hoc introductas, possunt per foramina petræ, intelligi tuta ac robusta latibula gratiæ, in quibus animæ virtuosæ quiescunt, et a suæ salutis hostibus se abscondunt durante hac vita. Hæc autem latibula, sunt humilis recognitio propriæ defectuositatis, spes divinæ subventionis, timor Dei sincerus, et mortificatio sui ipsius, refugiumque ad Deum, ei jugiter inhærere. Caverna vero maceriæ, est humilitatis profundum, seu penetrativa consideratio supernorum: inter quæ et nos, cœlum velut maceria mediat.
paras.en: [[2:14|My dove|columba mea]], that is, adorned with the properties of the dove, and beloved by me, [[2:14|in the clefts of the rock, in the hollow places of the wall|in foraminibus petræ, in caverna maceriæ]]. Besides the expositions of this brought in the preceding article, the clefts of the rock may be understood as the safe and strong hiding places of grace, in which virtuous souls rest and hide themselves from the enemies of their salvation while this life lasts. And these hiding places are the humble acknowledgment of one's own defectiveness, hope of God's help, the sincere fear of God, the mortification of oneself, and refuge in God, cleaving to him continually. The hollow place of the wall is the depth of humility, or the piercing consideration of the things above: between which and us heaven stands as a wall.

paras.t: Ostende mihi faciem tuam. Quum enim sim pastor bonus, diligenter volo agnoscere vultum pecoris mei: ideo mentem tuam jugiter orna, ut coram me resplendeat gratia et virtute, sapientia et fervore. Mihi quoque, id est vicariis meis superioribus tuis, secreta tua ostende, præsertim in foro confessionis, et quando tentatione, scrupulo, dubitatione seu anxietate gravaris; effunde quasi aquam ante me cor tuum.
paras.en: [[2:14|shew me thy face|Ostende mihi faciem tuam]]. For since [[John 10:11|I am the good shepherd|pastor bonus]], I wish diligently [[Prov 27:23|to know the countenance|agnoscere vultum]] of my flock: therefore adorn thy mind continually, that it may shine before me with grace and virtue, wisdom and fervour. To me also, that is, to my vicars, thy superiors, show thy secrets, especially in the court of confession, and when thou art burdened with temptation, scruple, doubt or anxiety; [[Lam 2:19|pour out thy heart like water|effunde quasi aquam ante me cor tuum]] before me.

paras.t: Sonet vox tua in auribus meis: id est, laudibus meis, precibus et doctrinis insiste; et omne quod loqueris, tale sit, ut acceptum sit mihi, et per approbationem audiatur a me. Impios namque non audio, neque agnosco, eo modo quo per Prophetam eis testatus sum: Quum multiplicaveritis preces, non audiam. In Evangelio quoque: Amen dico vobis, nescio vos unde sitis; discedite a me, operarii iniquitatis. Vox enim tua dulcis, videlicet clamor interior, utpote amor, virtuosa affectio, desiderium sanctum: quæ adeo placent Deo, ut propter ea etiam vox oris ex ipsis procedens dulcis et placens sit Domino.
paras.en: [[2:14|let thy voice sound in my ears|Sonet vox tua in auribus meis]]: that is, apply thyself to my praises, to prayers and to teachings; and let all that thou speakest be such as to be acceptable to me, and heard by me with approval. For the wicked I do not hear[[John 9:31||]], nor acknowledge, in the way in which I testified to them by the Prophet: [[Is 1:15|when you multiply prayer, I will not hear|Quum multiplicaveritis preces, non audiam]]. In the Gospel too: [[Matt 25:12|Amen I say to you|Amen dico vobis]], [[Luke 13:27|I know you not, whence you are. Depart from me, all ye workers of iniquity|nescio vos unde sitis; discedite a me, operarii iniquitatis]]. [[2:14|for thy voice is sweet|Vox enim tua dulcis]], namely the inner cry, such as love, virtuous affection, holy desire: which so please God that for their sake even the voice of the mouth proceeding from them is sweet and pleasing to the Lord.

paras.t: Capite nobis vulpes parvulas, quæ demoliuntur vineas. Parvulæ vulpes istæ, sunt fraus, dolus, hypocrisis, calliditas, duplicitas, vitia virtutum specie operta: quæ animas virtuosas spiritualiter destruunt, et quidquid gratiæ aut meriti habuerint, tollunt. Similiter, pravæ suggestiones, tentationum exordia, primi motus, inchoationes culparum: quæ mox in principio sunt penitus exstirpanda, ne paulatim totam inficiant animæ vineam. Has vulpes studeant præsidentes auferre de suorum cordibus subditorum, imo primo omnium a se ipsis. Nam vinea nostra floruit. Hoc unicuique bono pastori loquitur Christus, dum pastor congregationi sibi commissæ præest idonee: sicque congregatio illa est communis vinea Christi, et ejus vicarii.
paras.en: [[2:15|Catch us the little foxes that destroy the vines|Capite nobis vulpes parvulas, quæ demoliuntur vineas]]. These little foxes are fraud, guile, hypocrisy, craftiness, duplicity: vices covered with the appearance of virtues, which spiritually destroy virtuous souls and take away whatever grace or merit they have had. Likewise evil suggestions, the beginnings of temptations, first motions [that is, the first stirrings of the appetite, before reason has consented], the first beginnings of sins: which must be rooted out utterly at once, at the start, lest little by little they infect the whole vineyard of the soul. Let those who preside strive to remove these foxes from the hearts of their subjects, and indeed first of all from themselves. [[2:15|for our vineyard hath flourished|Nam vinea nostra floruit]]. This Christ says to every good shepherd, when the shepherd rules fitly the congregation entrusted to him: and so that congregation is the common vineyard of Christ and of his vicar.

paras.t: Dilectus meus mihi, et ego illi. Circa hoc ait Bernardus: O sancta anima, quid dilectus tuus tibi, et tu, quid illi? Quæ inter vos tam familiaris favorabilisque locutio, ut nec penitus tacere possitis, neque quod sentitis, exprimere valeatis? Habent enim suas voces ipsi affectus, quibus se aliquando produnt, etiam quando nolunt: ut timor meticulosas, dolor gemebundas, amor jucundas. Amor etenim flagrans ac vehemens, præsertim divinus, dum se intra se cohibere non valet, non attendit quo ordine, qua lege, quave serie verborum ebulliat, dummodo ex hoc nullum sui sentiat detrimentum.
paras.en: [[2:16|My beloved to me, and I to him|Dilectus meus mihi, et ego illi]]. On this Bernard says: O holy soul, what is thy beloved to thee, and thou, what to him? What is this speech between you, so familiar and so gracious, that you can neither keep wholly silent nor express what you feel? For the affections themselves have their own voices, by which they sometimes betray themselves even when they would not: fear fearful ones, grief groaning ones, love joyful ones. For love that is burning and vehement, especially divine love, when it cannot contain itself within itself, does not heed in what order, by what rule or in what sequence of words it bubbles forth, provided it feels no loss of itself thereby.

paras.t: Itaque, Dilectus meus mihi, et ego illi, id est, sponsus ille dulcissimus adhæret, placet, et congruit mihi, et ego illi. Qui pascitur inter lilia, id est, mundis meditationibus, virtuosis affectionibus, sanctis actibus delectatur, inquinamenta carnis et cordis abhorrens: quoniam non Deus volens iniquitatem ipse est, et omnem aversatur impietatem, imo odio sunt ei impii et impietas ejus. Si ergo vis sponsum istum reficere, et refici ab eodem, talibus liliis mentem tuam adorna, apprehensiones phantasticas, cogitationesque fœdas et omnem turpem ac sensualem exclude affectum, donec adspiret dies in quo remuneret sponsam.
paras.en: So then, [[2:16|My beloved to me, and I to him|Dilectus meus mihi, et ego illi]], that is, that most sweet Bridegroom cleaves to me, pleases me and suits me, and I him. [[2:16|who feedeth among the lilies|Qui pascitur inter lilia]], that is, he delights in pure meditations, virtuous affections and holy acts, abhorring the defilements of flesh and heart: for he is [[Ps 5:5|not a God that willest iniquity|non Deus volens iniquitatem]], and he turns away from all impiety; nay, [[Wis 14:9|the wicked and his wickedness are hateful|odio sunt ei impii et impietas ejus]] to him. If then thou wilt refresh this Bridegroom and be refreshed by him, adorn thy mind with such lilies, and shut out fantastic imaginings and foul thoughts and every base and sensual affection, [[2:17|Till the day break|donec adspiret dies]], in which he will reward his spouse.

paras.t: Revertere. Sponsus quippe interdum dispensative subtrahit et suspendit ad tempus ab anima pia consolationis suæ præsentiam, devotionem sensibilem, visitationem solitam et internam, atque alacritatem in cultu divino: ita quod anima talis interdum veretur se sponsum offendisse, et ideo esse relictam. Sponsus vero id agit, ne ipsa ex promptitudine et opulentia spirituali inaniter moveatur, aut securitate nimia resolvatur: sed propriam penset fragilitatem, seque humiliet, atque ad sponsum suspiret frequentius: et sic gratiæ mereatur augmentum, de cetero quoque custoditior exstet.
paras.en: [[2:17|Return|Revertere]]. For the Bridegroom at times, by a wise dispensation, withdraws and suspends for a time from the devout soul the presence of his consolation, sensible devotion, his wonted and inward visitation, and eagerness in the worship of God: so that such a soul sometimes fears she has offended the Bridegroom and has therefore been left. But the Bridegroom does this lest she be stirred to vanity by her readiness and spiritual wealth, or slackened by too much security: rather, that she may weigh her own frailty, humble herself, and sigh more often for the Bridegroom: and so may merit an increase of grace, and for the rest be more on her guard.

2.title: SEQUITUR EXPOSITIO EJUSDEM CAPITULI SECUNDI, DE SPONSO ET SPONSA SINGULARI.
2.title_en: Exposition of the same second chapter continued: of the Bridegroom and the singular bride

paras.t: Ego flos campi. Beatissima Virgo est vernantissimus, pulcherrimus ac redolentissimus flos campi, id est sæculi hujus : in quo tanquam loco certaminis sumus constituti, quia militia est vita nostra super terram. Ipsa quoque est flos campi, id est horti deliciarum, videlicet paradisi cœlestis. Et rursus, flos campi est, id est militantis Ecclesiæ in terra peregrinantis : cujus ipsa est mater, flos, regina, et advocata, suis orationibus ac meritis procurans Ecclesiæ ornamenta virtutum ac redolentiam meritorum. Denique, ipsa est flos cujuslibet animæ devotæ eam amantis : cujus memoriam nunquam ingreditur sine fructu, et sine suæ diffusione dulcedinis. Et lilium convallium. Ipsa instar lilii præclare venustat corda humilium. Rursum, ipsa suavissima et incomparabilis Virgo Deifera, est lilium convallium, id est proles floridissima suorum parentum humilium, a quibus velut speciosissimum lilium est exorta : nec Salomon in omni gloria sua ita ornatus fuit, ut lilium istud. Et sicut lilium est flos crescens in altum, et tamen repanda ac dependentia folia granaque aurea habens; sic optima et amabilissima Virgo crevit in omnium arcem virtutum, et nihilo minus excellentiam suarum virtutum per humilitatem depressit : fide quoque, spe et caritate ac donis Spiritus Sancti tanquam aureis granis ornatissima exstitit.
paras.en: [[2:1|I am the flower of the field|Ego flos campi]]. The most blessed Virgin is the most blooming, most beautiful and most fragrant [[2:1|flower of the field|flos campi]], that is, of this world, in which we are set as in a place of combat, since [[Job 7:1|The life of man upon earth is a warfare|militia est vita nostra super terram]] [Denis says *our life* for *the life of man*]. She is also the [[2:1|flower of the field|flos campi]], that is, of the garden of delights, namely of the heavenly paradise. And again, she is the [[2:1|flower of the field|flos campi]], that is, of the Church militant, on pilgrimage on earth: of which she is the mother, the flower, the queen and the advocate, by her prayers and merits obtaining for the Church the adornments of the virtues and the fragrance of merits. Lastly, she is the flower of every devout soul that loves her: whose memory she never enters without fruit and without pouring out her sweetness. [[2:1|and the lily of the valleys|Et lilium convallium]]. Like a lily she gloriously beautifies the hearts of the humble. Again, she, the most sweet and incomparable God-bearing Virgin, is the [[2:1|lily of the valleys|lilium convallium]], that is, the most flowering offspring of her humble parents, from whom she sprang like a most beautiful lily: [[Matt 6:29|not even Solomon in all his glory|nec Salomon in omni gloria sua]] was so adorned as this lily. And as the lily is a flower that grows up on high, and yet has leaves bent back and hanging down, and golden grains, so the most excellent and most lovable Virgin grew to the summit of all the virtues, and none the less kept the excellence of her virtues low by humility; and she stood forth most richly adorned with faith, hope and charity and the gifts of the Holy Ghost as with golden grains.

paras.t: Præterea Christus est flos campi, id est filius Virginis hujus, cujus uterus fuit mundissimus campus, omni castitate, temperantia, puritate ineffabiliter decoratus; et lilium convallium, descendens ex progenie patrum humilium ac parentum Virginis admirandæ : inter cujus parentes fuit omnino honorabile connubium, et torus immaculatus; et specialiter in eorum conventione, qua Virginem dignissimam genuerunt, omnimoda fuit honestas.
paras.en: Further, Christ is the [[2:1|flower of the field|flos campi]], that is, the son of this Virgin, whose womb was a most pure field, ineffably adorned with all chastity, temperance and purity; [[2:1|and the lily of the valleys|et lilium convallium]], descending from a line of humble fathers and from the parents of the admirable Virgin, between whose parents there was in every way [[Heb 13:4|Marriage honourable|honorabile connubium]] [[Heb 13:4|and the bed undefiled|et torus immaculatus]]; and especially in their coming together, by which they begot the most worthy Virgin, all was entirely honourable.

paras.t: Sicut lilium inter spinas, sic amica mea inter filias. Quamvis enim fuerint multæ virgines sanctæ, quarum quædam martyrii gloriam sunt adeptæ; tamen respectu hujus unicæ Virginis, singularis amicæ sponsi, quasi spinæ fuisse videntur, in quantum aliquid culpæ habebant : et quamvis in se fuerint mundæ, non tamen fuit in eis fomes prorsus exstinctus; fuerunt et aliis spinæ, qui ex earum intuitu, mucrone concupiscentiæ pungebantur, quamvis ipsæ virgines sanctæ, non fuerint in hoc ipso culpabiles. Porro hæc unica Dei delectabilissima Virgo, totius superbeatissimæ Trinitatis media et amica ac socia, ab omni culpa fuit prorsus immunis : fuit in ea fomes plene exstinctus; et tam intentissima castitate erat repleta, quod intuentium corda sic penetravit sua inæstimabili castitate virginea, quod a nullo potuit concupisci, imo potius exstinxit ad horam illorum libidinem.
paras.en: [[2:2|As the lily among thorns, so is my love among the daughters.|Sicut lilium inter spinas, sic amica mea inter filias.]] For though there have been many holy virgins, some of whom won the glory of martyrdom, yet compared with this one Virgin, the singular love of the Bridegroom, they seem to have been as thorns, in so far as they had some fault; and though they were clean in themselves, yet the *fomes* [that is, the tinder of sin, the leaning to evil left by original sin] was not wholly extinguished in them. They were thorns to others too, who at the sight of them were pricked by the point of concupiscence, though the holy virgins themselves were not to blame in this. But this one most delightful Virgin of God, the mediatrix [*media*, literally "the one in the midst"], friend and companion of the whole superblessed Trinity, was wholly free from all fault: in her the *fomes* was fully extinguished; and she was filled with chastity so intense that by her inestimable virginal chastity she so pierced the hearts of those who looked on her that she could be desired by no one; rather, she extinguished their lust for the time.

paras.t: Præterea Virgo gratissima, in qua et cum qua esse, fuit Deo deliciosum, commendat Filium suum, dicendo : Sicut malus inter ligna silvarum, sic dilectus meus inter filios. Nec enim ipsa sacratissima Virgo in tantum excedit ceteras filias, quantum unigenitus Filius ejus filios ceteros. Quem recte ait excedere filios, sicut malus ligna silvatica : siquidem omnes declinaverunt, simul inutiles facti sunt; et omnes nos quasi oves erravimus, unusquisque in viam suam declinavit. Etenim omnes peccaverunt, et egent gloria Dei. Atque, ut gloriosus dixit Joannes Baptista, Qui de terra est, de terra est, et de terra loquitur; qui autem de cœlo venit, super omnes est. At vero de hac arbore loquitur Alexander : Malus est arbor pulcherrima, cujus fructus sumi jubetur a filiis Israel cum palmarum spatulis, dum habitarent in umbraculis; et profert poma coloris aerii. Nitentissimus quoque viror foliorum ipsius, ita intuentibus est acceptus, ut quum radii solis tangunt superiora ejus, ex reverberatione fulgoris videatur aureis ramis ornatus. Hæc arbor nunquam suo fructu privatur; estque recta, alta, frondosa, delectans flore, recreans odore, reficiensque sapore. Ideo recte significat Virginis Filium, Dominum Jesum Christum, qui delectat nos flore suæ sanctissimæ conversationis, recreat odore suæ verissimæ prædicationis, et reficit sapore suæ suavissimæ consolationis : in quo nulla fuit curvitas culpæ, sed summæ perfectionis proceritas; cujus adspectus fuit consolatorius valde, et folia, id est verba ipsius, auro sapientiæ radiabant.
paras.en: Further, the most gracious Virgin, in whom and with whom it was a delight to God to be, commends her Son, saying: [[2:3|As the apple tree among the trees of the woods, so is my beloved among the sons|Sicut malus inter ligna silvarum, sic dilectus meus inter filios]]. For this most sacred Virgin does not surpass the other daughters so far as her only-begotten Son surpasses the other sons. And rightly she says that he surpasses the sons as the apple tree surpasses the trees of the wood: for [[Ps 13:3|They are all gone aside, they are become unprofitable together|omnes declinaverunt, simul inutiles facti sunt]]; and [[Is 53:6|All we like sheep have gone astray, every one hath turned aside into his own way|omnes nos quasi oves erravimus, unusquisque in viam suam declinavit]]. Indeed, [[Rom 3:23|all have sinned and do need the glory of God|omnes peccaverunt, et egent gloria Dei]]. And as the glorious John the Baptist said: [[John 3:31|He that is of the earth, of the earth he is, and of the earth he speaketh. He that cometh from heaven is above all|Qui de terra est, de terra est, et de terra loquitur; qui autem de cœlo venit, super omnes est]]. Now of this tree Alexander says: The apple tree is a most beautiful tree, whose fruit the children of Israel were commanded to take with the branches of palm trees while they dwelt in tabernacles[[Lev 23:40||]]; and it bears apples of an airy colour. The most shining green of its leaves, too, is so pleasing to the beholders that when the rays of the sun touch its top, it seems from the reflection of their brightness to be adorned with golden boughs. This tree is never without its fruit; and it is straight, tall, leafy, delighting with its flower, refreshing with its scent, and restoring with its taste. Rightly, then, it signifies the Virgin's Son, the Lord Jesus Christ, who delights us with the flower of his most holy life, refreshes us with the scent of his most true preaching, and restores us with the taste of his most sweet consolation: in whom there was no crookedness of fault, but the tallness of the highest perfection; whose countenance was very consoling, and whose leaves, that is, his words, shone with the gold of wisdom.

paras.t: Sub umbra illius quem desiderabam, sedi. Humillima et quietissima Virgo, Filii sui veram deitatem omnipotentiamque cognoscens, tanto perfectius sub ejus protectione quievit, et ejus auxilio innitebatur, quanto erat humilior. Conversando quoque in hoc mundo cum dilectissimo sponso ac filio suo, sub ejus pietate degebat, sub ejus exemplarissima conversatione profecit, et coram sermocinante resedit frequenter, verba prædicantis sponsi intentissime advertendo, in quibus et miro modo delectabatur, sicut subdendo fatetur : Et fructus ejus dulcis gutturi meo. Refecit utique Dominus majestatis munificentissimus, Unigenitus Patris, suam præstantissimam Matrem copiosissimis ac suavissimis refectionibus mentis, illuminando mirifice, inflammando deifice, exhilarando assidue, et renovando atque augendo in ea pretiosissima munera gratiarum continue. Amplius, suavissima cordis refectio fuit divinissimæ Virgini, Unicum suum quotidie intueri, audire et contrectare Verbum vitæ; et dum ipsa Domina angelorum, Filium Dei ex se natum corporaliter lactavit, educavit, deduxit, ipse omnipotens liberalissimus Filius, tam capacem et dilectissimam Matrem spiritualiter, copiosissime, indesinenter refecit, accendit, implevit.
paras.en: [[2:3|I sat down under his shadow, whom I desired|Sub umbra illius quem desiderabam, sedi]]. The most humble and most quiet Virgin, knowing the true Godhead and the omnipotence of her Son, rested under his protection and leaned on his help the more perfectly, the humbler she was. Living, too, in this world with her most beloved bridegroom and son, she passed her life under his loving care, grew under the pattern of his most exemplary life, and often sat before him as he spoke, listening most intently to the words of her bridegroom as he preached; and in these she took a wonderful delight, as she confesses in what follows: [[2:3|and his fruit was sweet to my palate|Et fructus ejus dulcis gutturi meo]]. The most bountiful Lord of majesty, the Only-begotten of the Father, truly restored his most excellent Mother with the most abundant and most sweet refreshments of the mind: enlightening her wonderfully, inflaming her divinely, gladdening her constantly, and continually renewing and increasing in her the most precious gifts of graces. Further, it was a most sweet refreshment of heart to the most divine Virgin to look every day upon her Only One, to hear and to handle the Word of life; and while she, the Lady of the angels, bodily suckled, reared and led about the Son of God born of her, he, the almighty and most generous Son, spiritually refreshed, kindled and filled his Mother, so capacious and so dearly loved, most abundantly and without ceasing.

paras.t: Introduxit me rex in cellam vinariam. Te introduxit, o beatissima Domina! Nec solum introduxit te in cellam vinariam; sed et in ipsum vinum, cui totaliter te intinxit, quia in abyssum divitiarum ac deliciarum suarum te prorsus immersit, omni benedictione te adimplevit, et jucunditatibus inebriavit frequenter, præsertim in annuntiatione angelica, in conceptione Filii Dei, in nativitate ejusdem, et alias sæpe.
paras.en: [[2:4|He brought me into the cellar of wine|Introduxit me rex in cellam vinariam]] [Denis reads *The king brought me*, as in 1:3]. He brought thee in, O most blessed Lady! And he brought thee not only [[2:4|into the cellar of wine|in cellam vinariam]], but into the wine itself, in which he dipped thee wholly; for he plunged thee utterly into the abyss of his riches and delights, filled thee with every blessing, and often inebriated thee with joys, above all at the angel's annunciation, at the conception of the Son of God, at his birth, and often at other times.

paras.t: Ordinavit in me caritatem : quia quidquid de naturali aut quocumque alio in me fuit amore, totum plene et potestative fuit subjectum caritati, et informatum ab eo, ac juxta ejus imperium etiam passiones appetitus sensitivi mei plenarie regebantur ac movebantur; nec unquam fuit in me inordinata affectio, neque ad Filium meum, quamvis unicum, speciosissimum, præstantissimum atque carissimum, fui unquam sensualiter affecta : sicut interdum Apostoli, propter quod audierunt ab eo : Si non abiero, Paracletus non veniet ad vos. Caritas quoque mea fuit circa sua objecta in suis actibus decentissime ordinata, ita quod Deum primo et maxime propter puram et infinitam bonitatem ipsius dilexi purissime; deinde, quoniam prior dilexit me, atque ad tanta ac talia me præ omni creatura elegit, ut scilicet essem mater ipsius, et propter cetera ejus beneficia generalia, specialia, ac singularia. Ad assumptam vero humanitatem Filii mei dulcissimi, habui caritatem valde præcipuam, imo et vehementissimum naturalem amorem gessi ad eum. Quamvis etiam a tempore quo uti cœpi ratione, valde dilexerim proximos, et in eorum caritate profecerim; tamen ab ea hora, qua propter hominum salvationem facta sum Genitrix Dei, inæstimabiliter dilexi genus humanum, et in ejus puro amore quotidie crevi. Imo nec passionem Filii mei, in quantum erat salvativa generis humani, abhorrui.
paras.en: [[2:4|he set in order charity in me|Ordinavit in me caritatem]]: for whatever love there was in me, natural or of any other kind, was all fully and with authority subject to charity and informed by it [that is, given its form by charity], and at its command even the passions of my sensitive appetite were fully ruled and moved; nor was there ever any inordinate affection in me, nor was I ever sensually affected even towards my Son, though he was my only one, most beautiful, most excellent and most dear: as the Apostles sometimes were, for which they heard from him: [[John 16:7|if I go not, the Paraclete will not come to you|Si non abiero, Paracletus non veniet ad vos]]. My charity, too, was most fittingly ordered in its acts towards its objects, so that I loved God first and most of all, most purely, for his pure and infinite goodness; then, because he [[1 John 4:19|first hath loved|prior dilexit]] me[[1 John 4:10||]], and chose me before every creature for things so great and of such a kind, namely to be his mother; and for his other benefits, general, special and singular. Towards the humanity taken up by my most sweet Son I had a very special charity; indeed I bore him also a most vehement natural love. And though from the time I began to use reason I loved my neighbours greatly and grew in charity towards them, yet from the hour in which I was made the Mother of God for the salvation of men, I loved the human race beyond all reckoning, and grew daily in a pure love of it. Indeed I did not even shrink from the passion of my Son, in so far as it was to save the human race.

paras.t: Fulcite me floribus, stipate me malis, quia amore langueo. Noverat docillima ac sapientissima Virgo, ante Filii sui passionem neminem posse ad beatificam Deitatis pertingere visionem : idcirco usque ad illud tempus patientius pertulit hujus exsilii incolatum: verum ex tunc cœpit ardentius ad cœlestem affici mansionem, præsertim post sui dilecti ascensionem. Unde ex tunc potissime languit caritate, suspirans ad immediatum, inseparabilem, et æternum sponsi amplexum lætissimum : ideo floribus concupivit fulciri ac malis stipari, id est cœlestibus consolationibus, copiosis profectibus, ac plurimorum conversionibus interim confoveri ac recreari : quod utique copiosissime fuit consecuta, ut subditur.
paras.en: [[2:5|Stay me up with flowers, compass me about with apples: because I languish with love.|Fulcite me floribus, stipate me malis, quia amore langueo.]] The most teachable and most wise Virgin knew that before the passion of her Son no one could attain to the beatific vision of the Godhead; therefore until that time she bore the sojourn of this exile more patiently. But from then on she began to be drawn more ardently towards the heavenly dwelling, above all after the ascension of her beloved. Hence from then on she languished most of all with charity, sighing for the most joyful embrace of the Bridegroom, immediate, inseparable and eternal; and so she longed to be stayed up with flowers and compassed about with apples, that is, in the meantime to be cherished and refreshed with heavenly consolations, abundant progress, and the conversions of very many: which she obtained most abundantly, as follows.

paras.t: Læva ejus sub capite meo, quia in præsenti me gratiosissime sustentavit; et dextera illius amplexabitur me. Jam namque in mea assumptione ad suam me dexteram collocavit, et assumptam cum corpore, corporaliter sibi univit; atque ad tam claram et voluptuosissimam suæ deitatis intuitionem promovit, quantam pura creatura sine personali unione videtur capere posse. Credimus quoque, o supercœlestis Domina, omnium creaturarum decus et gloria, te cum puero Jesu in sua sacra infantia (qua renovata est senectus et vetustas nostra) quandoque in eodem lecto dormivisse, atque infantulum Deum verum inter tua mundissima brachia collocasse, teque ab ejus dextera amplexatam. O quam incomparabilis et indicibilis est excellentia, beatitudo, et gloria tua! Quam propinquissima et familiarissima facta es Deo! Certe in quantum es Mater veri Dei, es dignitatis quodammodo infinitæ; et quanta fuit et est eminentia tuæ dignitatis, tanta et bonitatis, tanta quoque et felicitatis. Omnem ergo admirationem et capacitatem nostram transcendit beatitudo et gloria tua.
paras.en: [[2:6|His left hand is under my head|Læva ejus sub capite meo]], for in the present life he most graciously sustained me; [[2:6|and his right hand shall embrace me|et dextera illius amplexabitur me]]. For now at my assumption he has set me at his right hand, and has bodily united me to himself, taken up with my body; and he has raised me to as clear and as delightful a vision of his Godhead as a pure creature, without personal union [that is, without being united to God in one person, as Christ's humanity is], seems able to receive. We believe also, O Lady above the heavens, the beauty and glory of all creatures, that thou didst sometimes sleep in the same bed with the child Jesus in his holy infancy (by which our old age and oldness was renewed), and didst lay the little child, the true God, between thy most pure arms, and wast embraced by his right hand. O how incomparable and unspeakable are thy excellence, thy blessedness and thy glory! How very near and how very familiar to God thou hast been made! Surely, in so far as thou art the Mother of the true God, thou art of a dignity in a manner infinite; and as great as the eminence of thy dignity was and is, so great is that of thy goodness, and so great that of thy happiness. Thy blessedness and glory therefore pass all our wonder and all our grasp.

paras.t: Adjuro vos, filiæ Jerusalem, ne suscitetis neque evigilare faciatis dilectam, quoadusque ipsa velit. Post Christi ascensionem ac missionem paracleti Spiritus Sancti, multiplicatis fidelibus, et evidenti fide tenentibus sacrosanctam Virginem esse veri Dei Matrem, omnes eam in maxima et admirabili reverentia (ut vere decuit) habuerunt, atque ad ipsam in omni necessitate et rationabili causa habebant refugium : sed et plurimi magni ac sapientissimi etiam ex paganismo conversi, talem ac tantam videre et audire præcordialiter optaverunt, ut patet de S. Ignatio. Legitur item, quod grandis congregatio sanctarum virginum morabatur cum ea, ejus obsequio deputata. Commisit igitur sponsus cœlestis omnibus istis, ne importune hanc prædilectissimam sponsam et matrem suam accederent, ad revocandum eam de suo secreto et quietissimo actu et loco, ubi contemplativæ vitæ exercitiis, cum devotione sibi soli ac sponso cognita, excellentissime inhærebat. Verumtamen, quoniam sponsus noverat eam in proximorum caritate æstuantissimam esse, jugiterque paratam succurrere et suscitari pro rationabili causa, addidit : Quoadusque ipsa velit, utpote tempore congruo : in quo sine dubio semper fuit prompta, quoniam fructum passionis et mortis Filii sui ferventissime semper optavit.
paras.en: [[2:7|I adjure you, O ye daughters of Jerusalem|Adjuro vos, filiæ Jerusalem]], [[2:7|that you stir not up, nor make the beloved to awake, till she please|ne suscitetis neque evigilare faciatis dilectam, quoadusque ipsa velit]]. After the ascension of Christ and the sending of the Holy Ghost the Paraclete, when the faithful had been multiplied and held by a clear faith that the most holy Virgin was the Mother of the true God, all held her in the greatest and most wonderful reverence (as was truly fitting), and had recourse to her in every need and for every reasonable cause; and very many great and most wise men, converted even from paganism, longed from the heart to see and hear one so great and of such a kind, as is plain in the case of St Ignatius [that is, Ignatius of Antioch, to whom letters to the Blessed Virgin were ascribed]. We read too that a great company of holy virgins lived with her, set apart to serve her. The heavenly Bridegroom therefore charged all these not to come importunately to this his best-loved bride and mother so as to call her back from her hidden and most quiet act and place, where she clung most excellently to the exercises of the contemplative life, with a devotion known only to herself and to the Bridegroom. Yet because the Bridegroom knew that she burned most ardently with charity for her neighbours, and was always ready to help and to be stirred up for a reasonable cause, he added: [[2:7|till she please|Quoadusque ipsa velit]], that is, at a fitting time: at which without doubt she was always ready, for she always most fervently longed for the fruit of the passion and death of her Son.

paras.t: Vox dilecti mei est, qui modo præfacto hortatur ne suscitet. Ecce venit saliens in montibus, transiliens colles. Hoc rectissime dicere potuit Virgo excelsa, benedicta Maria, quando ab Archangelo Gabriele audivit : Ecce concipies in utero et paries filium, ac cetera quæ refert Evangelista. Imo tunc uno vehementissimo saltu a throno paterno in uterum prosiliit virginalem: ob cujus celeritatem aliasque rationes præhabitas, comparatur capreæ hinnuloque cervorum. Exsultavit enim ut gigas ad currendam viam. En ipse stat post parietem nostrum : id est, in carne mundissima, quam ex me assumpsit, suam latere voluit deitatem, me quoque cum Archangelo conferente, de proximo adstitit; prospiciens per cancellos, qualiter nostrum finiremus colloquium. Dum consentiendo dixissem, Ecce ancilla Domini, fiat mihi secundum verbum tuum : dicto celerius, imo instantanee prosiliit in me, et corpus assumpsit ex me.
paras.en: It is [[2:8|The voice of my beloved|Vox dilecti mei]], who in the manner just said urges that none stir her up. [[2:8|behold he cometh leaping upon the mountains, skipping over the hills|Ecce venit saliens in montibus, transiliens colles]]. This the exalted Virgin, blessed Mary, could most rightly say when she heard from the Archangel Gabriel: [[Luke 1:31|Behold thou shalt conceive in thy womb and shalt bring forth a son|Ecce concipies in utero et paries filium]], and the rest that the Evangelist relates. Indeed, then with one most vehement leap he sprang from the Father's throne into the virginal womb: for the swiftness of which, and for the other reasons given before, he is compared [[2:9|a roe, or a young hart|capreæ hinnuloque cervorum]]. For he [[Ps 18:6|Hath rejoiced as a giant to run the way|Exsultavit enim ut gigas ad currendam viam]]. [[2:9|Behold he standeth behind our wall|En ipse stat post parietem nostrum]]: that is, he willed to hide his Godhead in the most pure flesh which he took from me; and while I was conversing with the Archangel he stood close by, [[2:9|looking through the lattices|prospiciens per cancellos]] to see how we would end our conversation. When, consenting, I had said, [[Luke 1:38|Behold the handmaid of the Lord: be it done to me according to thy word|Ecce ancilla Domini, fiat mihi secundum verbum tuum]], quicker than speech, indeed in an instant, he sprang into me and took a body from me.

paras.t: En dilectus meus loquitur mihi. Qui enim per Gabrielem loquebatur mihi forinsecus, per se ipsum loquebatur mihi intrinsecus, me hortando ac incitando inspiratione occulta ad credendum Archangelo, ad consentiendum ejus oraculo, ad cooperandum summo ac divinissimo incarnationis mysterio. Et dixit mihi, instinctu secreto : Surge, a consideratione humillima tuæ propriæ parvitatis, ad actum nobilissimæ magnanimitatis : quatenus pietati meæ omnipotentiæ innitendo, credas mox agendum ex me, et fiendum ex te, atque complendum per te, quod tibi ore nuntiatur angelico, et omnem transcendit naturam, nec ulla fieri potest creata virtute. Propera, id est, festinanter sic age, crede, consenti; loquere verbum, præpara uterum, præbe materiam, ut concipiar a te, et gignar ex te, qui æternaliter sum conceptus et natus ex Patre, in quo idem est mihi concipi et gigni, quoniam generatio illa, intellectualis, immaterialis, intemporalis consistit. O amica mea singularis et unica, cujus respectu aliæ sunt ancillæ, quamvis et suo modo amicæ sint. Columba mea, in qua nunquam fuit radix amaritudinis, felleave austeritas, sed simplicitas sapientialis inviolata. Formosa mea, in naturalibus donis valde perfecta in genere tuo, corpore speciosa, mente ingeniosa, optimæ indolis privilegio decorata; ex naturali dispositione mitissima, piissima, honestissima, et ad omnem virtutem, imo universarum virtutum perfectionem, in termino excellentiæ dispositissima; venustissima moribus, splendidissima muneribus gratiarum infusis, opulentissima meritis : et talis ac tanta, ut speciem tuam non mediocriter concupiscam, quatenus post frequentiam angelorum, tumultuationemque hominum, tandem in te requiescam, tua pulchritudine delectatus, tua tranquillitate allectus.
paras.en: [[2:10|Behold my beloved speaketh to me|En dilectus meus loquitur mihi]]. For he who spoke to me outwardly through Gabriel spoke to me inwardly by himself, urging and stirring me by a hidden inspiration to believe the Archangel, to consent to his message, and to cooperate in the highest and most divine mystery of the incarnation. And he said to me by a secret prompting: [[2:10|Arise|Surge]] from the most humble consideration of thine own littleness to an act of the most noble greatness of soul: so that, leaning on my loving-kindness and omnipotence, thou mayest believe that what is announced to thee by the angel's mouth, which passes all nature and can be done by no created power, will presently be done by me, and be made of thee, and be fulfilled through thee. [[2:10|make haste|Propera]], that is, do so quickly: believe, consent; speak the word, make ready thy womb, give the matter, that I may be conceived by thee and begotten of thee, I who am eternally conceived and born of the Father, in whom being conceived and being begotten are for me the same, since that generation is intellectual, immaterial and outside time. O [[2:10|my love|amica mea]], singular and only, compared with whom the others are handmaids, though in their own way they too are loved friends [*amicæ*]. [[2:10|my dove|Columba mea]], in whom there was never a root of bitterness, nor the harshness of gall, but an unbroken wise simplicity. [[2:10|my beautiful one|Formosa mea]], very perfect in natural gifts in thy kind, beautiful in body, gifted in mind, adorned with the privilege of the best of natures; by natural disposition most gentle, most loving, most virtuous, and disposed to the very limit of excellence for every virtue, indeed for the perfection of all the virtues; most lovely in thy ways, most splendid in the infused gifts of graces, most rich in merits: and of such a kind and so great that I desire thy beauty not a little[[Ps 44:12||]], so that after the throng of the angels and the tumult of men I may at last rest in thee, delighted by thy beauty, drawn by thy tranquillity.

paras.t: Jam enim hiems transiit : id est, tempus est ut rigori legis terminus imponatur, et per me evangelica lex tradatur; imber abiit : id est, copia ac impetus ultionum, quas lex transgressoribus suis jussit infligi, mox finem accipient. Hiems quoque et imber, sunt obscuritas veteris Testamenti, et tempestas in qua lex data est; seu molestissima multitudo observantiarum legalium, quod fuit grave et importabile jugum, duræ cervici convenienter impositum, sed a lege evangelicæ libertatis tollendum. Unde ait Apostolus : Nox præcessit. Et princeps Apostolorum : Quid, inquit, tentatis imponere jugum super cervices discipulorum, quod neque nos, neque patres nostri portare potuimus?
paras.en: [[2:11|For winter is now past|Jam enim hiems transiit]]: that is, it is time for an end to be put to the rigour of the law, and for the law of the Gospel to be given through me; [[2:11|the rain is over|imber abiit]]: that is, the abundance and onslaught of the punishments which the law commanded to be inflicted on its transgressors will soon come to an end. The winter and the rain are also the obscurity of the Old Testament, and the storm in which the law was given; or else the most burdensome multitude of the legal observances, which was a heavy yoke and not to be borne, fittingly laid on a stiff neck, but to be taken away by the law of the freedom of the Gospel. Hence the Apostle says: [[Rom 13:12|The night is passed|Nox præcessit]]. And the prince of the Apostles: [[Acts 15:10|why|Quid]], he says, [[Acts 15:10|tempt you God to put a yoke upon the necks of the disciples which neither our fathers nor we have been able to bear?|tentatis imponere jugum super cervices discipulorum, quod neque nos, neque patres nostri portare potuimus?]] [Denis leaves out *God*, and puts *we* before *our fathers*.]

paras.t: Flores apparuerunt in terra nostra : id est, signa præclara ac florida mei adventus impleri cœperunt, et deinceps abundantius implebuntur, quia jam tempus hebdomadarum a Daniele prædictum advenit.
