So too holy Job speaks to God: [[Job 30:20|I cry to thee, and thou hearest me not: I stand up, and thou dost not regard me.|Clamo ad te, et non exaudis me; sto, et non respicis me]] [[Job 30:21|Thou art changed to be cruel toward me|mutatus es mihi in crudelem]]. Hence the Psalmist speaks to God: [[Ps 12:1|How long, O Lord, wilt thou forget me unto the end? how long dost thou turn away thy face from me?|Usquequo, Domine, oblivisceris me in finem? usquequo avertis faciem tuam a me?]] But we must not cease from this wholesome seeking, since it is written: [[Ps 104:4|Seek ye the Lord, and be strengthened: seek his face evermore.|Quærite Dominum, et confirmamini; quærite faciem ejus semper]] And it is certain that he who seeks will not be cheated of the effect and fruit of his seeking, so far as it rests with the most kind God; yet on the part of the seeker some hindrance could arise: therefore let a certain fear be mingled with hope. For hence it is written: [[Joel 2:14|Who knoweth but he will return, and forgive, and leave a blessing behind him|Quis scit, si convertatur et ignoscat Deus, et relinquat post se benedictionem]]? And so the king of Ninive also says: [[Jon 3:9|Who can tell if God will turn, and forgive: and will turn away from his fierce anger, and we shall not perish?|Quis scit, si convertatur et ignoscat Deus, et revertatur a furore iræ suæ, et non peribimus?]] Therefore there follows:

paras.t: Surgam, et circuibo civitatem, id est quamcumque congregationem fidelium, seu universalem Ecclesiam. Per vicos et plateas quæram quem diligit anima mea: id est, in hominibus activis et contemplativis, in majoribus et minoribus Dei servis quæram dilectum, quærendo ædificationem et instructionem ab ipsis, ac modum pertingendi ad gratiam Dei desideratam. Hoc est a singulis devotorum aliquid virtutis haurire, et instar prudentissimæ apis ex aliorum floribus mellificare, id est unumquemque sequi in bono virtutis, quo ipse magis abundat. Econtrario quidam perversi proximorum mala observant, recogitant, imitantur, et ex eis suas excusant iniquitates, sequentes quasdam aviculas, quæ ex stercoribus sibi præparant nidos. Quæsivi illum, et non inveni. Nam sicut piissima mater interdum abscondit se suo infanti, ut ille eam cum ploratu et majori quærat affectu, atque ad ipsam recurrere assuescat; sic sponsus aliquando sponsæ se subtrahit, ut illa gemendo, plorando, quærendo, affectando mereatur paulo post exuberantius invenire. Itaque, quod in tali casu sponsus non invenitur, dissimulatio est, non ira: attamen sponsa inde affligitur ac turbatur, juxta illud in Psalmo, Avertisti faciem tuam a me, et factus sum conturbatus.
paras.en: [[3:2|I will rise, and will go about the city|Surgam, et circuibo civitatem]], that is, any congregation of the faithful, or the universal Church. [[3:2|in the streets and the broad ways I will seek him whom my soul loveth|Per vicos et plateas quæram quem diligit anima mea]]: that is, among men of the active and of the contemplative life, among the greater and the lesser servants of God I will seek my beloved, seeking from them edification and instruction, and the way of attaining the grace of God that I desire. This is to draw something of virtue from each one of the devout, and, like the most prudent bee, to make honey from the flowers of others: that is, to follow each one in that good of virtue in which he most abounds. On the contrary, certain perverse men watch the evils of their neighbours, think them over, imitate them, and by them excuse their own iniquities, following certain little birds which make their nests of dung. [[3:2|I sought him, and I found him not|Quæsivi illum, et non inveni]]. For as a most loving mother sometimes hides herself from her infant, so that he may seek her with weeping and greater affection, and grow used to running back to her; so the spouse sometimes withdraws himself from the bride, so that by groaning, weeping, seeking and longing she may deserve a little later to find him more abundantly. So the fact that in such a case the spouse is not found is a pretence, not anger: yet the bride is afflicted and troubled by it, according to that in the Psalm, [[Ps 29:8|Thou turnedst away thy face from me, and I became troubled|Avertisti faciem tuam a me, et factus sum conturbatus]].

paras.t: Invenerunt me vigiles qui custodiunt civitatem. Vigiles isti, sunt omnes in caritate et diligentia fervidi, fraternæ salutis zelo accensi, qui pro communi bono Ecclesiæ sunt solliciti, qui animæ tam anxie ac salubriter suspirantis, ac dilectum quærenti, condolent, subvenireque conantur. Num quem diligit anima mea, vidistis? id est, si scitis ubi et qualiter inveniatur, mihi insinuate. Angeli autem visitant assidue animas sibi commissas, et intus eas affantur, quos animæ rogant pro directione et ope continua. Nec dubitant animæ virtuosæ, quin angeli sancti videant Deum per speciem, et sancti viri per fidem et sapientiæ donum; sed ex vehementia sui fervoris sic loquitur, velut si quis exeuntem de camera regis, interroget, an viderit regem.
paras.en: [[3:3|The watchmen who keep the city, found me|Invenerunt me vigiles qui custodiunt civitatem]]. These watchmen are all who are fervent in charity and diligence, fired with zeal for their brethren's salvation, who are careful for the common good of the Church, who feel for the soul that sighs so anxiously and so wholesomely and seeks her beloved, and try to help her. [[3:3|Have you seen him, whom my soul loveth?|Num quem diligit anima mea, vidistis?]] that is: if you know where and how he may be found, make it known to me. The angels, too, constantly visit the souls committed to them, and speak to them within; and the souls ask them for direction and continual help. Nor do virtuous souls doubt that the holy angels see God face to face [*per speciem*, by sight, as opposed to by faith], and holy men by faith and the gift of wisdom; but the bride speaks thus out of the vehemence of her fervour, as if one were to ask a man coming out of the king's chamber whether he had seen the king.

paras.t: Paululum quum pertransissem eos, inveni quem diligit anima mea. Non enim potui subsistere, gradumque figere in aliquo citra dilectum, qui creavit me propter se: ideo inquietum est cor meum, nisi ei jungatur. Ideo videns ipse perseverantiam meam, et afflictionem atque inquietudinem bonam, ex sui amoris fervore prodeuntes, misertus est mei, et ostendit se mihi: quem licet aliquo modo invenerim in præfatis vigilibus atque custodibus, non tamen tam plene, ut quietarer, et sicut optavi; sed ipsis quoque auxiliantibus et orantibus pro me, cupitam gratiæ affluentiam sum sortita.
paras.en: [[3:4|When I had a little passed by them, I found him whom my soul loveth|Paululum quum pertransissem eos, inveni quem diligit anima mea]]. For I could not stop, nor set my foot in anything short of my beloved, who created me for himself: therefore my heart is restless unless it be joined to him [an echo of Augustine, *Confessions* I, 1: "our heart is restless until it rest in thee"]. So he, seeing my perseverance, and the affliction and the good restlessness that came from the fervour of my love for him, had pity on me and showed himself to me: and though I had in some way found him in the watchmen and keepers spoken of, yet not so fully that I was at rest, nor as I wished; but, they too helping me and praying for me, I obtained the abundance of grace I longed for.

paras.t: Tenui eum, quoniam ipse est Dominus Deus salutis meæ, creator et salvator meus, qui universis ac singulis infinite est præferendus. Nec dimittam, imo omni maligno spiritui, omni tentationi et appetitioni ab ipso retrahere me volenti, in æternum resistam, nec a Deo ac sponso meo recedam: juxta illud Psalmi, Ego autem dixi in abundantia mea, Non movebor in æternum. Cum tali proposito ac desiderio Deum quærere et inventum tenere debemus, juxta illud quod scriptum est: In omni corde suo et in tota anima sua quæsierunt Dominum, et invenerunt. Nempe, qui sic quærunt, invenire merentur. Non enim tam incomparabile bonum cum desidia est quærendum; et magnam Omnipotenti infert injuriam, qui tepide et cum torpore cupit ei placere. Ideo Moyses asserit: Quumque quæsieris Dominum Deum tuum, invenies eum; si tamen toto corde et tota tribulatione animæ tuæ quæsieris eum. Verumtamen in tali ac tanto proposito cavendum, ne de suis viribus quis præsumat, sed speret pure in Domino, et innitatur super Deum suum.
paras.en: [[3:4|I held him|Tenui eum]], because he is the [[Ps 87:2|Lord, the God of my salvation|Dominus Deus salutis meæ]], my creator and saviour, who is to be preferred infinitely to all things together and to each one. [[3:4|and I will not let him go|Nec dimittam]]: rather, I will resist for ever every evil spirit, every temptation and desire that would draw me back from him, and I will not depart from my God and spouse: according to that of the Psalm, [[Ps 29:7|And in my abundance I said: I shall never be moved.|Ego autem dixi in abundantia mea, Non movebor in æternum]] With such a purpose and desire we ought to seek God and, having found him, to hold him, according to what is written: [[2 Par 15:15|with all their heart|In omni corde suo]] and with all their soul [[2 Par 15:15|they sought him, and they found him|quæsierunt Dominum, et invenerunt]] [Denis's wording, "with all their soul" (*in tota anima sua*) and "sought the Lord", differs from the Vulgate of this verse, which has "with all their will they sought him"; compare 2 Par 15:12]. For those who seek thus deserve to find. Indeed, so incomparable a good is not to be sought with sloth; and he does great wrong to the Almighty who wishes to please him tepidly and sluggishly. Therefore Moses declares: [[Deut 4:29|And when thou shalt seek there the Lord thy God, thou shalt find him: yet so, if thou seek him with all thy heart, and all the affliction of thy soul|Quumque quæsieris Dominum Deum tuum, invenies eum; si tamen toto corde et tota tribulatione animæ tuæ quæsieris eum]] [Denis omits *ibi*, "there"]. Yet in so great a purpose one must take care not to presume on one's own strength, but to hope purely in the Lord, and [[Is 50:10|lean upon his God|innitatur super Deum suum]].

paras.t: Itaque, Non dimittam illum, donec introducam illum in domum matris meæ, et in cubiculum genitricis meæ. Mater nostra, uno modo est gratia Dei ac sapientia, per quam regeneramur in Domino. Cujus gratiæ seu sapientiæ domus, est mens seu animæ intellectus: cubiculum vero potest dici ipsa synderesis, quæ semper remurmurat malo, atque ad bonum inclinat. In hanc domum ac thalamum debet sponsa introducere sponsum, quia non debet quiescere nec cessare ab inquisitione ac prece, quousque per gratiam gratum facientem sapientiamque infusam præcipuam, sponsus mentem suam atque synderesim firmiter inhabitare ac possidere omnino dignetur.
paras.en: And so: [[3:4|I will not let him go, till I bring him into my mother's house, and into the chamber of her that bore me|Non dimittam illum, donec introducam illum in domum matris meæ, et in cubiculum genitricis meæ]]. Our mother, in one way, is the grace and wisdom of God, by which we are born again in the Lord. The house of this grace or wisdom is the mind, or the soul's understanding; and the chamber may be called the synderesis itself [that is, the inborn habit of the first principles of moral action, the spark of conscience], which always murmurs against evil and inclines to good. Into this house and bridal chamber the bride must bring the spouse, for she must not rest nor cease from seeking and praying until, through sanctifying grace [*gratia gratum faciens*, the grace that makes one pleasing to God] and the excellent infused wisdom, the spouse deigns to dwell in her mind and synderesis firmly and to possess them entirely.

paras.t: Quæ est ista, quæ ascendit per desertum, sicut virgula fumi ex aromatibus myrrhæ et thuris et universi pulveris pigmentarii? Ecce anima virtuosa, Christi sponsa, quæ paulo ante desolata ac arida, per vicos et plateas, quasi mulier præ amore viri dilecti amissi insaniens, quæsivit dilectum: nunc desideratam gratiam alacritatis, illuminationis, inflammationis adepta, non videtur jam ita discurrens; sed tam radiose ascendit, ut paranymphi sodalesque sponsi super hoc admirentur, dicentes: Quæ est ista, quæ ascendit ad verticem caritatis, ad lucem contemplationis, ad plenitudinem cœlestis felicitatis?
paras.en: [[3:6|Who is she that goeth up by the desert, as a pillar of smoke of aromatical spices, of myrrh, and frankincense, and of all the powders of the perfumer?|Quæ est ista, quæ ascendit per desertum, sicut virgula fumi ex aromatibus myrrhæ et thuris et universi pulveris pigmentarii?]] Behold the virtuous soul, the bride of Christ, who a little before, desolate and dry, sought her beloved through the streets and the broad ways, like a woman out of her mind for love of the beloved husband she has lost: now, having obtained the grace she desired, of eagerness, enlightenment and kindling, she no longer seems to run to and fro thus, but goes up so radiantly that the bridesmen [*paranymphi*, the friends who escort the bride] and companions of the spouse wonder at it, saying: [[3:6|Who is she that goeth up|Quæ est ista, quæ ascendit]] to the summit of charity, to the light of contemplation, to the fulness of heavenly bliss?

paras.t: Per desertum, id est in carne ista mortali, in qua (secundum Apostolum) non habitat bonum; vel, Per desertum, id est inter passiones et opera partis sensitivæ ac vegetativæ, quas subjicit sibi. Per desertum etiam designatur vallis hæc lacrimarum. Iterum per desertum significatur religio a mundi voluptatibus, inquietudinibus, vanitatibusque remota.
paras.en: [[3:6|by the desert|Per desertum]], that is, in this mortal flesh, in which, according to the Apostle, no good dwells[[Rom 7:18||]]; or, [[3:6|by the desert|Per desertum]], that is, among the passions and works of the sensitive and vegetative part, which she subjects to herself. By the desert is also meant this vale of tears. Again, by the desert is signified the religious life, removed from the pleasures, restlessness and vanities of the world.

paras.t: Sicut virgula fumi ex aromatibus myrrhæ et thuris, etc., id est linealiter juste, tanquam ab omni privato commodo, et improbo sui amore purgata ac aliena, esuriens sitiensque semper justitiam, nec aliud cupiens nisi Deum et ejus amorem, honorem et gloriam, et nihil sui in se, tanquam plenarie abnegans et mortificans semetipsam: quæ etiam elevatio, cunctarum sibi invicem connexarum actibus delectationibusque virtutum ornatur. Felix anima, quæ sic jugiter cor sursum habet ad Dominum, quærens et sapiens quæ sursum sunt, non quæ super terram.
paras.en: [[3:6|as a pillar of smoke of aromatical spices, of myrrh, and frankincense|Sicut virgula fumi ex aromatibus myrrhæ et thuris]], etc. [*virgula*, a little rod or slender stem; hence "straight as a line"], that is, rising straight as a line in justice, as one cleansed of and estranged from all private advantage and wicked love of self, always hungering and thirsting after justice[[Matt 5:6||]], desiring nothing but God and his love, honour and glory, and nothing of her own in herself, as one who fully denies and mortifies herself: and this rising up is adorned with the acts and delights of all the virtues, which are linked with one another. Happy the soul that thus keeps her heart ever lifted up to the Lord, seeking[[Col 3:1||]] and minding [[Col 3:2|the things that are above, not the things that are upon the earth|quæ sursum sunt, non quæ super terram]].

paras.t: En lectulum Salomonis sexaginta fortes ambiunt ex fortissimis Israel. Lectulus Salomonis, est anima virtuosa, seu mens et tranquillitas ejus. Nam et anima justi, sedes est sapientiæ. Hunc lectulum ambit non solum angelus unus unicuique ad custodiam specialiter deputatus; sed et multi valde, aut etiam millia multa, præsertim tempore opportuno, prout quarto Regum patet de Eliseo, in cujus circuitu apparuerunt agmina angelorum. Similiter omnes electi in vita hac pro se invicem sollicitantur, et mutuo se confortant, ambiunt ac tuentur desiderando, orando, hortando. Ad quod monens Apostolus, Alter, inquit, alterius onera portate: et ipsemet Christus, In hoc, inquiens, cognoscent omnes quia discipuli mei estis, si dilectionem habueritis ad invicem. Hinc denuo loquitur Apostolus: Per caritatem servite invicem. Et Jacobus ait: Orate pro invicem, ut salvemini. Etenim totus populus christianus, est quasi unus exercitus Dei. In exercitu autem unus constipatur, ambitur, munitur, juvatur ab aliis. Ex fortissimis Israel, quia sunt ceteris Deum per fidem cognoscentibus fortiores: qui juxta expositionem præhabitam in præcedenti articulo, sunt ad bella doctissimi, gladiisque accincti.
paras.en: [[3:7|Behold threescore valiant ones of the most valiant of Israel, surrounded the bed of Solomon?|En lectulum Salomonis sexaginta fortes ambiunt ex fortissimis Israel]] The bed of Solomon is the virtuous soul, or her mind and its tranquillity. For the soul of the just man, too, is the seat of wisdom[[Prov 14:33||]] [the margin gives "cf. Prov. xiv, 33", which says that wisdom resteth in the heart of the prudent]. This bed is surrounded not only by the one angel specially appointed to each for his guarding, but also by very many, or even many thousands, especially at the fitting time, as appears in the fourth book of Kings in the case of Eliseus, round about whom hosts of angels appeared[[4 Kings 6:17||]]. Likewise all the elect in this life are concerned for one another, and comfort one another, surround and protect one another by desiring, praying and exhorting. Urging us to this, the Apostle: [[Gal 6:2|Bear ye|Alter]], he says, [[Gal 6:2|one another's burdens|alterius onera portate]]; and Christ himself: [[John 13:35|By this|In hoc]], he says, [[John 13:35|shall all men know that you are my disciples, if you have love one for another|cognoscent omnes quia discipuli mei estis, si dilectionem habueritis ad invicem]]. Hence the Apostle says again: [[Gal 5:13|by charity of the spirit serve one another|Per caritatem servite invicem]]. And James says: [[Jas 5:16|pray one for another, that you may be saved|Orate pro invicem, ut salvemini]]. For the whole Christian people is as it were one army of God; and in an army each one is closely flanked, surrounded, protected and helped by the others. [[3:7|of the most valiant of Israel|Ex fortissimis Israel]], because they are stronger than the others who know God by faith: who, according to the exposition given in the preceding article, are [[3:8|most expert in war|ad bella doctissimi]], and girded with swords.

paras.t: Ferculum fecit sibi rex Salomon de lignis Libani. Ferculum, seu habitaculum istud, est quælibet anima contemplativa, seu virtutum structura facta in anima: quæ structura constat ex lignis Libani, id est ex virtutibus pretiosis, redolentibus et excelsis.
paras.en: [[3:9|King Solomon hath made him a litter of the wood of Libanus:|Ferculum fecit sibi rex Salomon de lignis Libani]] This litter, or dwelling, is any contemplative soul, or the structure of the virtues built in the soul: and this structure is made of the wood of Libanus, that is, of precious, fragrant and lofty virtues.

paras.t: Columnas ejus fecit argenteas. Possunt per columnas intelligi quatuor virtutes cardinales, ædificium spirituale in anima fortiter sustentantes, videlicet justitia, prudentia, fortitudo, et temperantia. Justitia namque est præclarissima virtus, et non est Lucifer nec Hesperus ita admirabilis ac præclarus. Prudentia quoque non solum est virtus, sed et virtutum auriga, actuum moderatrix, splendor ac radius totius bonæ conversationis: per quam rationabile fit obsequium nostrum, et omnia decenter ac secundum ordinem fiunt in nobis, utpote congruo loco, suoque tempore, et recta intentione. Porro fortitudo est inclyta virtus, aggrediens viriliter ardua, nec timore mortis recedens a bonis, ac pro communi bono strenue certans. Temperantia vero, bestialium vitiorum ac voluptatum est refrenatrix, incipiens hominem facere spiritualem, et præcipue ipsum nobilitans ac decorans, dum a carnalibus vitiis (in quibus est maxima turpitudo) eum restringit, sicque ad actus intellectivæ partis eum aptificat.
paras.en: [[3:10|The pillars thereof he made of silver|Columnas ejus fecit argenteas]]. By the pillars may be understood the four cardinal virtues, which strongly hold up the spiritual building in the soul: namely justice, prudence, fortitude and temperance. For justice is a most glorious virtue, and neither the morning star nor the evening star is so wonderful and so bright [a saying of Aristotle, *Ethics* V, 1]. Prudence, too, is not only a virtue but the charioteer of the virtues, the governor of our acts, the splendour and ray of all good living: through it our service is made reasonable[[Rom 12:1||]], and all things are done in us decently and according to order[[1 Cor 14:40||]], that is, in the fitting place, at their own time, and with right intention. Fortitude, again, is a renowned virtue, which manfully undertakes hard things, does not draw back from good things for fear of death, and strives vigorously for the common good. Temperance is the bridle of the bestial vices and pleasures; it begins to make a man spiritual, and especially ennobles and adorns him, while it restrains him from the carnal vices (in which there is the greatest foulness), and so fits him for the acts of the intellectual part.

paras.t: Reclinatorium aureum, id est theologicarum virtutum connexionem ac ornamentum: quæ virtutes sunt ceteris digniores, et per eas potissime sponsus requiescit in anima, quoniam hæ virtutes circa Deum tanquam circa proprium objectum immediate et directe versantur. Ascensum purpureum, id est ordinationem seu gradus septem donorum Spiritus Sancti, in quibus ordo dignitatis perpenditur, et ab inferioribus ad superiora ascenditur.
paras.en: [[3:10|the seat of gold|Reclinatorium aureum]] [*reclinatorium*, a place to recline on], that is, he made the linking together and the adornment of the theological virtues: these virtues are worthier than the rest, and it is chiefly through them that the spouse rests in the soul, since these virtues are concerned with God immediately and directly, as with their proper object. [[3:10|the going up of purple|Ascensum purpureum]], that is, the order or steps of the seven gifts of the Holy Ghost, in which an order of dignity is observed, and one goes up from the lower to the higher.

paras.t: Media caritate constravit. Media seu pavimentum structuræ istius, sunt virtutes morales et actus earum: quas Dominus jussit caritate perfici ac formari, prout præcedenti articulo magis constat expositum. Quidam per media, intelligunt opera indifferentia: quæ scilicet in se non includunt rationem virtutis aut vitii, seu meriti sive demeriti; quæ tamen, si fiant ex caritate, virtuosa meritoriaque redduntur.
paras.en: [[3:10|the midst he covered with charity|Media caritate constravit]] [*constravit*, he paved or spread over]. The midst, or the floor, of this structure is the moral virtues and their acts, which the Lord has commanded to be perfected and formed by charity, as was explained more fully in the preceding article. Some understand by the midst indifferent works: that is, works which in themselves contain no character of virtue or vice, or of merit or demerit; but which, if they are done out of charity, are made virtuous and meritorious.

paras.t: Egredimini et videte, filiæ Sion, regem Salomonem. Istud juxta præinductam præcedentis articuli expositionem, dirigi potest ad quamlibet animam Christi sponsam.
paras.en: [[3:11|Go forth, ye daughters of Sion, and see king Solomon|Egredimini et videte, filiæ Sion, regem Salomonem]]. This, following the exposition given in the preceding article, may be addressed to any soul that is the bride of Christ.

3.title: EXPLANATIO EJUSDEM CAPITULI TERTII, DE CHRISTO ET SPONSA SINGULARI.
3.title_en: Explanation of the same third chapter: of Christ and the singular Bride

paras.t: In lectulo meo per noctes quæsivi quem diligit anima mea. Sponsus cœlestis non solum quæritur ab eis, qui caritatem et gratiam ejus nondum habent, sed ab his quoque, qui ipsum jam habent per caritatem et gratiam. Ideo scriptum est : Quærite faciem ejus semper. Imo ab habentibus eum quæritur multo perfectius, affectuosius et fructuosius, quam a non habentibus. Itaque habitus quæritur, ut plenius habeatur, et gratiosius adsit, ac per gratiæ incrementa assidue quasi de novo adveniat, sicque tandem gloriosius possideatur in patria. Quum igitur sacratissima ac suavissima Virgo, quamvis maxime confirmata in gratia, tamen viatrix fuit et incomparabili ardens dilectione, excellentissime quoque fuit proficiens omni die in universis charismatibus Spiritus Sancti (nec enim unigenitus et liberalissimus atque piissimus Filius ejus, tot guttas virginei lactis ex deificatis suæ dilectissimæ Matris uberibus suxit, quot illustrationibus et sacris ardoribus, recentissimis quoque visitationibus et præclaris profectibus electissimam ejus animam adimplevit) : certum est, quod ipsa divinissima et spiritualissima Virgo, in lectulo suo non solum spirituali, videlicet tranquillissima sui pectoris pace, sed etiam corporali, dilectum suum præ ceteris cunctis ineffabiliter ardentius, frequentius, stabilius, fructuosiusque quæsierit, intentissime deprecando, præcordialius desiderando, sublimius contemplando, copiosius obtinendo.
paras.en: [[3:1|In my bed by night I sought him whom my soul loveth|In lectulo meo per noctes quæsivi quem diligit anima mea]]. The heavenly Bridegroom is sought not only by those who do not yet have his charity and grace, but also by those who already have him through charity and grace. Therefore it is written: [[Ps 104:4|seek his face evermore|Quærite faciem ejus semper]]. Indeed, he is sought far more perfectly, more lovingly and more fruitfully by those who have him than by those who do not. So he who is already possessed is sought, that he may be possessed more fully and be present more graciously, and through the increase of grace come constantly as it were anew, and so at last be possessed more gloriously in the fatherland. Since, then, the most sacred and most sweet Virgin, though confirmed in grace in the highest degree, was yet a wayfarer [that is, still on the journey of this life, not yet in heaven], burning with a love beyond compare, and made most excellent progress every day in all the gifts of the Holy Ghost (for her only-begotten, most generous and most loving Son did not suck as many drops of virginal milk from the deified breasts of his most beloved Mother as he filled her most chosen soul with illuminations and holy ardours, with ever-fresh visitations and splendid advances): it is certain that this most divine and most spiritual Virgin, in her bed, not only the spiritual one, namely the most tranquil peace of her breast, but also the bodily one, sought her beloved beyond all others, ineffably more ardently, more often, more steadily and more fruitfully: praying most intently, desiring from the depth of her heart, contemplating more sublimely, obtaining more abundantly.

paras.t: Ad litteram demum, tempus nocturnum specialiter aptum est ad exercitia talia. Conformiter debemus et nos juxta nostræ modulum parvitatis quærere dilectum etiam in lectulo corporali : ita, ut cum præexaminatione et purgatione conscientiæ, pergamus ad lectum, et in meditatione devota seu orando obdormiamus : atque quam cito evigilaverimus, levemus cor nostrum ad Dominum, orando, meditando, laudando eumdem, sicque implendo quod admonet Jeremias : Consurge, lauda in nocte in principio vigiliarum, et effunde sicut aquam cor tuum ante conspectum Domini Dei tui.
paras.en: Further, in the literal sense, the night-time is especially suited to such exercises. In like manner we too, according to the small measure of our littleness, ought to seek the beloved in our bodily bed as well: so that we go to bed having first examined and cleansed our conscience, and fall asleep in devout meditation or in prayer; and as soon as we wake, lift up our heart to the Lord, praying, meditating and praising him, and so fulfilling what Jeremias counsels: [[Lam 2:19|Arise, give praise in the night, in the beginning of the watches: pour out thy heart like water, before the face of the Lord|Consurge, lauda in nocte in principio vigiliarum, et effunde sicut aquam cor tuum ante conspectum Domini]] thy God.

paras.t: Quæsivi illum, et non inveni. Hoc superficialiter potest exponi de triduo, in quo sanctissima Domina quæsivit dilectum, quum ille duodecim exsistens annorum, mansisset ea ignorante in urbe Jerusalem et in templo : in quo post triduum reperit eum. Quumque primo percepisset absentiam tam dilectissimi Filii, mæstissima facta, dicere potuit : Surgam mane de lecto, et circuibo civitatem Jerusalem : per vicos et plateas ejus quæram dilectum, præsertim inter cognatos et notos. Invenerunt me vigiles : quod ad litteram accidere potuit. Paululum quum pertransissem eos, inveni dilectum in templo in medio doctorum, interrogantem illos et audientem. Tenui eum, dicens : Fili, quid fecisti nobis sic? Ecce ego et pater tuus dolentes quærebamus te. Nec dimittam. Tunc quippe ardentissima mente amplexata fuit, et pectori suo purissimo adstrinxit amantissimum Puerum, plorans præ gaudio. Tamen, ut super Lucam loquitur Origenes, non ideo solum Filium suum tam dolorose quæsivit, quod putaverit eum errasse aut perditum esse, quum sciret eum esse verum Deum et hominem, cui nihil fortuitum aut improvisum posset accidere ; sed potius verebatur, ne forsan demigrasset ad alia aut ad cœlos redisset, iterum, quum sibi placuisset, descensurus. Sicut et aliquis studiosus quærit in Scripturis sanctis in difficilibus locis sensum earum cum quodam tormento, non quod putet errare Scripturas; sed quia quod continent nescit, nec invenire facile potest : propter quod dolens et anxius investigat, quod invenire non valet.
paras.en: [[3:1|I sought him, and found him not|Quæsivi illum, et non inveni]]. On the surface this can be explained of the three days in which the most holy Lady sought her beloved, when, being twelve years old[[Luke 2:42||]], he had stayed behind in the city of Jerusalem and in the temple without her knowing it[[Luke 2:43||]]: where after three days she found him. And when she first perceived the absence of so dearly beloved a Son, she was filled with grief and could say: [[3:2|I will rise|Surgam]] in the morning from my bed, [[3:2|and will go about the city|et circuibo civitatem]] of Jerusalem: [[3:2|in the streets and the broad ways I will seek|per vicos et plateas ejus quæram]] the beloved, especially [[Luke 2:44|among their kinsfolks and acquaintance|inter cognatos et notos]]. [[3:3|The watchmen|vigiles]] [[3:3|found me|Invenerunt me]]: which could have happened in the letter. [[3:4|When I had a little passed by them, I found|Paululum quum pertransissem eos, inveni]] the beloved in the temple, [[Luke 2:46|in the midst of the doctors|in medio doctorum]], asking them and hearing them. [[3:4|I held him|Tenui eum]], saying: [[Luke 2:48|Son, why hast thou done so to us? Behold thy father and I have sought thee sorrowing|Fili, quid fecisti nobis sic? Ecce ego et pater tuus dolentes quærebamus te]] [[3:4|I will not let him go|Nec dimittam]]. Then indeed she embraced him with a most ardent mind, and pressed the most loving Boy to her most pure breast, weeping for joy. Yet, as Origen says on Luke, it was not simply because she thought he had gone astray or was lost that she sought her Son so sorrowfully, since she knew him to be true God and man, to whom nothing by chance or unforeseen could happen; rather she feared that he had perhaps gone away elsewhere, or returned to heaven, to come down again when it pleased him. So too a diligent student seeks the sense of the holy Scriptures in difficult places with a kind of torment, not because he thinks the Scriptures are in error, but because he does not know what they contain and cannot easily find it: and therefore, grieving and anxious, he searches out what he cannot find.

paras.t: Donec introducam illum in domum matris meæ (fortassis beatæ Annæ) in qua habito; vel in templum aut synagogam, hoc est, quousque alia vice personaliter secum intrem materiale templum aut synagogam manufactam, et exeam, ne sic manum meam elapsus, remaneat me non sciente.
paras.en: [[3:4|till I bring him into my mother's house|Donec introducam illum in domum matris meæ]] (perhaps blessed Anne's), in which I live; or into the temple or synagogue: that is, until on another occasion I go in with him in person into the material temple or the synagogue made with hands, and come out again, lest, having thus slipped from my hand, he stay behind without my knowing it.

paras.t: Potest quoque inquisitio ista dilecti, referri ad tempus dominicæ passionis : in quo quum venerandissima Mater novisset Filium suum esse jam captum, cum fidelissima Maria Magdalene currebat per urbem Jerusalem, quousque percepit quod esset in domo pontificis; et quum mane educeretur ad præsidem, occurrit Filio suo : quem tenere, nec dimittere concupivit, imo et mori cum ipso, quousque anima sua, simul cum anima Filii pergeret ad sanctos in limbo.
paras.en: This seeking of the beloved can also be referred to the time of the Lord's passion: when the most venerable Mother knew that her Son had now been taken, she ran through the city of Jerusalem with the most faithful Mary Magdalene, until she learned that he was in the house of the high priest; and when in the morning he was led out to the governor, she met her Son: whom she longed to hold and not let go, nay, even to die with him, until her soul, together with her Son's soul, should go to the saints in limbo.

paras.t: Præterea spiritualiter loquendo, Deifera sponsa hæc Filium suum quæsivit in lectulo suo corporali ac spirituali, non sibi ipsi dumtaxat, sed et populo Judæorum, ac omnibus, pro quorum salute fuit sollicita et assidue preces fudit, ut eis gratiam conversionis, reformationis, ac consolationis internæ acquireret ; nec tamen pro omnibus illis exaudiebatur ad votum, propter illorum nimiam perversitatem. Quumque esset humillima, non tamen de meritis suis præsumpsit. Imo sanctorum Patriarcharum ac Prophetarum virtutes ac merita animo perlustravit, et per ea petiit aliquando exaudiri : sicque per vicos et plateas quæsivit dilectum : quem illis transmigratis invenit, quoniam meritis suis potius quam illorum, exaudiebatur pro plurimis. Ideo ait : Paululum quum pertransissem illos, inveni quem diligit anima mea. Tenui eum, nec dimittam, id est, non cessabo ab invocatione ipsius, donec introducam illum in domum matris meæ, et in cubiculum genitricis meæ, id est in animas congregationum, pro quibus oro, quatenus ipse eas inhabitare et reformare dignetur : quæ congregationes, sunt quædam particulares domus ac filiæ totius Synagogæ, cujus et ego filia sum.
paras.en: Moreover, speaking spiritually, this God-bearing Bride sought her Son in her bed, both bodily and spiritual, not for herself alone, but also for the Jewish people and for all for whose salvation she was concerned and for whom she constantly poured out prayers, to obtain for them the grace of conversion, of reformation and of inward consolation; yet she was not heard as she wished for all of them, because of their great perversity. And since she was most humble, she did not presume on her own merits; rather she went over in her mind the virtues and merits of the holy Patriarchs and Prophets, and sometimes asked to be heard through them: and so she sought the beloved [[3:2|in the streets and the broad ways|per vicos et plateas]]; and when she had passed beyond them she found him, since she was heard for very many on account of her own merits rather than theirs. Therefore she says: [[3:4|When I had a little passed by them, I found him whom my soul loveth|Paululum quum pertransissem illos, inveni quem diligit anima mea]]: [[3:4|I held him: and I will not let him go|Tenui eum, nec dimittam]], that is, I will not cease from calling upon him, [[3:4|till I bring him into my mother's house|donec introducam illum in domum matris meæ]], [[3:4|and into the chamber of her that bore me|et in cubiculum genitricis meæ]], that is, into the souls of the communities for which I pray, that he may deign to dwell in them and reform them: and these communities are, as it were, particular houses and daughters of the whole Synagogue, of which I too am a daughter.

paras.t: Quæ est ista, quæ ascendit per desertum, sicut virgula fumi ex aromatibus myrrhæ et thuris et universi pulveris pigmentarii ? De ascensu quotidiani profectus in omni virtute, sanctitate ac deiformi perfectione honorabilissimæ Virginis, omnes cives triumphantis ac militantis Ecclesiæ rite eumdem profectum pensantes, non immerito mirabantur vehementissime. Inæstimabiliter enim profecit singulis horis, quum haberet purissimum corpus animæ suæ omnino promptissime subditum atque obtemperans, fomitemque prorsus exstinctum, ac diligentiam animi summam ac indefessam, caritatem quoque æstuantissimam, stans indesinenter sub contactu Solis justitiæ, qui radios sapientiæ, flumina gratiæ, caritatis ardores assidue ac abundantissime influxit in eam. Sed et superdulcissimus Spiritus Sanctus Matrem ejus a quo ipse vere æternaliterque procedit, continuo incitavit, movit, accendit ad incrementa profectuum. Quid vero Pater æternus comparentali suæ non largiretur? Non dubium quin secretissime, frequentissime, exuberantissime inundavit eam. Ipsa quoque optime fertur ascendisse ut virgula fumi, quoniam ejus profectui non fuit admixta aliqua curvitas culpæ, nec negligentia ulla ; sed linealiter prorsus rectissime progrediebatur in omni bono, similis vapori resoluto ex incensione thymiamatis optimi, ex omni aromatica specie confecti : quia in profundo prætacto Virginis excellentissimæ, concurrebant plurimarum actus et ordinatissimæ contemperationes virtutum, suavissime redolentes apud Altissimum. Ascendit autem per desertum, per vallem hanc calamitatum ac fletuum, per terram peregrinationis præsentis, per Synagogam a Deo relictam.
paras.en: [[3:6|Who is she that goeth up by the desert, as a pillar of smoke of aromatical spices, of myrrh, and frankincense, and of all the powders of the perfumer?|Quæ est ista, quæ ascendit per desertum, sicut virgula fumi ex aromatibus myrrhæ et thuris et universi pulveris pigmentarii]] At the ascent of the daily progress of the most honourable Virgin in every virtue, holiness and godlike perfection, all the citizens of the Church triumphant and militant, duly weighing that progress, not without cause wondered exceedingly. For she advanced beyond all reckoning every hour, since she had a most pure body, wholly and most readily subject and obedient to her soul, the tinder [fomes: the inclination to sin left by original sin] entirely extinguished, the utmost and untiring diligence of mind, and the most burning charity, standing without ceasing under the touch of the Sun of justice, who constantly and most abundantly poured into her rays of wisdom, rivers of grace, ardours of charity. And the Holy Ghost too, sweet beyond all sweetness, continually stirred, moved and kindled to growth in progress the Mother of him from whom he himself truly and eternally proceeds. And what would the eternal Father not bestow on her who is the parent with him of one Son [comparentalis: literally 'co-parent']? Without doubt he flooded her most secretly, most often, most abundantly. She too is very fitly said to have gone up [[3:6|as a pillar of smoke|ut virgula fumi]] [virgula: literally 'a little rod', hence what follows on its straightness], since no crookedness of fault and no negligence was mixed with her progress; but she went forward in a straight line, wholly and most straightly, in every good, like the vapour released from the burning of the best incense, made of every kind of spice: because in the depth of the most excellent Virgin, touched on above, the acts and most ordered temperings of very many virtues came together, smelling most sweetly before the Most High. And she [[3:6|goeth up by the desert|Ascendit autem per desertum]]: through this valley of calamities and tears, through the land of our present pilgrimage, through the Synagogue forsaken by God.

paras.t: Insuper, ascensum ejus in sublimitate et profectu contemplationis nullus valet satis mirari : quam profundissime contemplabatur altitudinem imperscrutabilis consilii superbeatissimæ Trinitatis, super modo salvationis generis humani per incarnationem ac cetera mysteria Verbi æterni ex ea veraciter humanati. Quemadmodum enim amabilissimæ Virgini singulariter datum est, ut humanæ salutis mysteria ex ea et per eam efficerentur ; sic eminenter datum est ei, ut ab ea profundius contemplarentur. Postremo, quantum quotidie creverit in dilectione sincerissima Filii sui, imo totius superessentialis incircumscriptibilis Trinitatis, quis posset concipere ? quia quum fuerit ab omni sensuali affectione et inordinato amore mundissima aliena, atque in habitu caritatis perfectissima, maxime fuit disposita ad eminentissima caritatis augmenta : quia ex habitu caritatis processit in ferventissimos actus divini amoris ; et quo actus illi erant ferventiores, eo majus sortiebantur sanctæ caritatis augmentum.
paras.en: Further, no one can wonder enough at her ascent in the height and progress of contemplation: how most profoundly she contemplated the height of the unsearchable counsel of the Trinity, blessed above all blessedness, concerning the manner of saving the human race through the incarnation and the other mysteries of the eternal Word, truly made man of her. For as it was given singularly to the most lovable Virgin that the mysteries of human salvation should be wrought of her and through her, so it was given her in an eminent degree that they should be contemplated more deeply by her. Lastly, how much she grew every day in the most sincere love of her Son, nay, of the whole superessential and uncircumscribable Trinity, who could conceive? For since she was most purely free from every sensual affection and disordered love, and most perfect in the habit of charity, she was supremely disposed for the most eminent increases of charity: because from the habit of charity she went forth into most fervent acts of divine love; and the more fervent those acts were, the greater the increase of holy charity they won.

paras.t: Specialiter etiam possunt ista exponi de ascensu Virginis illustrissimæ ac regalis in sua assumptione in cœlos, quando velocissime ac splendidissime ascendit super universos angelicorum spirituum choros usque ad dexteram sponsi, et positus vel potius exhibitus est thronus Matri Regis universorum.
paras.en: These words can also be explained in particular of the ascent of the most illustrious and royal Virgin in her assumption into heaven, when most swiftly and most splendidly she went up above all the choirs of the angelic spirits to the right hand of the Bridegroom, and a throne was set, or rather presented, for the Mother of the King of all.

paras.t: En lectulum Salomonis sexaginta fortes ambiunt ex fortissimis Israel. Nulli puræ creaturæ tam eminenter ac vere competit esse lectulum, id est humilem lectum Salomonis seu Christi, ut glorificandissimæ Virgini : in qua summus ille Pacificus elegit concipi, incarnari, ac habitare in medio uteri ejus ; spiritualiter quoque gratiosissime in mente ipsius. Hanc igitur electissimam omnium creaturarum, statim ut in utero matris suæ concepta est, Deus Trinitas angelis sanctis custodiendam commisit, eamque frequenter vallavit et honoravit multitudo cœlestis militiæ, non tam ob indigentiam quam ob reverentiam ejus. Sed et gloriosi Apostoli ac ceteri utriusque sexus sancti primitivæ Ecclesiæ, ad eam multoties cum ingenti reverentia confluxerunt.
paras.en: [[3:7|Behold threescore valiant ones of the most valiant of Israel, surrounded the bed of Solomon?|En lectulum Salomonis sexaginta fortes ambiunt ex fortissimis Israel]] To no mere creature does it belong so eminently and so truly to be the little bed [lectulum, a diminutive], that is, the lowly bed, of Solomon or of Christ, as to the Virgin most worthy of glory: in whom that supreme Peacemaker [Solomon means 'peaceable'] chose to be conceived, to be made flesh and to dwell in the midst of her womb; and spiritually also, most graciously, in her mind. This most chosen of all creatures, then, as soon as she was conceived in her mother's womb, God the Trinity committed to the holy angels to guard; and a multitude of the heavenly host often surrounded and honoured her, not so much because of her need as out of reverence for her. And the glorious Apostles, too, and the other saints of either sex of the early Church, flocked to her many times with great reverence.

paras.t: Ferculum fecit sibi rex Salomon de lignis Libani. Præclarissima Virgo aptissime dicitur ferculum, id est thronus aut solium Salomonis, id est Salvatoris, in quo fuit Deus mundum reconcilians sibi : quoniam ipsa non solum portavit Unigenitum Dei in sua mente per fidem, caritatem, ac jugem memoriam, venerationemque præcipuam, juxta illud Apostoli, Habitare Christum per fidem in cordibus vestris; sed etiam in suo inviolatissimo utero tulit eum, ex se hominem factum. Hoc ferculum ipsemet Christus, secundum quod Deus, fecit, corpus benignissimæ Virginis per causas secundas formando, cujus et materiam in exordio produxit ex nihilo, animam quoque felicissimam ejus per se immediate creando. Spiritualiter etiam fecit hoc ferculum, sanctificando ac decorando illud per gratiam copiosam, juxta quod scriptum est : Sanctificavit tabernaculum suum Altissimus. Fecit autem illud ex lignis Libani : quia corpus immaculatissimæ Virginis constat ex membris sanctis et incorruptis, quibus Christus communicavit quod de ipso fuit prædictum : Nec dabis Sanctum tuum videre corruptionem. Porro animam Virginis benedictæ sanctificavit ex perfectis, invictis, excelsis, dulcissimisque virtutibus.
paras.en: [[3:9|King Solomon hath made him a litter of the wood of Libanus:|Ferculum fecit sibi rex Salomon de lignis Libani]] The most glorious Virgin is very fitly called a litter [ferculum: a seat or frame that is carried], that is, the throne or seat of Solomon, that is, of the Saviour, in which God was [[2 Cor 5:19|reconciling the world to himself|mundum reconcilians sibi]] [the margin gives 1 Cor. v, 19; the words are 2 Cor 5:19]: for she not only carried the Only-begotten of God in her mind, by faith, charity, unceasing remembrance and singular veneration, according to that word of the Apostle, [[Eph 3:17|That Christ may dwell by faith in your hearts|Habitare Christum per fidem in cordibus vestris]]; but she also bore him in her most inviolate womb, made man of her. This litter Christ himself made, as God, by forming the body of the most kind Virgin through secondary causes (its matter too he brought forth from nothing in the beginning), and by creating her most happy soul himself, immediately. Spiritually also he made this litter, by sanctifying and adorning it with abundant grace, according to what is written: [[Ps 45:5|the most High hath sanctified his own tabernacle|Sanctificavit tabernaculum suum Altissimus]]. And he made it [[3:9|of the wood of Libanus|ex lignis Libani]]: because the body of the most immaculate Virgin consists of holy and incorrupt members, to which Christ imparted what had been foretold of himself: [[Ps 15:10|nor wilt thou give thy holy one to see corruption|Nec dabis Sanctum tuum videre corruptionem]]. And the soul of the blessed Virgin he sanctified with perfect, unconquered, lofty and most sweet virtues.

paras.t: Columnas fecit argenteas. Unde in Proverbiis scribitur : Sapientia ædificavit sibi domum, excidit columnas septem. Per quas septem dona Spiritus Sancti accipiuntur, quæ fulciunt et sustentant animam eis ornatam. Dona namque in adjutorium dantur virtutum, et eas expedire dicuntur, id est promptas facere ad agendum : in adjutorium, inquam, theologicarum virtutum, prout primo Moralium docet Gregorius; et ex respectu illarum virtutum dicuntur argenteas, quia inferiora ac nitida.
paras.en: [[3:10|The pillars thereof he made of silver|Columnas fecit argenteas]]. Hence it is written in Proverbs: [[Prov 9:1|Wisdom hath built herself a house, she hath hewn her out seven pillars.|Sapientia ædificavit sibi domum, excidit columnas septem]] By these are understood the seven gifts of the Holy Ghost, which prop up and sustain the soul adorned with them. For the gifts are given in aid of the virtues, and are said to make them ready, that is, prompt to act: in aid, I say, of the theological virtues, as Gregory teaches in the first book of the Morals; and in respect of those virtues they are called silver, as being lower than they, and bright.

paras.t: Reclinatorium aureum, id est ardentissimam caritatem, per quam pudicissima Virgo proxime disponebatur ad conceptionem Verbi æterni. Per fidem tamen fundamentaliter disponebatur ad hoc. Propter quod dixit Elisabeth : Beata quæ credidisti, etc. Per humilitatem quoque de propinquo et per modum congruitatis : quia non decuit summum nisi ab humillima concipi, quatenus pietas ac gratia Dei recognoscerentur in omnibus. Ideo ipsa dixit : Quia respexit humilitatem ancillæ suæ. Caritas vero præfervida, qua Dei honorem et proximorum æstuantissime concupivit salvationem, maxime Deo eam univit, dignificavit, ac placentissimam fecit. In caritate igitur beatissimæ Dominæ Deus quievit, resedit, ac ferebatur. Qui enim manet in caritate, in Deo manet, et Deus in eo; et qui diligit Deum, unus spiritus est cum eo. Caritas quoque adstringit, amplexatur, et alligat sibi dilectum.
paras.en: [[3:10|the seat of gold|Reclinatorium aureum]] [reclinatorium: a place to lean or recline on], that is, the most burning charity, by which the most chaste Virgin was proximately disposed for the conception of the eternal Word. Yet it was by faith that she was fundamentally disposed for it; and therefore Elisabeth said: [[Luke 1:45|blessed art thou that hast believed|Beata quæ credidisti]], etc. By humility too she was disposed closely and by way of congruity [that is, as what was fitting, not as strict merit]: for it was not fitting that the Most High should be conceived except by the humblest of women, so that the goodness and grace of God might be recognized in all things. Therefore she herself said: [[Luke 1:48|Because he hath regarded the humility of his handmaid|Quia respexit humilitatem ancillæ suæ]]. But her most fervent charity, by which she longed most burningly for the honour of God and the salvation of her neighbours, united her most closely to God, made her worthy and most pleasing to him. In the charity of the most blessed Lady, then, God rested, sat down, and was carried [ferebatur, 'was carried': a play on ferculum, a thing for carrying]. For [[1 John 4:16|he that abideth in charity abideth in God, and God in him|Qui enim manet in caritate, in Deo manet, et Deus in eo]]; and he who loves God [[1 Cor 6:17|is one spirit|unus spiritus est]] with him [the Apostle has: he who is joined to the Lord]. Charity also binds, embraces and ties the beloved to itself.

paras.t: Ascensum purpureum. Posuit enim ascensiones in corde suo in valle hac lacrimarum, hoc est ordinatum ac successivum profectum ab imo humilitatis usque ad apicem caritatis. Denique ascensus purpureus fuit dolorosa compassio, qua affectuosissima ac benignissima Mater Filio suo paulatim tanto intentius condolebat, quanto passio ejus magis appropinquavit : ita quod ipso die Parasceves propter vehementissimum suæ compassionis dolorem, plus quam martyr effecta est. Fuitque dolor talis, consolationibus ejus frequenter admixtus. Quemadmodum enim dulcissime mirabiliterque gaudebat, infantem puerum Jesum vultu placido conspectando, virgineis brachiis deferendo, amplectendo, rosea facie osculando, sacris uberibus nutriendo : sic plane recolendo quod a Simeone audierat, Tuam ipsius animam pertransibit gladius : imo quod a Gabriele sancto perceperat dictum esse ad Joseph de puero, Ipse salvum faciet populum suum a peccatis eorum; quod item ex Prophetis et Psalmis noverat prophetatum de amantissimo Filio suo : Foderunt manus meas et pedes meos, ac multa similia : vehementissime condolebat, et concutiebantur omnia viscera ejus materna super innocentissimo Filio suo, ita ut cum David dicere videretur : O Jesu fili mi, fili mi Jesu ! quis mihi det, ut ego moriar pro te?
paras.en: [[3:10|the going up of purple|Ascensum purpureum]]. For she set ascents in her heart[[Ps 83:6||]] in this vale of tears[[Ps 83:7||]]: that is, an ordered progress, step by step, from the depth of humility to the summit of charity. Lastly, the going up of purple was the sorrowful compassion with which the most loving and most kind Mother suffered with her Son, little by little the more intently the nearer his passion drew: so that on the very day of the Parasceve [that is, Good Friday], through the most vehement sorrow of her compassion, she became more than a martyr. And that sorrow was often mingled with her consolations. For as she rejoiced most sweetly and wonderfully in looking with a calm face on the infant boy Jesus, carrying him in her virginal arms, embracing him, kissing his rosy face, nursing him at her sacred breasts: so, plainly, when she recalled what she had heard from Simeon, [[Luke 2:35|thy own soul a sword shall pierce|Tuam ipsius animam pertransibit gladius]]; nay, what she had learned from holy Gabriel had been said to Joseph about the child, [[Matt 1:21|he shall save his people from their sins|Ipse salvum faciet populum suum a peccatis eorum]]; and likewise what she knew had been prophesied of her most loving Son in the Prophets and Psalms, [[Ps 21:17|They have dug my hands and feet|Foderunt manus meas et pedes meos]], and many like things: she suffered with him most vehemently, and all her mother's bowels were shaken over her most innocent Son, so that she seemed to say with David [in his lament over Absalom]: O Jesus my son, my son Jesus! [[2 Kings 18:33|would to God that I might die for thee|quis mihi det, ut ego moriar pro te]]?

paras.t: Media caritate constravit : id est, quidquid sacratissima Virgo in se habuit, gessit aut pertulit, sponsus ac Filius ejus plenissimo amore Dei et proximorum ornavit : ita quod præfatus piissimæ Matris dolor, sicut ex naturali amore ac materno affectu, quo afficiebatur ad Filium suum, præcipue profluxisse videtur ; sic ex infusa caritate, qua divinæ majestatis honorationem ac mundi redemptionem præcordialissime affectavit, dolor ille mitigabatur, et de fructu passionis Filii sui ingessit ei consolationem non parvam.
paras.en: [[3:10|the midst he covered with charity|Media caritate constravit]]: that is, whatever the most sacred Virgin had in herself, did or suffered, her Bridegroom and Son adorned with the fullest love of God and of neighbour: so that, as the aforesaid sorrow of the most loving Mother seems to have flowed chiefly from the natural love and motherly affection with which she was moved towards her Son, so by the infused charity, with which she longed from the depth of her heart for the honouring of the divine majesty and the redemption of the world, that sorrow was softened, and charity brought her no small consolation from the fruit of her Son's passion.

paras.t: Consequenter sapientissima Virgo fructum incarnationis, passionisque Filii sui ardentissime cupiens fructificare in omnibus, adhortatur : Egredimini et videte, o filiæ Sion, regem Salomonem in diademate, quo coronavit eum mater sua, id est in assumpta humanitate præclarissime decorata, regia, sacerdotali, et judiciaria potestate magnifice sublimata, quam assumpsit ex me ; atque in glorificatione humanitatis ejusdem : quam glorificationem a me matre sua accepit, in quantum fui occasio, medium ac subjectum ex quo suæ incarnationis, et ministratrix substantiæ suæ humanationis, per quam, exaltationem et glorificationem corporis sui accidentaleque præmium meruit et accepit. Exinanivit enim se, formam servi accipiens ; et humiliavit semetipsum, factus obediens Patri usque ad mortem crucis : propter quod Deus exaltavit illum, et dedit illi nomen quod est super omne nomen. Hæc ergo, o filiæ Sion, id est, devotæ animæ, considerate, ut gratæ sitis Salvatori, ejusque humilitatem sectando, mereamini glorificationis ipsius participes fieri. Cetera ex præinductis expositionibus patent.
paras.en: Next, the most wise Virgin, longing most ardently that the fruit of the incarnation and passion of her Son should bear fruit in all, exhorts: [[3:11|Go forth, ye daughters of Sion, and see king Solomon in the diadem, wherewith his mother crowned him|Egredimini et videte, o filiæ Sion, regem Salomonem in diademate, quo coronavit eum mater sua]]: that is, in the humanity he assumed, most gloriously adorned and magnificently raised up with kingly, priestly and judicial power, which he took from me; and in the glorification of that same humanity: which glorification he received from me his mother, inasmuch as I was the occasion, the means and the subject from which [came the matter] of his incarnation [the Latin here seems to lack a word], and the minister of the substance of his becoming man, through which he merited and received the exaltation and glorification of his body, and an accidental reward [that is, a joy added to the essential bliss of heaven]. For he [[Phil 2:7|emptied himself, taking the form of a servant|Exinanivit enim se, formam servi accipiens]]; and he [[Phil 2:8|humbled himself, becoming obedient|humiliavit semetipsum, factus obediens]] to the Father [[Phil 2:8|unto death, even to the death of the cross|usque ad mortem crucis]]: [[Phil 2:9|For which cause, God also hath exalted him and hath given him a name which is above all names|propter quod Deus exaltavit illum, et dedit illi nomen quod est super omne nomen]]. Consider these things therefore, O [[3:11|daughters of Sion|filiæ Sion]], that is, devout souls, that you may be grateful to the Saviour, and by following his humility may deserve to become sharers in his glorification. The rest is clear from the expositions given above.

4.title: ELUCIDATIO CAPITULI QUARTI : QUAM PULCHRA ES, AMICA MEA ! DE CHRISTO ET ECCLESIA.
4.title_en: Explanation of the fourth chapter: How beautiful art thou, my love! Of Christ and the Church

paras.t: Modo in fine præcedentis capituli Ecclesia animas credentium fuit hortata ad considerandum mysteria incarnationis glorificationisque sponsi sui. Videns igitur sponsus ingentem suæ Ecclesiæ caritatem, fervidum zelum, sinceram intentionem, sollicitudinemque pervigilem pro Salvatoris sui honorificentia, cultu et gloria, et pro subditorum salute, vicem rependit, et commendat eamdem, dicendo quasi cum admiratione et ingeminatione, ad insinuandum magnitudinem rei, et affirmationem suæ sententiæ: Quam pulchra es, amica mea! quam pulchra es, sancta et universalis Ecclesia! in qua sunt semper aliquæ sanctæ et perfectæ personæ, et pulcherrima et pulchrificantia sacramenta gratiæ contentiva, ac sancta officia, supernaturaliaque divinorum charismatum ornamenta. Itaque, pulchra es in naturalibus, tanquam ad superbeatissimæ Trinitatis imaginem et similitudinem condita; pulchrior facta per Baptisma gratiarumque munera; pulcherrima, per sanctitatem et contemplationem sublimem, caritatisque perfectionem.
paras.en: Just now, at the end of the preceding chapter, the Church exhorted the souls of believers to consider the mysteries of the incarnation and glorification of her Spouse. The Spouse, then, seeing the great charity of his Church, her fervent zeal, her sincere intention, and her watchful care for the honour, worship and glory of her Saviour and for the salvation of those under her, repays her in turn and commends her, saying as if with wonder and with repetition, to convey the greatness of the matter and the firmness of his judgment: [[4:1|How beautiful art thou, my love|Quam pulchra es, amica mea]]! [[4:1|how beautiful art thou!|quam pulchra es,]] O holy and universal Church, in whom there are always some holy and perfect persons, and most beautiful and beautifying sacraments which contain grace, and holy offices, and the supernatural adornments of the divine gifts [that is, *charismata*, the graces freely given]. So then, thou art beautiful in thy natural gifts, as made to the image and likeness of the most blessed Trinity[[Gen 1:26||]][[Gen 1:27||]]; made more beautiful by Baptism and the gifts of grace; most beautiful through holiness and lofty contemplation, and the perfection of charity.

paras.t: Oculi tui columbarum: id est, columbinos oculos habes, scilicet purum intuitum ac pudicum, dirigendo visum tuum ad sponsum cœlestem, aliundeque avertendo, quemadmodum pudicissima sponsa suum dumtaxat inspicit sponsum; simplicem quoque habes intentionem a felle amaritudinis alienam, et duplicitatem, æmulationem, hypocrisim odis. Absque eo quod intrinsecus latet, id est, præter beatitudinem æternalem tibi paratam, quam degustasti, et quæ in tuis meritis continetur sicut effectus in causa, et sicut fructus in flore, ac forma in inchoatione. Unde ait Apostolus: Habetis fructum vestrum in sanctificationem, finem vero vitam æternam.
paras.en: [[4:1|thy eyes are doves' eyes|Oculi tui columbarum]]: that is, thou hast the eyes of a dove, namely a pure and chaste gaze, directing thy sight to thy heavenly Spouse and turning it away from all else, as a most chaste bride looks at her own bridegroom alone; thou hast also a single intention, free of the gall of bitterness, and thou hatest duplicity, envy and hypocrisy. [[4:1|besides what is hid within|Absque eo quod intrinsecus latet]]: that is, besides the eternal beatitude prepared for thee, which thou hast tasted, and which is contained in thy merits as an effect in its cause, as the fruit in the flower, and as the form in its beginning. Hence the Apostle says: [[Rom 6:22|you have your fruit unto sanctification, and the end life everlasting|Habetis fructum vestrum in sanctificationem, finem vero vitam æternam]].

paras.t: Vel: Pulchra es in conversatione exteriori, virtuosa et exemplari; pulchra quoque in prædicatione salubri, ac ædificatoria locutione: quæ pulchritudines aliqualiter apparent ad sensum, sed ex interiori et insensibili pulchritudine dependent ac oriuntur. De qua sequitur: Absque eo quod intrinsecus latet, id est, præter puritatem tuam internam, caritatis fervorem, contemplationis splendorem, indesinentem profectum mentalem, quæ homines latent, Deoque patent. Homo enim videt in facie, Deus autem intuetur cor.
paras.en: Or: thou art beautiful in thy outward conduct, virtuous and exemplary; beautiful also in wholesome preaching and edifying speech: and these beauties are in some measure apparent to the senses, but they depend on and arise from an inward beauty that the senses do not perceive. Of this there follows: [[4:1|besides what is hid within|Absque eo quod intrinsecus latet]]: that is, besides thy inward purity, the fervour of thy charity, the splendour of thy contemplation, thy unceasing progress of mind, which are hidden from men and open to God. For [[1 Kings 16:7|man seeth those things that appear, but the Lord beholdeth the heart|Homo enim videt in facie, Deus autem intuetur cor]] [Denis's wording, "man seeth the face", is looser than the verse].

paras.t: Capilli tui sicut greges caprarum, quæ ascenderunt de monte Galaad. In capillis multa considerantur. Primo, quod ex capite immediate nascuntur, et illud ornant, atque subtiles sunt, et præ multitudine innumerabiles esse videntur. Quidam igitur per capillos Ecclesiæ, intelligunt ejus prælatos: quia matri Ecclesiæ proximius hærent, et per quos ipsa parit et instruit ornatque alios. Alii per capillos accipiunt contemplativos: qui subtiles esse censentur, et a carnalitate, rudimentisque sensuum extenuati, ac graciles conversatu. Nonnulli per capillos, ob eorum multitudinem, intelligunt plebem communem ac copiam subditorum: qui recte obediendo, sunt ornamenta capitum, id est superiorum suorum. Omnes hi assimilantur gregibus caprarum: quæ, sicut præhabitum est, sunt acutissimi visus, et agiles motu, et in montanis pascentes. Sic præfati per fidem illuminatam et sapientiam salutarem intuentur acute, et discernunt vera a falsis, salubria a nocivis; celeriter quoque divina exsequuntur præcepta, et in ecclesiasticis sacramentis atque Scripturis aluntur; invicem quoque coordinati sunt: quæ mutua ordinatio multitudinem valde perornat. Hinc quæ a Deo sunt, ordinata esse feruntur. Porro Galaad interpretatur, tumulus testis, vel acervus testimonii, ut patet in Genesi. Idcirco per montem Galaad, designatur sacræ Scripturæ sublimitas, in qua est abundantia testimoniorum de Christo. Et etiam per montem hunc significatur sacramentorum ubertas, gratiæ ac virtutum fertilitas: quibus omnibus optime nutriuntur fideles, sicut ad litteram in monte Galaad bona pro pecoribus pascua abundabant. Itaque, de hoc monte ascendunt fideles per spiritualem profectum ad regnum cœlorum.
paras.en: [[4:1|Thy hair is as flocks of goats, which come up from mount Galaad|Capilli tui sicut greges caprarum, quæ ascenderunt de monte Galaad]]. Many things are to be considered in hair. First, that it grows straight from the head and adorns it, and that it is fine, and seems countless for its multitude. Some, then, understand by the hair of the Church her prelates, because they cling most closely to Mother Church, and through them she brings forth, instructs and adorns others. Others take the hair to be the contemplatives, who are reckoned fine, worn thin from carnality and from the crudeness of the senses, and slender in their way of life. Some, because of its multitude, understand by the hair the common people and the great number of subjects, who by obeying rightly are the ornaments of their heads, that is, of their superiors. All these are likened to flocks of goats, which, as was said before, are very sharp of sight, nimble in movement, and graze on the mountains. So those just named, through enlightened faith and saving wisdom, see sharply and tell the true from the false, the wholesome from the harmful; they also carry out the divine commandments swiftly, and are fed on the sacraments of the Church and on the Scriptures; and they are ordered one with another, and this mutual order greatly adorns the multitude. Hence it is said that the things that are of God are ordered[[Rom 13:1||]]. Further, Galaad is interpreted "the mound of the witness" or "the heap of testimony", as is plain in Genesis[[Gen 31:47||]][[Gen 31:48||]]. Therefore by mount Galaad is meant the loftiness of holy Scripture, in which there is an abundance of testimonies concerning Christ. And by this mountain is also signified the richness of the sacraments and the fertility of grace and of the virtues, on all of which the faithful are excellently fed, as in the literal sense there was an abundance of good pasture for the flocks on mount Galaad. And so from this mountain the faithful go up by spiritual progress to the kingdom of heaven.

paras.t: Dentes tui sicut greges tonsarum, quæ ascenderunt de lavacro. Greges ovium tonsarum ascendentes de aqua, in qua lotæ sunt, tam a quantitate et onere suæ lanæ, quam a sordibus sub lana latentibus, alleviatæ sunt ac purgatæ. Sic dentes Ecclesiæ, id est prædicatores, doctores, et propugnatores fidei christianæ (qui animarum cibaria, scilicet sacras doctrinas terunt, frangunt, transfundantque proximis), ab omni carnalium vitiorum mollitie, ab onere sollicitudinis immoderatæ, a superfluitate temporalium rerum, atque a fœditate culparum temporalibus annexarum, debent esse exonerati et emundati, atque ad baptismalis innocentiæ puritatem reducti: quatenus, qui futuram vitam, et ejus æternam, incomparabilem ac perfectam beatitudinem prædicant et commendant, inveniantur terrena contemnere, et ad futuram felicitatem toto affectu accelerare; qui etiam lacrimis pœnitentiæ, fletuque oriente ex desiderio ac dilatione cœlestis patriæ, debent se ipsos quotidie baptizare, ut sint purgati, illuminati, perfecti, quorum officium est alios purgare, illuminare, perficere. Hinc Christus suos ad prædicandum mittens discipulos: Nihil, inquit, tuleritis in via, neque sacculum, neque pecuniam, nec duas tunicas habeatis.
paras.en: [[4:2|Thy teeth as flocks of sheep, that are shorn, which come up from the washing|Dentes tui sicut greges tonsarum, quæ ascenderunt de lavacro]]. Flocks of shorn sheep, coming up from the water in which they have been washed, are lightened and cleansed both of the quantity and weight of their wool and of the dirt hidden under the wool. So the teeth of the Church, that is, the preachers, doctors and defenders of the Christian faith (who grind and break the food of souls, namely the sacred teachings, and pass it on to their neighbours), ought to be unburdened and cleansed of all the softness of carnal vices, of the burden of immoderate care, of the superfluity of temporal things, and of the foulness of the sins bound up with temporal things, and brought back to the purity of baptismal innocence: so that those who preach and commend the life to come and its eternal, incomparable and perfect beatitude may be found to despise earthly things and to hasten with all their affection towards the happiness to come. They ought also to baptize themselves daily with tears of penance, and with weeping that springs from desire for the heavenly fatherland and from its delay, so that they may be purified, enlightened and perfected, whose office it is to purify, enlighten and perfect others. Hence Christ, sending his disciples to preach, says: [[Luke 9:3|Take nothing|Nihil]], he says, [[Luke 9:3|for your journey|tuleritis in via]], [[Luke 9:3|nor scrip|neque sacculum]], [[Luke 9:3|nor money; neither have two coats|neque pecuniam, nec duas tunicas habeatis]].

paras.t: Omnes gemellis fetibus: id est, oves sic tonsæ, duplum habent fetum, saltem in terris quibusdam; et sterilis non est inter eas. Sic præfati dentes Ecclesiæ, duplici fecunditate debent fulgere, videlicet exhibitione exempli, et sermone salubri. In virtutibus quoque debent ceteris fructuosiores exsistere; et duo caritatis præcepta implendo, tam Deo quam hominibus, id est sibi ipsis ac proximis, fructificare: sique creditis sibi talentis uti cum lucro, concessamque eis gratiam communicare atque influere populo, ut dicere queant: Domine, mna tua decem mnas fecit.
paras.en: [[4:2|all with twins|Omnes gemellis fetibus]]: that is, sheep shorn in this way bear twin young, at least in some lands; [[4:2|and there is none barren among them|et sterilis non est inter eas]]. So the teeth of the Church just named ought to shine with a twofold fruitfulness, namely the showing of example and wholesome speech. They ought also to be more fruitful in virtues than the rest, and, by fulfilling the two commandments of charity, to bear fruit both to God and to men, that is, to themselves and to their neighbours: and so to use with profit the talents entrusted to them, and to share the grace granted them and pour it into the people, so that they can say: [[Luke 19:16|Lord, thy pound hath gained ten pounds.|Domine, mna tua decem mnas fecit.]]

paras.t: Sicut vitta coccinea, labia tua. Labia Ecclesiæ sunt homines studiosi in Scripturis periti, et sacra dogmata scribentes, aut aliis proponentes: qui comparantur vittis coccineis, id est rubeis ligaturis, quibus restringuntur capilli ne defluant; et hoc, duplici ratione: primo, quia doctrinæ et locutiones eorum sunt sibi invicem coordinatæ, contextæ, et cohærentes, sicut fila in vittis; secundo, quoniam sicut vittæ restringunt capillos, sic verba idoneæ prædicationis refrenant cogitationum distractiones, et affectionum inordinationes, mentesque audientium in Deum recolligunt. Et quia de Christi salutifera passione, et qualiter per eam simus redempti, debent assidue prædicare, merito vittis assimilantur coccineis. Hoc utique faciunt, dum instruunt populum, qualiter omni hora perpendere debeat in divinæ majestatis aspectu se omnia agere, et metuendum Dei judicium atque amarissimam Christi passionem semper pensare, et illud Psalmographi, Oculi mei semper ad Dominum, ruminare frequenter in corde. Et eloquium tuum dulce, quia delectabile et jucundum, amorosum, salubre, facundum, exemplare et consolatorium: juxta quod scriptum est, Quam dulcia faucibus meis eloquia tua! Hoc eloquium, est sacra Scriptura, stilo plana, sententiis plena, mysteriis gravida: in quo Deus Trinitas vere creditur, cognoscitur et laudatur, Christi mysteria continentur, divina præcepta, consilia, testimonia, hortamenta ac varia scripta sunt documenta, et novissima hominum describuntur.
paras.en: [[4:3|Thy lips are as a scarlet lace|Sicut vitta coccinea, labia tua]]. The lips of the Church are studious men, skilled in the Scriptures, who write the sacred teachings or set them before others. They are compared to scarlet laces [*vittae*, the bands or fillets that bind the hair], that is, to red bands with which the hair is bound so that it does not fall loose; and this for two reasons: first, because their teachings and words are ordered, woven together and coherent with one another, like the threads in the bands; secondly, because as the bands bind the hair, so the words of fitting preaching rein in the distractions of the thoughts and the disorders of the affections, and gather the minds of the hearers back into God. And because they ought to preach unceasingly of the saving passion of Christ, and of how we have been redeemed by it, they are rightly likened to scarlet bands. This they do when they teach the people how at every hour they should consider that they do all things in the sight of the divine majesty, and always ponder the fearful judgment of God and the most bitter passion of Christ, and often ruminate in the heart that word of the Psalmist: [[Ps 24:15|My eyes are ever towards the Lord|Oculi mei semper ad Dominum]]. [[4:3|and thy speech sweet|Et eloquium tuum dulce]]: because it is delightful and pleasant, loving, wholesome, eloquent, exemplary and consoling; according to what is written: [[Ps 118:103|How sweet are thy words to my palate!|Quam dulcia faucibus meis eloquia tua!]] This speech is holy Scripture, plain in style, full in meaning, pregnant with mysteries: in which God the Trinity is truly believed, known and praised; the mysteries of Christ are contained; the divine commandments, counsels, testimonies, exhortations and various teachings are written; and the last things of men are described.

paras.t: Sicut fragmen mali punici, ita genæ tuæ. Genæ Ecclesiæ, sunt personæ contemplativæ, pacificæ, pudicæ, ac dulces in sua conversatione. In genis namque fit osculum, et pulcher apparet color, ac cito apparet verecundiæ rubor, atque amplior teneritudo sentitur. Hæ personæ comparantur non malo punico, sed fragmini ejus, seu frusto mali granati: per quod sponsus significatur, cujus perfectio a nemine valet plenarie imitari, aut participari; sed unusquisque pro modulo gratiæ sibi collatæ, imitatur ipsum pro parte, et in istis aut illis virtutibus secundum aliquem gradum. Nempe in malo seu pomo punico invenitur exterior quædam asperitas, et dulcedo interior, granorum collectio, decor coloris, venusta quoque varietas ex albi rubeique coloris permixtione. Ita in Christo fuit asperitas exterioris vestitus. Unde ait in Psalmo: Posui vestimentum meum cilicium; itemque, Ego autem, quum mihi molesti essent, induebar cilicio. Intus vero fuit in superiori parte animæ Salvatoris dulcor beatificæ fruitionis. Fuit quoque in eo granorum, id est omnium virtutum ac donorum, collectio, in totius excellentiæ termino; et decor coloris, id est honestissimus ac summe exemplaris apparatus exterior in vultu, incessu, gestu, sermone et factis; venustissima item varietas ex permixtione albi rubeique coloris, id est præclarissima unio divinæ ac humanæ naturæ, et communio actuum utriusque, idiomatum etiam communicatio, quia in ipso divina adscribuntur homini, et Deo humana. Nam et Deus dicitur passus, et homo vocatur unigenitus Filius Dei: in quibus semper pensandum quid propter quod dicatur. Propter quod magnus et divinus Dionysius Christi actionem vocat theandricam, id est deivirilem.
paras.en: [[4:3|Thy cheeks are as a piece of a pomegranate|Sicut fragmen mali punici, ita genæ tuæ]]. The cheeks of the Church are persons contemplative, peaceable, chaste and gentle in their way of life. For on the cheeks the kiss is given, and a lovely colour appears, and the blush of modesty quickly shows, and a greater tenderness is felt. These persons are compared not to a pomegranate but to a piece of one, a fragment of a pomegranate; for by the pomegranate is signified the Spouse, whose perfection no one can wholly imitate or share; but each, according to the measure of grace given him, imitates him in part, and in these or those virtues, in some degree. For in the pomegranate there is found a certain roughness without and sweetness within, a gathering of seeds, beauty of colour, and also a lovely variety from the mingling of white and red. So in Christ there was the roughness of his outward clothing. Hence he says in the Psalm: [[Ps 68:12|I made haircloth my garment|Posui vestimentum meum cilicium]]; and again: [[Ps 34:13|But as for me, when they were troublesome to me, I was clothed with haircloth|Ego autem, quum mihi molesti essent, induebar cilicio]] But within, in the higher part of the Saviour's soul, there was the sweetness of beatific fruition. There was also in him the gathering of seeds, that is, of all virtues and gifts, at the summit of all excellence; and beauty of colour, that is, a most seemly and supremely exemplary outward bearing, in his face, his gait, his gestures, his speech and his deeds; and likewise a most lovely variety from the mingling of white and red, that is, the most glorious union of the divine and human natures, and the sharing of the acts of each, and also the communication of idioms [that is, the attributing to the one Person of what belongs to either nature], since in him divine things are ascribed to the man, and human things to God. For God is said to have suffered, and the man is called the only-begotten Son of God; in which we must always weigh what is said by reason of what. For this reason the great and divine Dionysius calls Christ's action theandric, that is, divine-human.

paras.t: Tales ergo sunt genæ Ecclesiæ, absque eo quod intrinsecus latet, id est præter interiorem ejus soli Deo notam perfectionem, sicut expositum est. Habet quippe in secretissimo cordis sinu, in apice mentis mysticam theologiam et sapientialem pudorem, quo coram sponso erubescit in quocumque reprehensibiliter se habere, aut quantumcumque parum offendere.
paras.en: Such, then, are the cheeks of the Church, [[4:3|besides that which lieth hid within|absque eo quod intrinsecus latet]]: that is, besides her inward perfection, known to God alone, as has been explained. For she has, in the most secret bosom of the heart, at the summit of the mind, mystical theology and a wise modesty, by which she blushes before her Spouse to behave blameworthily in anything, or to offend in however small a way.

paras.t: Sicut turris David collum tuum, quæ ædificata est cum propugnaculis. Collum, inter caput et corpus, est medium, nectitque ea in unum; et ipsum erigitur, ut undique longius ac latius circumspiciatur, et imminentibus resistatur periculis.
