Recte ergo per collum Ecclesiæ, accipiuntur custodes et curati, qui præsident: qui inter Christum caput omnium, et inter populum mediant, et Deo reconciliant plebem, cui et dona gratiæ desuper impetrant, ac sacramenta ministrant; oculum quoque circumspectionis dirigunt et circumferunt undique, considerando statum, impugnationes, indigentiamque Ecclesiæ, ut super his avisent et cautum reddant populum Dei. Isti elevantur in altum, non elatione, sed prælatione, magnanimitate, perfectione, et circumspectione. Ideo assimilantur turri David ædificatæ cum propugnaculis, id est pinnis murorum, ex quibus contra hostes pugnatur. Sic et isti pro subditis et sibi commissis, contra adversarios salutis talium, præliantur orando, virtuose vivendo, hortando, instruendo, corripiendo.
paras.en: [[4:4|Thy neck, is as the tower of David, which is built with bulwarks|Sicut turris David collum tuum, quæ ædificata est cum propugnaculis]]. The neck is between the head and the body, and joins them into one; and it is raised up, so that one may look about further and more widely on every side, and resist the dangers that threaten. Rightly, then, by the neck of the Church are understood the guardians and pastors [*curati*, those with the cure of souls] who preside: who stand between Christ, the head of all, and the people, and reconcile the people to God, obtain for them the gifts of grace from on high, and minister the sacraments to them; and they turn and carry the eye of watchfulness round on every side, considering the state of the Church, the attacks upon her and her needs, so that they may take counsel about these things and make the people of God wary. These are raised on high, not by pride but by prelacy, by greatness of soul, perfection and watchfulness. Therefore they are likened to the tower of David built with bulwarks, that is, with battlements on the walls, from which one fights against the enemy. So these too, for their subjects and those entrusted to them, fight against the enemies of their salvation by praying, by living virtuously, by exhorting, instructing and rebuking.

paras.t: Mille clypei pendent ex ea, id est in muris turris Davidicæ, in signum apparatuum bellicorum ipsius; omnis armatura fortium. Legitur autem secundo Regum et primo Paralipomenon David rex habuisse triginta septem fortes, tres fortiores, tresque fortissimos: inter quos ipsemet exstitit unus, ut aliqui opinantur. Unde quum dicitur, Mille clypei, videtur numerus determinatus sumi pro indeterminato. Sic, imo incomparabiliter magnificentius, per gyrum ecclesiasticæ sublimitatis et in congregatione fidelium, est omnium armatura virtutum, innumerabilesque clypei, ad defendendum fidem Ecclesiæ contra universos ipsius hostes invisibiles atque visibiles. Clypei isti, sunt auctoritates, testimonia et doctrinæ sacræ Scripturæ et sanctorum Patrum ac catholicorum doctorum, miracula, sanctitas et virtutes fidelium, aliaque diversa multa ac copiosa Spiritus Sancti charismata. Unde de evangelicæ legis doctrina Apostolus scribit: Quæ in nos confirmata est, contestante Deo signis et virtutibus et prodigiis, et variis Spiritus Sancti distributionibus. His sensis et armis convincuntur hæreticæ pravitates, omnisque infidelitatis perversitas.
paras.en: [[4:4|a thousand bucklers hang upon it|Mille clypei pendent ex ea]]: that is, on the walls of David's tower, as a sign of its warlike equipment; [[4:4|all the armour of valiant men|omnis armatura fortium]]. Now we read in the second book of Kings and the first of Paralipomenon that King David had thirty-seven valiant men, three more valiant, and three most valiant, among whom he himself was one, as some think[[2 Kings 23:8||]][[1 Par 11:10||]]. Hence when it says "a thousand bucklers", a definite number seems to be taken for an indefinite one. So, and indeed incomparably more magnificently, all round the height of the Church and in the congregation of the faithful there is the armour of all the virtues, and countless bucklers, to defend the faith of the Church against all her enemies, invisible and visible. These bucklers are the authorities, testimonies and teachings of holy Scripture and of the holy Fathers and the Catholic doctors, the miracles, holiness and virtues of the faithful, and the many other diverse and abundant gifts of the Holy Ghost. Hence the Apostle writes of the teaching of the law of the Gospel that it [[Heb 2:3|was confirmed unto us|Quæ in nos confirmata est]], [[Heb 2:4|God also bearing them witness by signs and wonders and divers miracles and distributions of the Holy Ghost|contestante Deo signis et virtutibus et prodigiis, et variis Spiritus Sancti distributionibus]]. By these senses [*sensis*, perhaps for *sensibus*] and arms the wickedness of heretics and all the perversity of unbelief are refuted.

paras.t: Duo ubera tua, sicut duo hinnuli capreæ gemelli. De duobus uberibus sponsi, dictum est super illud: Quia meliora sunt ubera tua vino. Porro duo Testamenta, seu doctrina legis Mosaicæ ac sapientia Evangelicæ legis, quæ dicuntur duo ubera sponsi, tanquam datoris ac Domini, sunt etiam ubera sponsæ seu universalis Ecclesiæ, tanquam recipientis, ministerialiterque utentis. Et quia hæc sponsa humiliter se suo conformat sponso: ideo sicut in Christo duo ubera etiam intelliguntur caritas ejus ac pietas; ita et ubera ista Ecclesiæ et prælatorum ipsius, sunt caritas et pietas, seu discretio et misericordia, vel diligentia pastoralis et quotidiana instructio: per quæ omnia subditos suos maternaliter fovet, nutrit, lactat Ecclesia, sicut Paulus testatur: Libentissime impendam et superimpendar ipse pro animabus vestris; et iterum, Facti sumus parvuli in medio vestri, quomodo si nutrix foveat filios suos. Rursus, duo ubera Ecclesiæ, sunt sustentatio filiorum ejus, tam spiritualis quam corporalis. Verum, secundum Gregorium, duo ubera sunt duo prædicantium ordines, quorum unus missus est ad Judæos, alter ad gentes, prout Paulus fatetur: Qui operatus est Petro in apostolatum circumcisionis, operatus est et mihi inter gentes. — Ubera ista Ecclesiæ, comparantur gemellis hinnulis capreæ: quoniam spirituali renovatione sunt florida, humilitateque parva, ac invicem concordantia et connexa, dilectionem quoque et concordiam inter superiores ac subditos, et inter subditos inter se, inter superiores etiam inter se facientia; iterum, quoniam instar hinnulorum capreæ procedunt in actus virtutum celerrime, ac interiori visus acumine vigent.
paras.en: [[4:5|Thy two breasts like two young roes that are twins|Duo ubera tua, sicut duo hinnuli capreæ gemelli]]. Of the two breasts of the Spouse we have spoken on the words: [[Cant 1:1|for thy breasts are better than wine|Quia meliora sunt ubera tua vino]]. Further, the two Testaments, or the teaching of the law of Moses and the wisdom of the law of the Gospel, which are called the two breasts of the Spouse as the giver and Lord, are also the breasts of the bride, the universal Church, as the one who receives them and uses them as a minister. And because this bride humbly conforms herself to her Spouse, therefore, as in Christ the two breasts are also understood as his charity and his tenderness, so these breasts of the Church and of her prelates are charity and tenderness, or discretion and mercy, or pastoral diligence and daily instruction: by all of which the Church cherishes, nourishes and suckles her subjects like a mother, as Paul testifies: [[2 Cor 12:15|I most gladly will spend and be spent myself for your souls|Libentissime impendam et superimpendar ipse pro animabus vestris]]; and again: [[1 Thess 2:7|we became little ones in the midst of you, as if a nurse should cherish her children|Facti sumus parvuli in medio vestri, quomodo si nutrix foveat filios suos]]. Again, the two breasts of the Church are the sustenance of her children, both spiritual and bodily. But according to Gregory the two breasts are the two orders of preachers, one of which was sent to the Jews and the other to the Gentiles, as Paul declares: [[Gal 2:8|he who wrought in Peter to the apostleship of the circumcision wrought in me also among the Gentiles|Qui operatus est Petro in apostolatum circumcisionis, operatus est et mihi inter gentes]]. These breasts of the Church are compared to the twin young of the roe because they are flourishing with spiritual renewal, little by humility, and in harmony and joined with one another, and they make love and concord between superiors and subjects, among subjects themselves, and among superiors themselves; and again because, like the young of the roe, they go forth very swiftly into the acts of the virtues, and are strong in the inward keenness of their sight.

paras.t: Qui pascuntur in liliis: id est, quæ ubera, seu pastores significati per hinnulos, spiritualiter nutriuntur in splendidis ac suavibus Sanctorum sententiis, doctrinis, virtutibus et exemplis, præsertim in candore castimoniæ et puritatis flagrantia. Donec adspiret dies, id est, clara cognitio Dei per speciem, seu dies æternitatis, aut retributio diei generalis judicii veniat, et inclinentur umbræ, id est, obscuritas cognitionis præsentis, tenebræ hujus exsilii, umbraque mortis cessent. Interim enim durat lactatio uberum Ecclesiæ in hac vita; sed in die æternitatis ac beatifica visione cessabit, quia ex tunc erit Deus omnia in omnibus, militansque Ecclesia ad triumphantem translata, et unum cum illa effecta, immediate ac plene a Deo illuminabitur ac pascetur.
paras.en: [[4:5|which feed among the lilies|Qui pascuntur in liliis]]: that is, these breasts, or the pastors signified by the young roes, are spiritually fed on the bright and sweet sayings, teachings, virtues and examples of the Saints, above all in the whiteness of chastity and the fragrance of purity. [[4:6|Till the day break|Donec adspiret dies]]: that is, until the clear knowledge of God by sight, or the day of eternity, or the requital of the day of the general judgment come, [[4:6|and the shadows retire|et inclinentur umbræ]]: that is, until the obscurity of our present knowledge, the darkness of this exile and the shadow of death cease. For meanwhile the suckling at the breasts of the Church lasts in this life; but in the day of eternity and the beatific vision it will cease, because from then on [[1 Cor 15:28|God may be all in all|erit Deus omnia in omnibus]], and the Church militant, carried over to the Church triumphant and made one with her, will be enlightened and fed by God immediately and fully.

paras.t: Vadam ad montem myrrhæ, et ad collem thuris. Per myrrham amaram, et corpora a corruptionibus præservantem, significatur austeritas vitæ pœnitentialis, rigor justitiæ, mortificatio carnis; per thus vero, quod dulciter redolet, et in cultu divino accenditur, insinuatur fervor devotionis, suavitas orationis, et contemplativæ redolentia vitæ. Itaque sponsus testatur: Vadam ad montem myrrhæ: id est, eos misericorditer visitabo, qui in arduis pœnitentiæ exercitiis occupantur, et rigori pœnitentiæ sunt intenti, et se ipsos salubriter mortificare nituntur, et dicunt: Quoniam propter te mortificamur tota die; itemque, Propter verba labiorum tuorum ego custodivi vias duras. Hos ergo sponsus consolatur ac refovet, et gratiæ dona auget in eis. Et ad collem thuris, id est ad eos qui in eminentia devotionis, dulcedine orationis, et contemplativæ vitæ redolentiis conquiescunt. Hi familiarius desuper invisuntur, gratiosius adimplentur, et nutriuntur in croceis, et introeuntes domum mentis, cum sapientia delectantur. Itaque per montem myrrhæ, possunt intelligi in vita activa constituti; per collem thuris, contemplativi. Et quamvis sublimior sit contemplativorum vita, quam activorum; activi tamen per montem, contemplativi per collem signantur: quoniam multo plures sunt activi, quam contemplativi; et quoniam contemplatio vitæ hujus, permodica est respectu futuræ. Sed quia in multis offendimus omnes, necesse habemus primo montem myrrhæ accedere, et per pœnitentiæ opera nos purgare; sicque per exercitia viæ illuminativæ, per orationes intentas et meditationes suaves, ad collem thuris venire.
paras.en: [[4:6|I will go to the mountain of myrrh, and to the hill of frankincense|Vadam ad montem myrrhæ, et ad collem thuris]]. By myrrh, which is bitter and preserves bodies from corruption, is signified the austerity of the penitential life, the rigour of justice, the mortification of the flesh; and by frankincense, which smells sweet and is burned in divine worship, is meant the fervour of devotion, the sweetness of prayer, and the fragrance of the contemplative life. So the Spouse declares: [[4:6|I will go to the mountain of myrrh|Vadam ad montem myrrhæ]]: that is, I will mercifully visit those who are busy in the hard exercises of penance, intent on its rigour, and striving to mortify themselves to their salvation, and who say: [[Ps 43:22|Because for thy sake we are killed all the day long|Quoniam propter te mortificamur tota die]]; and again: [[Ps 16:4|for the sake of the words of thy lips, I have kept hard ways|Propter verba labiorum tuorum ego custodivi vias duras]]. These, then, the Spouse consoles and refreshes, and increases the gifts of grace in them. [[4:6|and to the hill of frankincense|Et ad collem thuris]]: that is, to those who rest in the height of devotion, in the sweetness of prayer and in the fragrances of the contemplative life. These are visited from on high more familiarly, are filled more graciously, and are brought up in saffron [*nutriuntur in croceis*; the Douay-Rheims has "brought up in scarlet"][[Lam 4:5||]], and, entering the house of the mind, take delight with wisdom. So by the mountain of myrrh can be understood those set in the active life, and by the hill of frankincense the contemplatives. And though the life of contemplatives is loftier than that of the active, yet the active are signified by a mountain and the contemplatives by a hill: because the active are far more numerous than the contemplatives, and because the contemplation of this life is very slight in comparison with that of the life to come. But since [[Jas 3:2|in many things we all offend|in multis offendimus omnes]], we must first go to the mountain of myrrh and purify ourselves by the works of penance, and so, through the exercises of the illuminative way, through earnest prayers and sweet meditations, come to the hill of frankincense.

paras.t: Tota pulchra es, amica mea, et macula non est in te. Hoc concordat Apostoli verbis, dicentis: Elegit sibi gloriosam Ecclesiam non habentem maculam neque rugam, nec aliquid ejusmodi, sed ut sit sancta et immaculata: quod tamen, secundum Hieronymum super Jeremiam, et Bernardum in sermone quodam, competit Ecclesiæ pro statu futuro. Attamen convenit ei aliquo modo etiam in præsenti, quantum ad membra sua principaliora seu meliora: quoniam semper sunt in Ecclesia aliqui sancti, imo et multi, in quibus non est macula culpæ mortalis. Potest quoque contingere, quod aliqui sint tam custoditi ac fervidi coram Deo, quod interdum ad aliquantulum temporis sint etiam sine veniali: dum pro suis quotidianis culpis quotidie tantam pœnitentiam agunt, et tantum accenduntur in Deo, atque de minimis culpis sic erubescunt, quod non solum pro eis satisfaciunt plene, imo etiam crescunt in caritate et in omni virtute, ita quod evolant, si in tali dispositione obierint. Est ergo Ecclesia tota pulchra, id est ab inquinamentis carnis ac spiritus munda: in appetitu sensitivo, per virtutes morales a passionum immoderantiis reformata; in intellectu, per fidem, scientiam, prudentiam, consilium, sapientiam decorata; in voluntate vero, per spem, caritatem, justitiam; in memoria, per stabilitatem in istis: multis quoque virtuosis abundans operibus, ac ædificatoriis verbis, meritisque præclaris; et in quibusdam personis, etiam sanctitate virtutibusque heroicis pollens.
paras.en: [[4:7|Thou art all fair, O my love, and there is not a spot in thee.|Tota pulchra es, amica mea, et macula non est in te.]] This agrees with the words of the Apostle, who says that he chose for himself [[Eph 5:27|a glorious church, not having spot or wrinkle or any such thing; but that it should be holy and without blemish|gloriosam Ecclesiam non habentem maculam neque rugam, nec aliquid ejusmodi, sed ut sit sancta et immaculata]]. Yet this, according to Jerome on Jeremias and Bernard in one of his sermons, belongs to the Church in her future state. Nevertheless it fits her in some way in the present too, as regards her chief or better members: for there are always in the Church some saints, indeed many, in whom there is no stain of mortal sin. It can also happen that some are so watchful and fervent before God that at times, for a little while, they are even without venial sin: when for their daily faults they do so much penance every day, are so inflamed in God, and so blush at the least faults, that they not only make full satisfaction for them but even grow in charity and in every virtue, so that they would fly straight up [to heaven] if they died in that disposition. The Church, then, is all fair, that is, clean of defilement of the flesh and of the spirit[[2 Cor 7:1||]]: in the sensitive appetite, reformed from the excesses of the passions by the moral virtues; in the intellect, adorned with faith, knowledge, prudence, counsel and wisdom; in the will, with hope, charity and justice; in the memory, with steadfastness in these; abounding also in many virtuous works, edifying words and glorious merits; and in certain persons strong even in holiness and heroic virtues.

paras.t: Nec his obstat, quod Ecclesia asseritur deformata, imo et meretrix facta, ut aliqui dicunt super illud Isaiæ: Quomodo facta est meretrix civitas fidelis? Totum enim integrale, secundum diversitatem suarum partium, diversas sumit denominationes. Unde Apostolus Corinthiis scribens: In omnibus, inquit, divites facti estis in illo (puta in Christo), ita ut nihil vobis desit in ulla gratia. Et tamen eisdem paulo post loquitur: Quum sit inter vos zelus et contentio, nonne carnales estis, et secundum hominem ambulatis? Itemque: Non potui vobis loqui quasi spiritualibus, sed quasi carnalibus. Dicitur ergo Ecclesia deformata, aversa, exsanguis, seu meretrix facta, quantum ad credentes scilicet, caritatem et opera non habentes, imo vero vitiis sordidatos, quorum animæ non sunt sponsæ Christi, sed adulteræ diaboli. De hoc Gregorius super Job, et Alexander de Hales super tertium Sententiarum plenius sunt locuti.
paras.en: Nor does it stand against this that the Church is said to be deformed, and even to have become a harlot, as some say on the words of Isaias: [[Is 1:21|How is the faithful city, that was full of judgment, become a harlot?|Quomodo facta est meretrix civitas fidelis?]] For an integral whole [that is, a whole made up of parts] takes different names according to the diversity of its parts. Hence the Apostle, writing to the Corinthians, says: [[1 Cor 1:5|in all things|In omnibus]], he says, [[1 Cor 1:5|you are made rich in him|divites facti estis in illo]] (that is, in Christ), so that [[1 Cor 1:7|nothing is wanting to you in any grace|nihil vobis desit in ulla gratia]]. And yet a little later he says to the same people: [[1 Cor 3:3|whereas there is among you envying and contention, are you not carnal and walk you not according to man?|Quum sit inter vos zelus et contentio, nonne carnales estis, et secundum hominem ambulatis?]] And again: [[1 Cor 3:1|could not speak to you as unto spiritual, but as unto carnal|Non potui vobis loqui quasi spiritualibus, sed quasi carnalibus]]. The Church, then, is called deformed, turned away, bloodless, or become a harlot, as regards those believers, namely, who have not charity and works, but are rather defiled with vices, whose souls are not brides of Christ but adulteresses of the devil. Gregory on Job, and Alexander of Hales on the third book of the Sentences, have spoken of this more fully.

paras.t: Veni de Libano, sponsa mea, veni de Libano, veni. Ecce ter sponsam invitat venire : primo, ad commendationem beatissimæ Trinitatis, quæ est unus sponsus omnium beatorum spirituum atque fidelium animarum, quamvis ratio sponsi magis proprie conveniat Verbo incarnato, ut dictum est; secundo, ad ampliorem excitationem, sicut in Jeremia, Terra, terra, terra, audi verbum Domini; tertio, ad insinuandum sui amoris fervorem ad sponsam suam. Ter quoque hortatur ut veniat, quatenus mentis cogitatu, oris sermone, et operum exhibitione, ad ipsum accedat. Et rursus, quia per tres virtutes theologicas fit spiritualis iste accessus. Itaque, veni per fidem, spem, et caritatem, de Libano, id est de mentis renovatione ac puritate : Libanus enim, candidatio interpretatur.
paras.en: [[4:8|Come from Libanus, my spouse, come from Libanus, come|Veni de Libano, sponsa mea, veni de Libano, veni]]. See, he invites the spouse three times to come: first, to commend the most blessed Trinity, which is the one Spouse of all the blessed spirits and of faithful souls, although the character of spouse belongs more properly to the Word incarnate, as has been said; second, to rouse her the more, as in Jeremias: [[Jer 22:29|O earth, earth, earth, hear the word of the Lord|Terra, terra, terra, audi verbum Domini]]; third, to suggest the fervour of his love for his spouse. He also urges her three times to come, so that she may draw near to him by the thought of the mind, by the word of the mouth, and by the showing forth of works. And again, because this spiritual drawing near is made through the three theological virtues. So: come through faith, hope and charity, [[4:8|from Libanus|de Libano]], that is, from renewal and purity of mind; for Libanus is interpreted *whitening*.

paras.t: Secundum Gregorium, per Libanum, designatur Baptismus, in quo purgatur Ecclesia, fidemque recipit, per quam una cum gratia ad coronam vocatur. Simili modo posset per Libanum pœnitentia, contritio, seu confessio accipi : omnia enim in confessione lavantur.
paras.en: According to Gregory, Libanus signifies Baptism, in which the Church is cleansed and receives the faith, through which, together with grace, she is called to the crown. In like manner Libanus could be taken for penance, contrition or confession: for all things are washed away in confession[[Ps 31:5||]][[Prov 28:13||]].

paras.t: Veni de Libano, id est de justa conversatione ad beatificam visionem; veni, de merito ad præmium, de fide ad speciem, de curriculo ad quietem, de tempore ad æternitatem, de luctu ad bravium, de via ad patriam, de periculo ad securitatem, de miseriis ad salutem; coronaberis de capite Amana, de vertice Sanir et Hermon, de cubilibus leonum, de montibus pardorum, id est, coronam gloriæ sortieris pro diligentia et labore, quo convertisti ad fidem principes et magnates sæculi hujus. Amana enim interpretatur inquietus seu turbulentus: Sanir vero, fœtor; Hermon, anathema. Sicque per Amana intelliguntur homines passionati, tyranni et persecutores justorum, de quibus loquitur Isaias, Impii quasi mare fervens, quod quiescere non potest; per Sanir autem, gulosi et lubrici, qui fœditatibus serviunt carnis, de quibus exponitur illud Joelis, Computruerunt jumenta in stercore suo; per Hermon, superbi et spiritualibus vitiis dediti, qui sunt anathema et separati a Domino. Per leones demum exprimuntur homines feroces, voraces, et violenti; per pardos, simulatores et callidi ac immisericordes, quoniam pardus est animal crudele, varietatem et maculas habens colorum. Similiter diversis vitiis indurati, signantur per pardum, juxta quod loquitur Jeremias : Si Æthiops potest mutare pellem suam, et pardus varietates suas, et vos poteritis benefacere, quum didiceritis malum.
paras.en: [[4:8|Come from Libanus|Veni de Libano]], that is, from just living to the beatific vision; [[4:8|come|veni]], from merit to reward, from faith to sight, from the race to rest, from time to eternity, from mourning to the prize, from the way to the fatherland, from danger to safety, from miseries to salvation; [[4:8|thou shalt be crowned from the top of Amana, from the top of Sanir and Hermon, from the dens of the lions, from the mountains of the leopards|coronaberis de capite Amana, de vertice Sanir et Hermon, de cubilibus leonum, de montibus pardorum]]: that is, thou shalt obtain the crown of glory for the diligence and labour with which thou hast converted to the faith the princes and great men of this world. For Amana is interpreted *restless* or *turbulent*; Sanir, *stench*; Hermon, *anathema*. And so by Amana are understood men of passion, tyrants and persecutors of the just, of whom Isaias speaks: [[Is 57:20|the wicked are like the raging sea, which cannot rest|Impii quasi mare fervens, quod quiescere non potest]]; by Sanir, the gluttonous and lustful, who serve the foulnesses of the flesh, of whom that saying of Joel is expounded: [[Joel 1:17|The beasts have rotted in their dung|Computruerunt jumenta in stercore suo]]; by Hermon, the proud and those given to spiritual vices, who are anathema and separated from the Lord. By lions, lastly, are expressed men fierce, greedy and violent; by leopards, dissemblers, the crafty and the merciless, since the leopard is a cruel animal, with variety and spots of colour. So too those hardened in divers vices are signified by the leopard, according to what Jeremias says: [[Jer 13:23|If the Ethiopian can change his skin, or the leopard his spots: you also may do well, when you have learned evil|Si Æthiops potest mutare pellem suam, et pardus varietates suas, et vos poteritis benefacere, quum didiceritis malum]].

paras.t: Porro, secundum Glossam, per leones et pardos dæmones designantur : de quibus precamur, Ne tradas bestiis animam confitentem tibi. Unde et princeps ait Apostolorum : Adversarius vester diabolus, tanquam leo rugiens circuit, quærens quem devoret. Horum montes atque cubilia sunt iniqui, in quorum cordibus regnabant ac habitabant. Coronaberis ergo de capite Amana, id est pro conversione capitaneorum ac principalium inter eos, qui per Amana sunt expressi; de vertice quoque Sanir et Hermon, id est, pro eo quod avertisti ad me sublimiores inter eos, qui per Sanir et Hermon notantur. Hinc conversis per se scribit apostolus Paulus : Quæ enim est spes nostra, aut gaudium, aut corona gloriæ ? Nonne vos ante Dominum ?
paras.en: Further, according to the Gloss, the demons are signified by the lions and leopards: concerning whom we pray, [[Ps 73:19|Deliver not up to beasts the souls that confess to thee|Ne tradas bestiis animam confitentem tibi]] [Denis has the singular: *the soul that confesseth to thee*]. Hence the prince of the Apostles also says: [[1 Pet 5:8|your adversary the devil, as a roaring lion, goeth about seeking whom he may devour|Adversarius vester diabolus, tanquam leo rugiens circuit, quærens quem devoret]]. Their mountains and dens are the wicked, in whose hearts they reigned and dwelt. [[4:8|Thou shalt be crowned|Coronaberis]] therefore [[4:8|from the top of Amana|de capite Amana]], that is, for the conversion of the captains and chief men among those who are expressed by Amana; and also [[4:8|from the top of Sanir and Hermon|de vertice quoque Sanir et Hermon]], that is, for having turned to me the more exalted among those who are marked by Sanir and Hermon. Hence the apostle Paul writes to those converted through him: [[1 Thess 2:19|For what is our hope or joy or crown of glory? Are not you, in the presence of our Lord|Quæ enim est spes nostra, aut gaudium, aut corona gloriæ ? Nonne vos ante Dominum]]?

paras.t: Nec mirum, o sponsa, quod toties te invito ad gloriam. Nam Vulnerasti cor meum, soror mea, sponsa : id est, tu, Ecclesia, quæ es soror per conformitatem naturæ quam assumpsi, et sponsa per caritatem præcipuam, in tantum me provocasti ad tuum amorem, tamque dilecta et cara es mihi, quod præ tuo amore et desiderio tuæ salutis mortem sustinui, et tuæ damnationi vehementissime condolui, et quasi vulnere amoris fui percussus. Ideo repeto : vulnerasti cor meum in uno oculorum tuorum, id est per columbinum illum intuitum quem habes ad me, et per puram ac simplicem intentionem qua meum intendis honorem. Vel, In uno oculorum tuorum, id est in unitate fidei qua me cernis. Habes enim oculum scientiæ naturalis, seu lumen naturalis ingenii. Habes quoque oculum fidei, quo supernaturalia intueris, per quem mihi amplius places, quoniam justus ex fide vivit. Et in uno crine colli tui. Per crines Ecclesiæ, sicut præhabitum est, uno modo intelligitur populi multitudo; et per collum, ipsi prælati, qui inter Christum caput et corpus communitatis sunt medii, et caput corpori illi annectunt. Sicque per unum crinem colli, insinuatur unitas plebis fidelis suis præsidentibus adhærentis, ut sic capiti (quod est Christus) per obedientiam conjungantur : quod præcipue placet sponso, qui suis ait vicariis : Qui vos audit, me audit; et qui vos spernit, me spernit. Propter quod monet Apostolus : Obedite præpositis vestris, et subjacete illis.
paras.en: Nor is it any wonder, O spouse, that I invite thee so often to glory. For [[4:9|Thou hast wounded my heart, my sister, my spouse|Vulnerasti cor meum, soror mea, sponsa]]: that is, thou, the Church, who art my sister by likeness of the nature I took on, and my spouse by a special charity, hast so far provoked me to love of thee, and art so beloved and dear to me, that for love of thee and desire of thy salvation I underwent death, and grieved most vehemently over thy damnation, and was as it were struck with the wound of love. Therefore I repeat: [[4:9|thou hast wounded my heart with one of thy eyes|vulnerasti cor meum in uno oculorum tuorum]], that is, through that dove-like gaze which thou hast toward me, and through the pure and simple intention with which thou seekest my honour. Or, [[4:9|with one of thy eyes|In uno oculorum tuorum]], that is, in the unity of the faith by which thou seest me. For thou hast the eye of natural knowledge, or the light of natural wit. Thou hast also the eye of faith, with which thou beholdest supernatural things, and by which thou pleasest me more, since [[Rom 1:17|The just man liveth by faith|justus ex fide vivit]]. [[4:9|And with one hair of thy neck|Et in uno crine colli tui]]. By the hairs of the Church, as was said before, is understood in one way the multitude of the people; and by the neck, the prelates themselves, who stand between Christ the head and the body of the community, and join the head to that body. And so by one hair of the neck is suggested the unity of the faithful people cleaving to those set over them, so that they may thus be joined by obedience to the head (which is Christ)[[1 Cor 11:3||]][[Eph 4:15||]]: which especially pleases the Spouse, who says to his vicars: [[Luke 10:16|He that heareth you heareth me: and he that despiseth you despiseth me|Qui vos audit, me audit; et qui vos spernit, me spernit]]. For this reason the Apostle admonishes: [[Heb 13:17|Obey your prelates and be subject to them|Obedite præpositis vestris, et subjacete illis]].

paras.t: Præterea (ut apparet) sponsus hic loquitur per modum amantium, qui frequenter ex intuitu alicujus partis seu rei personæ dilectæ, ita in ejus accenduntur amore, ut quasi vulnerati amore perhibeantur; qui etiam ex oculorum et capillorum dilectæ adspectu solent ad eam affici valde. Sic ergo nunc asserit sponsus : Vulnerasti cor meum, soror mea, sponsa, in uno oculorum tuorum, et in uno crine colli tui, id est, in tantum te amo, ut etiam quæcumque pars tua seu res tibi conjuncta, meam dilectionem inflammet. Imo qui diligit vehementer personam, si viderit aliquam ei multum consimilem, mox medullitus grandi affectu concutitur. Quumque oculi Ecclesiæ dicantur doctores et magistri fidelium, præsertim gloriosi Apostoli ac beatissimi Evangelistæ, posset per unum oculorum intelligi discipulus ille, quem diligebat Jesus, S. Joannes; et per unum crinem, amorosa Maria Magdalene, imo potissime beatissima virgo Maria.
paras.en: Moreover (as appears), the Spouse speaks here in the manner of lovers, who often, from the sight of some part or thing of the person beloved, are so kindled with love of her that they are said to be as it were wounded with love; and who are also wont to be greatly moved toward the beloved by the sight of her eyes and hair. So now the Spouse declares: [[4:9|Thou hast wounded my heart, my sister, my spouse, thou hast wounded my heart with one of thy eyes, and with one hair of thy neck|Vulnerasti cor meum, soror mea, sponsa, in uno oculorum tuorum, et in uno crine colli tui]], that is, I love thee so much that even any part of thee, or anything joined to thee, inflames my love. Indeed, one who loves a person vehemently, if he sees someone very like her, is at once shaken to the marrow with great affection. And since the doctors and masters of the faithful are called the eyes of the Church, above all the glorious Apostles and the most blessed Evangelists, by one of the eyes could be understood that disciple [[John 13:23|whom Jesus loved|quem diligebat Jesus]], St. John; and by one hair, the loving Mary Magdalen, nay, most of all the most blessed Virgin Mary.

paras.t: Quam pulchræ sunt mammæ tuæ, soror mea, sponsa! Mammæ Ecclesiæ, sicut inductum est, sunt caritas Dei et proximi, vel pietas et doctrina, seu utriusque Testamenti scientia, vel ipsi prædicatores atque prælati : quæ utique mammæ, pulchræ sunt valde, virtuosæ, ornatæ, divinæ, atque uberibus sponsi consimiles. Pulchriora sunt ubera tua vino, id est omni temporali materialique bono ac poculo, quia salubrius alunt ac dulcius. Meliora sunt etiam ubera evangelicæ compassionis ac consolationis, vino rigoris legalis. Similiter doctrina Christi, melior atque perfectior est doctrina Moysis. Juxta quem modum in Proverbiis legitur : Melior est sapientia cunctis opibus. At vero sicut corporeæ mammæ sunt pulchræ, quum fuerint plenæ ac rigidæ, albæ ac modicæ : sic spiritualia ubera pulchra censentur, quum per prædicationem et comminationem divinæ justitiæ fuerint rigida ; per commemorationem divinæ pietatis et futuræ glorificationis, plena; per doctrinam sinceram, nil falsitatis includentem, alba; per planum humilemque sermonem, modica.
paras.en: [[4:10|How beautiful are thy breasts, my sister, my spouse|Quam pulchræ sunt mammæ tuæ, soror mea, sponsa!]]! The breasts of the Church, as was brought in before, are the charity of God and of the neighbour, or piety and doctrine, or the knowledge of both Testaments, or the preachers and prelates themselves: which breasts are indeed very beautiful, virtuous, adorned, divine, and like the breasts of the Spouse. [[4:10|thy breasts are more beautiful than wine|Pulchriora sunt ubera tua vino]], that is, than every temporal and material good and drink, because they nourish more wholesomely and more sweetly. Better too are the breasts of evangelical compassion and consolation than the wine of the rigour of the law. Likewise the doctrine of Christ is better and more perfect than the doctrine of Moses. In the same way we read in Proverbs: [[Prov 8:11|wisdom is better than all|Melior est sapientia cunctis]] riches [Denis has *opibus*, riches, where the Vulgate has *pretiosissimis*, the most precious things]. But just as bodily breasts are beautiful when they are full and firm, white and small, so spiritual breasts are judged beautiful when they are firm through preaching and the threat of divine justice; full, through the recalling of divine mercy and of future glorification; white, through sincere doctrine containing nothing false; small, through plain and humble speech.

paras.t: Rursus, ut asserit Beda, prædicatores et pastores Ecclesiæ interdum comparantur mammis, aliquando oculis, quandoque dentibus : mammis, eo quod consolentur pusillanimes ac infirmos, et instruant subditos ; oculis, quoniam sapientiam loquuntur inter perfectos, et bona a malis, vera a falsis discernunt ; dentibus, quia corripiunt inquietos ac reos. Et odor unguentorum tuorum super omnia aromata: id est, dulcedo, delecta fama, quam tu, o sponsa Ecclesia, habes, ex tuis unguentis, id est supernaturalibus donis Spiritus Sancti, et infusis virtutibus, præsertim ex fide, spe, caritate, præstantior, spiritualior, divinior est aromatibus materialibus universis, et etiam virtutibus naturalibus acquisitis, philosophicisque scientiis, operibus quoque bonis ex genere, quæ a malis hominibus fieri queunt.
paras.en: Again, as Bede says, the preachers and pastors of the Church are sometimes compared to breasts, sometimes to eyes, sometimes to teeth: to breasts, because they comfort the faint-hearted and the weak, and instruct those under them; to eyes, because they [[1 Cor 2:6|speak wisdom among the perfect|sapientiam loquuntur inter perfectos]], and discern good from evil and true from false; to teeth, because they [[1 Thess 5:14|rebuke the unquiet|corripiunt inquietos]] and the guilty. [[4:10|and the sweet smell of thy ointments above all aromatical spices|Et odor unguentorum tuorum super omnia aromata]]: that is, the sweetness, the choice fame, which thou, O spouse, the Church, hast from thy ointments, that is, from the supernatural gifts of the Holy Ghost and the infused virtues, above all from faith, hope and charity, is more excellent, more spiritual and more divine than all material spices, and also than the acquired natural virtues and the sciences of the philosophers, and than the works good in their kind [that is, good by the nature of the act, as distinct from works made meritorious by grace] which can be done by evil men.

paras.t: Favus distillans labia tua, sponsa : id est, melliflua verba habes ; et labia tua, videlicet prælati et prædicatores, saluberrima atque dulcissima sermocinantur eloquia de bonitate, amabilitate, excellentia et beatitudine Dei in semetipso, atque de omni misericordia, caritate, munificentia ejus ad rationales creaturas, præsertim ad Christianos, de beneficiis ac promissis ipsius, de mysteriis Christi, et de ceteris quæ in divinis continentur Scripturis.
paras.en: [[4:11|Thy lips, my spouse, are as a dropping honeycomb|Favus distillans labia tua, sponsa]]: that is, thou hast honey-flowing words; and thy lips, namely the prelates and preachers, speak most wholesome and sweetest discourses of the goodness, loveliness, excellence and beatitude of God in himself, and of all his mercy, charity and munificence toward rational creatures, above all toward Christians; of his benefits and promises, of the mysteries of Christ, and of the other things contained in the divine Scriptures.

paras.t: Mel et lac sub lingua tua : id est, doctrinam habes salubrem ac dulcem pusillis incipientibusque convenientem ; qualiter scilicet debeant carnalia atque mortalia vitare peccata, exteriorem componere hominem, exteriores sensus reprimere, linguam domare, ad humilitatem, mansuetudinem, patientiam, caritatem se dare, et divina ac ecclesiastica observare præcepta. Et ista designantur per lac, quod cibus est puerorum. Unde et princeps apostolici chori hortatur : Quasi modo geniti infantes rationabiles, lac concupiscite. Paulus quoque : Quasi parvulis, inquit, lac vobis dedi. Interdum tamen per lac, innocentia et puritas designantur. Et potest hoc loco per lac intelligi doctrina ad Christi humanitatem ac ejus mysteria, virtutes ac opera pertinens : quod scilicet Unigenitus Dei propter nos factus est homo, et conversatus in mundo in summa paupertate, profundissima humilitate, immobili patientia, ardentissima caritate, et tandem acerbissimam mortem perpessus ; et qualiter debeamus eum sequi in istis. Per mel vero, doctrina spectans ad divinitatem ejus : qualiter ab æterno invariabiliter natus sit ex Patre, se ipsum in se concipiente, intelligente ac proferente, cujus prolatio est generatio Verbi æterni, quod est unigenitus Filius ejus. Iterum, per mel accipi potest doctrina proficientibus ac perfectis conveniens : qualiter debeant se jugiter interius exercere, et mentem Deo unire, eumque contemplari sinceriter, amare ardenter, tenere, stringere, et amplecti stabiliter. Unde dixit Apostolus : Perfectorum est solidus cibus; et, Sapientiam loquimur inter perfectos. Hinc ait Fulgentius : In sacra Scriptura seu sermone dominico, est quod omni professioni congruat, quod omni ætati conveniat.
paras.en: [[4:11|honey and milk are under thy tongue|Mel et lac sub lingua tua]]: that is, thou hast wholesome and sweet doctrine, suited to little ones and beginners: how, namely, they ought to shun carnal and mortal sins, order the outward man, restrain the outward senses, tame the tongue, give themselves to humility, meekness, patience and charity, and keep the divine and ecclesiastical commandments. And these things are signified by milk, which is the food of children. Hence the prince of the apostolic choir exhorts: [[1 Pet 2:2|As newborn babes, desire the rational milk|Quasi modo geniti infantes rationabiles, lac concupiscite]] [Denis reads *rationabiles*, making the babes, not the milk, "rational"]. Paul too: [[1 Cor 3:1|As unto little ones|Quasi parvulis]], he says, [[1 Cor 3:2|I gave you milk|lac vobis dedi]]. Sometimes, however, innocence and purity are signified by milk. And in this place milk may be understood as the doctrine that concerns the humanity of Christ and his mysteries, virtues and works: namely that the Only-begotten of God was made man for our sake[[John 1:14||]], and lived in the world in the utmost poverty, the deepest humility, unshaken patience and most ardent charity, and at last suffered a most bitter death; and how we ought to follow him in these. By honey, the doctrine regarding his divinity: how from eternity he was unchangeably born of the Father, who conceives, understands and utters himself in himself, whose uttering is the generation of the eternal Word, which is his only-begotten Son. Again, by honey may be taken the doctrine suited to the proficient and the perfect: how they ought to exercise themselves continually within, and unite the mind to God, and contemplate him sincerely, love him ardently, and hold, clasp and embrace him steadfastly. Hence the Apostle said: [[Heb 5:14|strong meat is for the perfect|Perfectorum est solidus cibus]]; and, [[1 Cor 2:6|we speak wisdom among the perfect|Sapientiam loquimur inter perfectos]]. Hence Fulgentius says: In holy Scripture, or the Lord's discourse, there is what befits every calling and what suits every age.

paras.t: Et odor vestimentorum tuorum, sicut odor thuris. Virtutes et dona Spiritus Sancti, ac meritorii actus, sunt vestimenta, ornamenta ac arma Ecclesiæ et uniuscujusque fidelis. De quibus in Isaia ait Ecclesia : Induit me Dominus vestimentis salutis, et indumento justitiæ circumdedit me. Ad quod pertinet illud in Psalmo : Adstitit regina a dextris tuis in vestitu deaurato. Itaque vestimenta dicuntur, quoniam contra æstum concupiscentiæ, et frigora invidiæ atque accidiæ, ac cæterorum intemperiem et immoderantiam vitiorum defendunt. Dicuntur etiam ornamenta, quia coram Deo pulchrificant, et ad intuendum delectabilem efficiunt ipsam Ecclesiam, ac membra ipsius, juxta illud in Apocalypsi : Vestimentis albis induaris, ut non appareat confusio nuditatis tuæ. Vocantur et arma, quia per ea resistitur hostibus humanæ salutis, vitia expugnantur, tentatio vincitur, et homo legitime certans, coronari meretur. Propter quod hortatur Apostolus : Induite vos armaturam Dei, ut possitis stare adversus insidias diaboli. Et rursus : Accipite, inquit, armaturam Dei, ut possitis resistere in die malo. Horum igitur vestimentorum odor, fama, delectatio, suavitasque interna, est sicut odor thuris : quoniam sicut odor thuris dulciter afficit odoratum sive olfactum, sic odor ille spiritualium vestium, mentem; et sicut thus odorem non fundit, nisi incendatur, sic nec vestes illæ redolent coram Deo, nisi divino inflammentur amore, atque ex igne caritatis procedant. Amplius, quia per thuris odorem solet orationis fervor seu devotio designari, juxta illud in Apocalypsi, Ascendit fumus aromatum de orationibus Sanctorum; et in Psalmo, Dirigatur oratio mea sicut incensum in conspectu tuo : hinc odor vestimentorum illorum, est sicut odor thuris, quoniam meritorii actus habent vim orationis, et gratiam adipiscuntur ac gloriam; imo sine eis oratio est inefficax, juxta quod scriptum est : Qui declinat aurem suam ne audiat legem, oratio ejus erit exsecrabilis. Ideo scriptum est : Scimus quoniam peccatores Deus non audit; sed si quis cultor est Dei, et voluntatem ejus facit, hunc exaudit.
paras.en: [[4:11|and the smell of thy garments, as the smell of frankincense|Et odor vestimentorum tuorum, sicut odor thuris]]. The virtues and gifts of the Holy Ghost, and meritorious acts, are the garments, ornaments and arms of the Church and of each of the faithful. Of these the Church says in Isaias: [[Is 61:10|he hath clothed me with the garments of salvation: and with the robe of justice he hath covered me|Induit me Dominus vestimentis salutis, et indumento justitiæ circumdedit me]]. To this belongs that in the Psalm: [[Ps 44:10|The queen stood on thy right hand, in gilded clothing|Adstitit regina a dextris tuis in vestitu deaurato]]. They are called garments, then, because they defend against the heat of concupiscence, the cold of envy and of sloth [*accidia*, the vice of spiritual sloth], and the inclemency and excess of the other vices. They are also called ornaments, because they make the Church herself and her members beautiful before God and delightful to behold, according to that in the Apocalypse: [[Apoc 3:18|mayest be clothed in white garments: and that the shame of thy nakedness may not appear|Vestimentis albis induaris, ut non appareat confusio nuditatis tuæ]]. And they are called arms, because by them the enemies of man's salvation are resisted, vices are overcome, temptation is conquered, and man, striving lawfully, deserves to be crowned. For this reason the Apostle exhorts: [[Eph 6:11|Put you on the armour of God, that you may be able to stand against the deceits of the devil|Induite vos armaturam Dei, ut possitis stare adversus insidias diaboli]]. And again: [[Eph 6:13|take unto you|Accipite]], he says, [[Eph 6:13|the armour of God, that you may be able to resist in the evil day|armaturam Dei, ut possitis resistere in die malo]]. The smell of these garments, then, their fame, delight and inward sweetness, is [[4:11|as the smell of frankincense|sicut odor thuris]]: for as the smell of frankincense sweetly affects the sense of smell, so the smell of those spiritual garments affects the mind; and as frankincense gives off no smell unless it is kindled, so neither are those garments fragrant before God unless they are inflamed with divine love and proceed from the fire of charity. Further, because the fervour or devotion of prayer is wont to be signified by the smell of frankincense, according to that in the Apocalypse, [[Apoc 8:4|the smoke of the incense of the prayers of the saints ascended up|Ascendit fumus aromatum de orationibus Sanctorum]], and in the Psalm, [[Ps 140:2|Let my prayer be directed as incense in thy sight|Dirigatur oratio mea sicut incensum in conspectu tuo]]: therefore the smell of those garments is as the smell of frankincense, since meritorious acts have the force of prayer, and obtain grace and glory; nay, without them prayer is ineffectual, according to what is written: [[Prov 28:9|He that turneth away his ears from hearing the law, his prayer shall be an abomination|Qui declinat aurem suam ne audiat legem, oratio ejus erit exsecrabilis]]. Therefore it is written: [[John 9:31|we know that God doth not hear sinners: but if a man be a server of God and doth his, will, him he heareth|Scimus quoniam peccatores Deus non audit; sed si quis cultor est Dei, et voluntatem ejus facit, hunc exaudit]].

paras.t: Hortus conclusus, soror mea, sponsa, hortus conclusus, fons signatus : id est, tu, Ecclesia, per similitudinem recte hortus vocaris; nec solum hortus, sed et hortus conclusus. Hortus es, quem ego hortulanus cœlestis colo, purgo, fecundo : in qua tanquam in pulcherrimo horto oriuntur flores virtutum, fructus actuum meritoriorum; gramina cœlestium ferculorum, id est gratiæ ecclesiasticorum sacramentorum, quibus homines, jumentis assimilati, seu tanquam pium obediensque jumentum effecti, reficiuntur; arbores fructuosæ atque frondosæ, id est homines virtuosi : in quo horto jugiter perseverat viriditas supernæ floritionis, ac fecunditatis internæ viror venustus. Hic hortus conclusus est, quia multiplici circumvallatus munimine : quia Salvator ponitur in eo murus et antemurale, et Dominus in circuitu ejus. Angelicæ quoque virtutes eum custodiunt, sed et prælati ipsius ac prædicatores, et viri sancti, pro communi bono Ecclesiæ semper solliciti ac orantes. Vallatur etiam et clauditur ac munitur hic hortus vallo caritatis, timore filiali, custodia cordis, circumspectione prudentiæ, quotidiano profectu, oratione assidua, documentis Scripturæ : ne hæretici, schismatici, infideles, iniqui, aut invisibiles hostes valeant eum ingredi et demoliri. Possunt tamen pulsare, atque forinsecus impugnare, et quasi primam januam introire suggerendo, corporaliterque vexare; sed consensum nequeunt extorquere, aut mentem dejicere, nisi ipsemet hortus iste, seu exsistentes in eo, sponte aperiant ac permittant. Ideo monet Apostolus : Nolite locum dare diabolo. Jacobus quoque : Resistite, inquit, diabolo, et fugiet a vobis.
paras.en: [[4:12|My sister, my spouse, is a garden enclosed, a garden enclosed, a fountain sealed up|Hortus conclusus, soror mea, sponsa, hortus conclusus, fons signatus]]: that is, thou, the Church, art rightly called a garden by likeness; and not only a garden, but a garden enclosed. Thou art a garden which I, the heavenly gardener, till, cleanse and make fruitful: in which, as in a most beautiful garden, spring up the flowers of the virtues and the fruits of meritorious acts; the grasses of heavenly fare, that is, the graces of the Church's sacraments, by which men are refreshed who are made like to beasts of burden, or rather made as it were a dutiful and obedient beast; and fruitful and leafy trees, that is, virtuous men: in which garden the greenness of heavenly flowering and the lovely verdure of inward fruitfulness abide continually. This garden is enclosed, because it is walled round with manifold defences: for [[Is 26:1|a saviour, a wall and a bulwark shall be set therein|Salvator ponitur in eo murus et antemurale]], and [[Ps 124:2|the Lord is round about|Dominus in circuitu ejus]] it. The angelic powers also guard it[[Ps 90:11||]], and so do its prelates and preachers, and holy men, ever solicitous and praying for the common good of the Church. This garden is also walled, closed and fortified by the rampart of charity, by filial fear, the guard of the heart, the circumspection of prudence, daily progress, assiduous prayer and the teachings of Scripture: lest heretics, schismatics, infidels, the wicked or invisible enemies be able to enter it and lay it waste. They can, however, knock and assail it from without, and as it were enter the first gate by suggestion, and vex it bodily; but they cannot extort consent or cast down the mind, unless this garden itself, or those who dwell in it, open of their own accord and allow it. Therefore the Apostle warns: [[Eph 4:27|Give not place to the devil|Nolite locum dare diabolo]]. James too: [[Jas 4:7|resist|Resistite]], he says, [[Jas 4:7|the devil: and he will fly from you|diabolo, et fugiet a vobis]].

paras.t: Fons signatus, id est opertus, ne aquæ immundæ, id est falsæ doctrinæ, fluant in eum. Dicitur ergo Ecclesia fons, quoniam aqua sapientiæ salutaris abundat in ea, fluenta divinorum charismatum, fons gratiæ, fons olei, fons luminis : quibus sancta mater Ecclesia potat, refocillat, et reficit filios suos et universos spiritualiter sitientes, ad eam pro salutis poculo accedentes, dicens : Omnes sitientes, venite ad aquas. Est etiam in Ecclesia fons Baptismi, fons contritionis et lacrimarum, fons evangelicæ legis, ex quo rivi sapientiæ undique derivantur. Et vocatur, fons signatus, ob causam prætactam, et etiam propter incomprehensibilem altitudinem sensuum ejus, et propter sacramentorum ejus mysteriorumque Christi imperscrutabilem profunditatem. Attamen fidelibus aliqualiter patet, imo omnibus exhibetur ac propinatur a prædicatoribus evangelicæ legis, qui sapientibus et insipientibus, fidelibus ac infidelibus debitores se esse fatentur. Unde scriptum est : Erit fons patens domui David, et habitantibus Jerusalem.
paras.en: [[4:12|a fountain sealed up|Fons signatus]], that is, covered, lest unclean waters, that is, false doctrine, flow into it. The Church, then, is called a fountain, since the water of saving wisdom abounds in her, the streams of the divine gifts, the fountain of grace, the fountain of oil, the fountain of light: with which holy Mother Church gives drink to, revives and refreshes her children and all who thirst spiritually and come to her for the cup of salvation, saying: [[Is 55:1|All you that thirst, come to the waters|Omnes sitientes, venite ad aquas]]. There is also in the Church the fountain of Baptism, the fountain of contrition and tears, the fountain of the law of the Gospel, from which streams of wisdom are drawn off on every side. And it is called [[4:12|a fountain sealed up|fons signatus]] for the reason touched on, and also because of the incomprehensible height of its senses, and the unsearchable depth of its sacraments and of the mysteries of Christ. Yet it lies open in some measure to the faithful; nay, it is shown and given to drink to all by the preachers of the law of the Gospel, who confess themselves debtors [[Rom 1:14|to the wise and to the unwise|sapientibus et insipientibus]], to the faithful and to the unfaithful. Hence it is written: [[Zach 13:1|there shall be a fountain open to the house of David, and to the inhabitants of Jerusalem|Erit fons patens domui David, et habitantibus Jerusalem]].

paras.t: Insuper, sicut in horto continentur quædam manducabilia, ut poma, pira, et uvæ; quædam medicinalia, ut aquæ, herbæ, et species aromaticæ; quædam etiam ad abluendum, irrigandum ac delectandum, ut fontes et rivi ac flores : sic in Ecclesia sunt plurimi cibi ac potus spirituales, et medicamina contra criminum vulnera, aquæ Baptismi, rivuli doctrinarum, et flores virtutum atque sententiarum.
paras.en: Moreover, as a garden holds some things to eat, as apples, pears and grapes; some medicinal things, as waters, herbs and aromatic spices; and some also for washing, watering and delight, as fountains, streams and flowers: so in the Church there are very many spiritual foods and drinks, and medicines against the wounds of sins, the waters of Baptism, the rivulets of doctrines, and the flowers of virtues and of sentences.

paras.t: Emissiones tuæ paradisus malorum punicorum cum pomorum fructibus. Emissiones horti istius deliciosi seu sanctæ Ecclesiæ, sunt ea quæ emittuntur ex ea, vel ipsi actus emittendi. Emittit itaque hortus iste ex se bonæ famæ odorem, virtutum fragrantiam, optimos fructus spiritus (de quibus ait Apostolus : Fructus spiritus est caritas, gaudium, pax, etc.), fluenta doctrinæ, miracula, signa, prodigia, et homines sanctos, virtuosos ac sapientes, per quos convertit quamplurimos. Istæ emissiones sunt paradisus malorum punicorum, id est deliciosa possessio, opulentia, atque suavitas malorum granatorum, id est pretiosa encænia, et exhibitio hominum caritate ardentium. quorum et multi pro fide amoreque sponsi, sanguinem suum fuderunt : sicque proprio rubricati cruore, recte dicuntur malogranata, quæ rubent extrinsecus, et suavi vigent odore, ac refectiva sunt dulciter ; sicut et martyres sancti ac homines fervidi, proximos exemplis suis alliciunt et accendunt, ac corda reficiunt devotorum. Ideo additur, Cum pomorum fructibus, id est cum fructuosa conversatione ædificationeque hominum quos lucrifaciunt Christo : qui sunt quasi cibaria, dum Christo incorporantur poma ejus, qui est lignum vitæ, lignum sapientiæ, lignum jugiter viride universarum virtutum, in medio paradisi, id est triumphantis ac militantis Ecclesiæ, situm.
paras.en: [[4:13|Thy plants are a paradise of pomegranates|Emissiones tuæ paradisus malorum punicorum]] [[4:13|with the fruits of the orchard|cum pomorum fructibus]]. The *emissions* [Latin *emissiones*, the things sent forth, which the Douay-Rheims renders *plants*] of this delightful garden, holy Church, are the things sent forth from her, or the very acts of sending forth. This garden, then, sends forth from itself the smell of good fame, the fragrance of the virtues, the best fruits of the spirit (of which the Apostle says: [[Gal 5:22|the fruit of the Spirit is, charity, joy, peace|Fructus spiritus est caritas, gaudium, pax]], etc.[[Gal 5:23||]]), streams of doctrine, miracles, signs, wonders, and holy, virtuous and wise men, through whom she converts very many. These emissions are [[4:13|a paradise of pomegranates|paradisus malorum punicorum]], that is, a delightful possession, abundance and sweetness of pomegranates: that is, precious *encænia* [things newly made, or dedications], and the showing forth of men burning with charity, many of whom have shed their blood for the faith and love of the Spouse: and so, reddened with their own blood, they are rightly called pomegranates, which are red outside, flourish with a sweet smell, and refresh sweetly; as the holy martyrs and fervent men draw and kindle their neighbours by their example and refresh the hearts of the devout. Therefore is added, [[4:13|with the fruits of the orchard|Cum pomorum fructibus]] [Latin *poma*, fruits of trees], that is, with the fruitful living and edification of the men whom they gain for Christ: who are as it were food, while they are incorporated, as his fruits, into him who is the tree of life, the tree of wisdom, the tree ever green with all the virtues, set in the midst of paradise[[Gen 2:9||]], that is, of the Church triumphant and militant.

paras.t: Cypri cum nardo. Cypri est hic nominativus numeri pluralis, ut sit sensus : Præfatæ emissiones tuæ, o sponsa, sunt cypri cum nardo, id est ita mihi acceptæ, ut arbores aromaticæ quæ cypri dicuntur, et herba quæ nardus vocatur, acceptæ sunt indigentibus atque utentibus eis. Cyprus quippe est aromatica arbor, in Ægypto crescens, cujus semen candidum ac odoriferum in oleo coquitur atque exprimitur, et inde unguentum regale optimumque efficitur. Ideo eos significat, qui de infidelitatis caligine ad fidei lumen conversi, oleo Spiritus Sancti unguntur, et igne tribulationis durius excoquuntur, ut sic unguentum Christo summo regi delectabile efficiantur : ita quod Dominus et Salvator per eos medetur vitiis proximorum. Isti quoque nardo inunguntur. Nardus namque est aromatica herba spicosa, odorifera, calida, et declivis, humilitatem caritate formatam, fructuosam, bonæque famæ diffusivam, significans : quam plane virtutem jugiter amplectuntur, qui oleo Spiritus Sancti fuerint uncti. Cyprus etiam semine suo odorifero et candenti potest continentiam designare, præsertim quoniam Christus in Evangelio de triplici castimonia, scilicet virginali, viduali, et conjugali, sub nomine seminis loquens : Semen, inquit, cecidit in terram, et ortum, fecit fructum, aliud centesimum, aliud sexagesimum, aliud trigesimum.
paras.en: [[4:13|Cypress with spikenard|Cypri cum nardo]]. *Cypri* is here a nominative plural, so that the sense is: These emissions of thine, O spouse, are [[4:13|cypress with spikenard|cypri cum nardo]], that is, as acceptable to me as the aromatic trees called *cypri* and the herb called spikenard are acceptable to those who need and use them. For the cyprus is an aromatic tree growing in Egypt, whose white and fragrant seed is boiled in oil and pressed out, and from it a royal and excellent ointment is made. It therefore signifies those who, turned from the darkness of unbelief to the light of faith, are anointed with the oil of the Holy Ghost and boiled hard in the fire of tribulation, so that they may thus be made an ointment delightful to Christ the supreme King: so that through them the Lord and Saviour heals the vices of their neighbours. These are also anointed with spikenard. For spikenard is an aromatic herb, spiky, fragrant, warm and low-growing, signifying humility formed by charity, fruitful, and spreading good fame: which virtue they plainly embrace continually who have been anointed with the oil of the Holy Ghost. The cyprus, too, by its fragrant and shining white seed, can signify continence, especially since Christ in the Gospel, speaking under the name of seed of threefold chastity, namely virginal, widowed and conjugal, says: The seed, he says, fell on the ground, and springing up yielded fruit, [[Matt 13:8|some an hundred fold, some sixty fold, and some thirty fold|aliud centesimum, aliud sexagesimum, aliud trigesimum]][[Mark 4:8||]] [the margin gives Matt. xiii, 8 and Mark iv, 8; Denis's opening words, *et ortum fecit fructum*, are closer to Luke 8:8].

paras.t: Insuper emissiones tuæ, o Ecclesia, sunt nardus et crocus. Quid per nardum denotetur, jam patuit. Per crocum vero (quæ est herba folia coloris aurei habens, ac tanti fervoris est ut febricitantibus refrigerium præstet) designantur personæ quæ caritatis fervore ac sapientiæ calefactivo fulgore ornantur : ita ut in se ipsis ac aliis æstum concupiscentiæ et cupiditatis exstinguant, desideriumque supernorum accendant bonorum, ac aureum exemplaritatis producant ornatum. Quibus humilitas valde necessaria esse cognoscitur : propter quod hic nardus repetitur. Nam et per nardum potest dominicæ memoria passionis intelligi. Quia unguentum nardi, rigorem depellit algentium, et membra ipso inuncta calefacere perhibetur; sic et meditatio passionis Christi intenta, accendit ad imitationem vestigiorum ipsius, torpore acediæ ac timoris excluso : quæ meditatio tam accommoda est ad spiritualem profectum, sicut humilitas.
paras.en: Moreover thy emissions, O Church, are [[4:14|Spikenard and saffron|nardus et crocus]]. What is denoted by spikenard has already appeared. By saffron (which is a herb with leaves of a golden colour, and of such heat that it gives relief to the feverish) are signified persons adorned with the fervour of charity and the warming brightness of wisdom: so that in themselves and in others they quench the heat of concupiscence and covetousness, kindle the desire of heavenly goods, and bring forth the golden ornament of example. For these humility is known to be very necessary: and for this reason spikenard is repeated here. For by spikenard the remembrance of the Lord's passion can also be understood. For as the ointment of spikenard is said to drive out the stiffness of those numb with cold and to warm the limbs anointed with it, so too intent meditation on the passion of Christ kindles to the imitation of his footsteps, shutting out the torpor of sloth and of fear: and this meditation is as well fitted to spiritual progress as humility.

paras.t: Fistula et cinnamomum. Fistula seu casia, corticem habet durum, purpureum et amarum, valens ad curandum viscerum afflictionem, estque brevis staturæ : idcirco significat eos qui arduam pœnitentiæ exercitationem incedunt, et sua ac proximorum peccata acerbe deplorant, sicque purpureo caritatis splendore venusti sunt. At vero cinnamomum aromatica arbor est, nigri cinereive coloris, virtute ac odore præcipua, et frutice brevis, ad medicamina præstantior fistula : cujus etiam cinnamomi cortex, est pretiosus, instar cannæ rotundus ac gracilis. Idcirco per cinnamomum expressi sunt hi qui ex caritate et humilitate obediunt prompte, propter quod valde virtuosi ac boni odoris censentur, curativi superbiæ ac inobedientiæ proximorum. Universos hos et sanctas eorum virtutes emittit, gignit, diffundit Ecclesia, cum universis lignis Libani, id est sicut et ceteros fideles, virtute sublimes, ac gratiæ candidatos. Libanus enim mons est in quo pulchræ et altæ arbores crescunt, et candidatio interpretatur.
paras.en: [[4:14|sweet cane and cinnamon|Fistula et cinnamomum]]. The *fistula* [Latin, "pipe"; the Douay-Rheims's *sweet cane*], or cassia, has a hard bark, purple and bitter, good for curing affliction of the bowels, and is short of stature: therefore it signifies those who undertake the hard exercise of penance, and bitterly bewail their own and their neighbours' sins, and are thus made comely with the purple splendour of charity. Cinnamon, again, is an aromatic tree, black or ash-coloured, eminent in virtue and smell, a low shrub, better for medicines than the *fistula*; and the bark of this cinnamon is precious, round and slender like a reed. Therefore by cinnamon are expressed those who obey promptly out of charity and humility, for which reason they are judged very virtuous and of good odour, healers of the pride and disobedience of their neighbours. All these, and their holy virtues, the Church sends forth, begets and spreads abroad, [[4:14|with all the trees of Libanus|cum universis lignis Libani]], that is, as also the other faithful, lofty in virtue and whitened with grace. For Libanus is a mountain on which beautiful and tall trees grow, and it is interpreted *whitening*.

paras.t: Insuper, o Ecclesia, emissiones tuæ sunt myrrha et aloe cum omnibus primis unguentis. Myrrha, est arbor Arabiæ, habens in altitudine cubitos quinque, similis spinæ, guttaque ejus viridis et amara; sponte emanans, est pretiosior ea quæ cortice læso elicitur : ideo mortificationem carnis designat, quæ in principio sentitur amara, sed spe fructus æterni florescit; et pungit, ut spina, sed a vitiorum præservat putredine; et tunc maxime complacet Deo, dum tempore sanitatis ac juventutis sponte assumitur. Porro aloe est arbor pretiosa, præclari suavissimique odoris : propter quod antiqui lignum ejus, loco thymiamatis olim circa altaria adolebant seu incendebant. Cujus succus est amarissimus, tamen unguentis plurimis congruus: unde et corpora mortua a putrefactione præservat, sicut et myrrha. Hinc in Evangelio legitur Nicodemus mixturam myrrhæ et aloes quasi libras centum attulisse ad ungendum corpus dominicum, de cujus resurrectione fidem non habebat explicitam. Interdum itaque myrrha et aloe pro arboribus, interdum pro earum fructibus seu effectibus accipiuntur : et nunc personæ exprimuntur contemplativæ dignissimæ, quæ vitæ hujus deplangunt vitia et ærumnas, et optimus Christi odor sunt undique, atque se ipsos ac alios ab interiori præservant corruptione, sua conversatione orationeque sancta. Per omnia vero prima (id est nobiliora) unguenta, intelliguntur contemperationes actuum altissimarum virtutum, ut fidei, spei, caritatis, atque donorum.
paras.en: Moreover, O Church, thy emissions are [[4:14|myrrh and aloes with all the chief perfumes|myrrha et aloe cum omnibus primis unguentis]]. Myrrh is a tree of Arabia, five cubits in height, like a thorn, and its gum is green and bitter; that which flows of its own accord is more precious than that drawn out by wounding the bark: therefore it signifies the mortification of the flesh, which at first is felt to be bitter, but flourishes in the hope of eternal fruit; and it pricks like a thorn, but preserves from the rottenness of vices; and it pleases God most when it is taken up of one's own accord in time of health and youth. Aloe, again, is a precious tree, of a splendid and very sweet smell: for which reason the ancients used once to burn its wood around the altars in place of incense. Its juice is very bitter, yet suited to many ointments: hence it also preserves dead bodies from putrefaction, as myrrh does. Hence we read in the Gospel that Nicodemus brought [[John 19:39|a mixture of myrrh and aloes, about an hundred pound weight|mixturam myrrhæ et aloes quasi libras centum]] to anoint the Lord's body, though he had no explicit faith in his resurrection. Myrrh and aloes, then, are taken sometimes for the trees, sometimes for their fruits or effects: and here are expressed most worthy contemplative persons, who bewail the vices and miseries of this life, and are everywhere the good odour of Christ, and preserve themselves and others from inward corruption by their holy living and prayer. By all the chief (that is, the nobler) perfumes are understood the blendings [*contemperationes*] of the acts of the highest virtues, as of faith, hope and charity, and of the gifts.

paras.t: Fons hortorum, puteus aquarum viventium, quæ fluunt impetu de Libano. Quidam exponunt hæc tanquam sint verba sponsæ sponsum laudantis, eo quod omnia bona præfata ex ipso sponso tanquam ex splendidissimo, opulentissimo ac munificentissimo fonte principaliter oriantur ; qui etiam est puteus, id est, imperscrutabilis quædam abyssus aquarum viventium, id est supernorum charismatum, vitam gratiæ conferentium ac vitam gloriæ promerentium. Gregorius vero, Anselmus, Beda, ac alii exponunt ita, ut sint adhuc verba Christi, sponsam, id est Ecclesiam, commendantis : quæ est fons hortorum, quoniam universalis Ecclesia particulares Ecclesias instruit, irrigat, perfundit, fecundat, sicut fons hortos. Est quoque puteus aquarum viventium, id est profunda origo Baptismi ac sacramenti Confessionis, in quibus cuncta abluuntur peccata, sapientia quoque, gratia ac virtutes infunduntur et reparantur : quæ aquæ dicuntur vivæ, quoniam jugiter fluunt a sacramentis suas virtutes indeficienter habentibus : quemadmodum aquæ vivæ vocantur, quæ profluunt ex vena fontana incessante, fecunda, et erumpente, diffundenteque rivos ; ad distinctionem aquarum quæ ex pluviis, nivibus, stagnisve manant ad tempus, non jugiter.
paras.en: [[4:15|The fountain of gardens: the well of living waters, which run with a strong stream from Libanus.|Fons hortorum, puteus aquarum viventium, quæ fluunt impetu de Libano.]] Some expound these as the words of the bride praising the Bridegroom, because all the goods aforesaid spring principally from the Bridegroom himself as from a most splendid, most opulent and most munificent fountain; who is also [[4:15|the well|puteus]], that is, an unsearchable abyss, [[4:15|of living waters|aquarum viventium]], that is, of heavenly gifts, which confer the life of grace and merit the life of glory. But Gregory, Anselm, Bede and others expound it so that these are still the words of Christ commending the bride, that is, the Church: who is [[4:15|The fountain of gardens|fons hortorum]], since the universal Church instructs, waters, bedews and makes fruitful the particular Churches, as a fountain does gardens. She is also [[4:15|the well of living waters|puteus aquarum viventium]], that is, the deep source of Baptism and of the sacrament of Confession, in which all sins are washed away, and wisdom, grace and virtues are poured in and restored: and these waters are called living, since they flow continually from sacraments which hold their power unfailingly: just as those waters are called living which flow from a spring-vein that is ceaseless, abundant and bursting forth, sending out streams; as distinct from waters that come from rains, snows or pools for a time, not continually.

paras.t: Denique aquæ istæ fluunt impetu de Libano, id est cito et copiose de puritate interna et candidatione mentali, vel ex Scriptura divina mundissima, vel ex gratia gratificante habituali, quæ dicitur essentiam creaturæ intellectualis perficere, et in habitus virtutum ac donorum ramificare. Fluunt quoque de Libano, id est a capite Christo, monte altissimo, in quo est gratia capitis, se derivans ac diffundens in membra : de cujus plenitudine accepimus omnes. Postremo, impetu fluunt de Libano, id est a superpulcherrimo Spiritu Sancto, cujus impetus lætificat civitatem Dei.
paras.en: Lastly, these waters [[4:15|run with a strong stream from Libanus|fluunt impetu de Libano]], that is, swiftly and abundantly, from inward purity and whiteness of mind, or from the most pure divine Scripture, or from habitual sanctifying grace [*gratia gratificans*, the grace that makes one pleasing to God], which is said to perfect the essence of the intellectual creature and to branch out into the habits of the virtues and gifts. They flow also from Libanus, that is, from Christ the head, the loftiest mountain, in whom is the grace of headship [*gratia capitis*, the grace Christ has as head of the Church], deriving and pouring itself into the members: [[John 1:16|of his fulness we all have received|de cujus plenitudine accepimus omnes]]. Finally, they flow with a strong stream from Libanus, that is, from the Holy Ghost, beautiful above all, whose [[Ps 45:5|stream of the river maketh the city of God joyful|impetus lætificat civitatem Dei]].

paras.t: Surge, Aquilo ; et veni, Auster. Ista sunt verba sponsi. Solet autem per Aquilonem, qui est ventus durissimus ac constringens, diabolus designari ; item adversitas, seu gravis tentatio, torpor quoque pigritiæ, et frigus invidiæ, igni caritatis contrarium. Per Austrum vero, qui est dulcis et calidus ventus, accipitur Spiritus Sanctus, seu gratia et caritas ; item prosperitas ac consolatio spiritualis.
paras.en: [[4:16|Arise, O north wind, and come, O south wind|Surge, Aquilo ; et veni, Auster]]. These are the words of the Bridegroom. Now by the north wind, which is a very harsh and binding wind, the devil is wont to be signified; also adversity, or grievous temptation, and also the torpor of sloth and the cold of envy, contrary to the fire of charity. By the south wind, which is a sweet and warm wind, is taken the Holy Ghost, or grace and charity; also prosperity and spiritual consolation.

paras.t: Potest itaque locus iste dupliciter explanari. Christus etenim interdum permittit Ecclesiam suam per adversa ac prospera impugnari : quatenus nec adversis frangatur, nec prosperis extollatur ; sed in utrisque constans ac superans, diffundat virtutum suarum fragrantiam, et supernorum suavitatem donorum quæ habet, exemplariter manifestet. Itaque, Surge, id est, exsurge et vade, o Aquilo ; et veni, Auster, id est, prosperitas mundi, perfla hortum meum, id est, super Ecclesiam te effunde ; et fluent aromata illius, id est, virtutes ejus innotescent, fragrabunt, ac prævalebunt. Porro interdum Salvator ad tempus eripit et præservat Ecclesiam suam a dæmonum tentamentis, adversitatibus, et malignis spiritibus ; sicque sensus est : Surge, id est, recede, o Aquilo, id est, dæmon cum machinationibus tuis ; et veni, Auster, id est, tu, Spiritus Sancte, cum donis tuis visita hortum meum, id est Ecclesiam ; et fluent aromata illius, id est, virtutes ejus ac merita abundabunt, seque diffundent : quoniam sine ope et affluentia actualique motione tua nihil valet Ecclesia, nec fluere seu meritorie agere queunt ejus aromata.
paras.en: This place, then, can be explained in two ways. For Christ sometimes permits his Church to be assailed by adversity and by prosperity, so that she may be neither broken by adversity nor lifted up by prosperity; but, constant and victorious in both, may spread abroad the fragrance of her virtues, and show forth by example the sweetness of the heavenly gifts she has. So: [[4:16|Arise|Surge]], that is, rise up and go, [[4:16|O north wind|Aquilo]]; [[4:16|and come, O south wind|et veni, Auster]], that is, prosperity of the world, [[4:16|blow through my garden|perfla hortum meum]], that is, pour thyself out upon the Church; [[4:16|and let the aromatical spices thereof flow|et fluent aromata illius]] [Denis reads *fluent*, "shall flow", for the Vulgate's *fluant*], that is, her virtues will become known, will be fragrant and will prevail. Again, the Saviour sometimes for a time snatches away and preserves his Church from the temptations of the demons, from adversities and from evil spirits; and so the sense is: [[4:16|Arise|Surge]], that is, withdraw, [[4:16|O north wind|Aquilo]], that is, demon, with thy machinations; [[4:16|and come, O south wind|et veni, Auster]], that is, thou, Holy Ghost, with thy gifts visit [[4:16|my garden|hortum meum]], that is, the Church; [[4:16|and let the aromatical spices thereof flow|et fluent aromata illius]], that is, her virtues and merits will abound and spread themselves abroad: since without thy help and abundance and actual moving the Church avails nothing, nor can her spices flow, that is, act meritoriously.

4.title: DECLARATIO EJUSDEM CAPITULI QUARTI, DE CHRISTO ET ANIMA VIRTUOSA.
4.title_en: Declaration of the same fourth chapter: of Christ and the virtuous soul

paras.t: Qui a cœlesti appetit sponso laudari, laudibus ejus devote insistat. Nam sponsa particularis, anima amorosa, quæ præcedenti capitulo sponsum cœlestem sincera laudavit intentione, nunc commendatur ab ipso. Etenim ipse in Evangelio contestatur : Qui me confessus fuerit coram hominibus, confitebor et ego eum coram Patre meo. Itaque ait : Quam pulchra es, amica mea ! quam pulchra es ! Quasi dicat : Pulchritudinem meam admirata es ac laudasti, et ejus comparatione te fœdam et contemptibilem reputasti, ac mihi displicere vereris ; sed noli metuere, quoniam qui se parvi pendit ac despicit, a me magni penditur et laudatur, sicut in Evangelio sum locutus : Quod hominibus altum est, abominatio est ante Deum. Nec dubium quin econtra. Considerata ergo tua naturali imbecillitate ac fragilitate, mira et magna est pulchritudo, fortitudo, stabilitas tua, quas per dona gratiæ, et laborem tuum, diligentiamque sortita es ; et tanto commendabilior est pulchritudo, perfectio, virtuositas, sapientia tua, per gratiam et conatum tuum adepta, quanto major est naturalis defectuositas tua : et tamen naturalis pulchritudo tua, o anima rationalis, qua superbenedictæ Trinitatis imago vocaris, utpote splendore intellectus ornata, libertate voluntatis fulcita, tenacitate memoriæ decorata, omnem sensibilem pulchritudinem, etiam solis et lunæ ac siderum, vincit. Vere sublimiter pulchra es, quæ a tantæ pulchritudinis sponso digna es tam reverenter laudari. Denique, taliter pulchra est anima, quæ passionum fœditate non inquinatur, quæ carnalitati fortiter dominatur ; cujus ratio per sapientiam, prudentiam, scientiam splendet, cujus voluntas caritate Dei et proximi ardet, cujus cor circa Deum omnino affigitur, atque in divinis totaliter occupatur ; quæ Deo exhibet conscientiæ puritatem, et proximis ædificationis fulgorem, quæ in verbis ac sensibus, in vultu, in progressu servat moralitatem.
paras.en: Let him who longs to be praised by the heavenly Bridegroom devote himself earnestly to his praises. For the particular bride, the loving soul, who in the preceding chapter praised the heavenly Bridegroom with sincere intention, is now commended by him. For he himself bears witness in the Gospel: He [[Matt 10:32|that shall confess me before men, I will also confess him before my Father|Qui me confessus fuerit coram hominibus, confitebor et ego eum coram Patre meo]][[Luke 12:8||]]. And so he says: [[4:1|How beautiful art thou, my love, how beautiful art thou!|Quam pulchra es, amica mea ! quam pulchra es !]] As if to say: Thou hast marvelled at my beauty and praised it, and in comparison with it thou hast thought thyself foul and contemptible, and thou fearest to displease me; but do not be afraid, since he who thinks little of himself and despises himself is thought much of by me and praised, as I said in the Gospel: [[Luke 16:15|that which is high to men is an abomination before God|Quod hominibus altum est, abominatio est ante Deum]]. And no doubt the reverse is true as well. Considering, then, thy natural weakness and frailty, wonderful and great is thy beauty, thy strength, thy steadfastness, which thou hast gained through the gifts of grace and through thy labour and diligence; and thy beauty, perfection, virtue and wisdom, won by grace and by thy own striving, are the more praiseworthy the greater is thy natural defectiveness.
