And yet thy natural beauty, O rational soul, by which thou art called the image of the superblessed Trinity, adorned as thou art with the splendour of understanding, upheld by freedom of will, graced with a retentive memory, surpasses all the beauty of the senses, even that of the sun and moon and stars. Truly thou art sublimely beautiful, who art worthy to be praised so reverently by a Bridegroom of such beauty. In short, that soul is so beautiful which is not defiled by the foulness of the passions, which rules strongly over the flesh; whose reason shines with wisdom, prudence and knowledge, whose will burns with charity towards God and neighbour, whose heart is wholly fixed upon God and wholly occupied with divine things; which shows God purity of conscience and shows its neighbours the brightness of edification; which keeps good conduct in words and senses, in countenance and in bearing.

paras.t: Oculi tui columbarum : quoniam nosti quantum detester omnem calliditatem, duplicitatem, impudentiam, obliquitatem, hypocrisim. Nam sicut similitudo parit concordiam, complacentiam, et amorem ; sic dissimilitudo origo est discordiæ, displicentiæ, atque aversionis. Hinc ego in natura deitatis, infinitæ simplicitatis exsistens, et essentialiter sanctus ac virtuosus, simplicitatem diligo columbinam, ac puram mentis intentionem ; duplicitatem vero, simulationem, fraudem, versutiam toto corde abhorreo. Absque eo quod intrinsecus latet, id est præter tuam secretissimam exercitationem internam, qua supergloriosissimæ Trinitatis gloriam contemplaris, et emanationem ac communicationem ejus ad intra, naturalem, superliberalissimam, ac superplenissimam, mutuam quoque intuitionem, dilectionem, complacentiam et fruitionem trium supervenerabilium Personarum : qualiter unaquæque æterna, increata, incircumscripta, et penitus infinite perfecta Persona, aliam cum infinita jucunditate ac claritate invariabiliter intuetur, cum infinito ardore diligit atque amplectitur, et sibi invicem superdulcissime complacent, ac se mutuo superdeliciosissime perfruuntur, tamque superbeatissimam et supervoluptuosissimam ducunt ac possident vitam.
paras.en: [[4:1|thy eyes are doves' eyes|Oculi tui columbarum]]: for thou knowest how I loathe all cunning, doubleness, shamelessness, crookedness and hypocrisy. For as likeness begets concord, good pleasure and love, so unlikeness is the origin of discord, displeasure and aversion. Hence I, existing in the nature of the Godhead, which is of infinite simplicity, and being essentially holy and virtuous, love the simplicity of the dove and pure intention of mind; but doubleness, pretence, fraud and craft I abhor with my whole heart. [[4:1|besides what is hid within|Absque eo quod intrinsecus latet]]: that is, besides thy most secret inward exercise, in which thou contemplatest the glory of the superglorious Trinity, and its emanation and communication within itself [Latin ad intra: the processions of the divine Persons within the Godhead, as against God's works outside it], natural, superabundantly liberal and superabundantly full; and also the mutual beholding, love, good pleasure and enjoyment of the three most venerable Persons: how each eternal, uncreated, uncircumscribed and wholly, infinitely perfect Person unchangeably beholds the other with infinite delight and clearness, loves and embraces it with infinite ardour, and how they take most sweet pleasure in one another and most delightfully enjoy one another, and so lead and possess a life supremely blessed and supremely delightful.

paras.t: Capilli tui sicut greges caprarum. Capilli animæ virtuosæ, sunt contemplationes, meditationes, et cogitationes ex intellectu immediate nascentes, affectiones quoque et dilectiones ex voluntate progredientes : quæ dum circa Deum et creaturas ordinate versantur, ita quod ex consideratione et affectione creaturarum, ad Creatoris notitiam, admirationem, dilectionem consurgunt, atque ex Creatoris contemplatione et amore intenso, creata hæc sensibilia et terrena parvi pendunt ac aspernantur, et deserunt, celeriterque ad Deum resiliunt et conscendunt ; tunc ordinatæ, et pulchræ, copiosæque sunt, et veloces sicut greges caprarum. Ideo quidquid eminentiæ aut decoris in rebus creatis conspicimus, mox ad Creatoris notitiam referamus : quoniam quidquid bonitatis, pulchritudinis, perfectionis in entibus est creatis, in Deo infinite perfectius gloriosiusque consistit. Similiter quidquid amabilitatis aut delectabilitatis in creaturis se nobis obtulerit, ad summi infinitique boni ordinemus amorem, tamque incomparabiliter et ardenter afficiamur ad illud superpulcherrimum, ac superdulcissimum, infinitumque bonum, ut nil aliud nisi in ipso et secundum ipsius voluntatem amemus, ne impleatur in nobis illud Sapientiæ : Creaturæ Dei factæ sunt in odium, et in tentationem animæ hominum, et in muscipulam pedibus insipientium.
paras.en: [[4:1|Thy hair is as flocks of goats|Capilli tui sicut greges caprarum]]. The hairs of the virtuous soul are the contemplations, meditations and thoughts that spring directly from the intellect, and also the affections and loves that proceed from the will. When these are busied in due order about God and creatures, so that from the consideration of creatures and affection for them they rise up to the knowledge, wonder and love of the Creator, and from the contemplation and intense love of the Creator they think little of these created things of sense and earth, scorn them and leave them, and swiftly spring back and climb up to God: then they are well ordered, beautiful and abundant, and swift like flocks of goats. Therefore whatever excellence or grace we see in created things, let us at once refer it to the knowledge of the Creator, since whatever goodness, beauty and perfection there is in created beings exists in God in an infinitely more perfect and glorious way. Likewise whatever lovableness or delightfulness offers itself to us in creatures, let us direct it to the love of the highest and infinite good, and let us be drawn so incomparably and ardently towards that supremely beautiful, supremely sweet and infinite good that we love nothing else except in it and according to its will; lest there be fulfilled in us that word of Wisdom: [[Wis 14:11|the creatures of God are turned to an abomination, and a temptation to the souls of men, and a snare to the feet of the unwise|Creaturæ Dei factæ sunt in odium, et in tentationem animæ hominum, et in muscipulam pedibus insipientium]].

paras.t: Dentes tui sicut greges tonsarum, quæ ascenderunt de lavacro. Anima rationalis, per intellectum et voluntatem reflexiva est super proprios actus et rediens ad se ipsam : ideo considerare debet proprios actus et examinare an vere sint virtuosi et puri, ac dijudicare se ipsam. Talis ergo discussio, examinatio, discretio, dijudicatio propriorum actuum interiorum et exteriorum ac sui ipsius, sunt dentes animæ veraciter sapientis : qui ovibus tonsis ac lotis ordinatæ incedentibus comparantur : quia sicut ab ovibus talibus ablatæ sunt lanæ et sordes, et confusi incessus sive discursus ; sic præfatæ discussiones et considerationes a vitiis sunt mundatæ, et culpas admixtas ab actibus animæ separant, ipsamque animam purgant, ac ordinant in se ipsa et actibus suis : quod prorsus salubre est, quum dicat Apostolus, Si nos ipsos dijudicaremus, non utique judicaremur. Hinc per Aggæum Dominus jubet : Ponite corda vestra super vias vestras. Et in Proverbiis legitur : Cogitationes justorum, judicia. Hoc est quod jubet et Moyses : Custodi temetipsum et animam tuam sollicite. Quod quam acceptum sit Deo, constat per id quod ipse Dominus contestatur ad Jeremiam : Si separaveris pretiosum a vili, quasi os meum eris. Istud sanctus Job egit, qui dixit : Vias meas in conspectu Dei arguam, et ipse erit salvator meus. Nempe qui ita se discutit, lavat utique per singulas noctes culparum lectum animæ suæ, et thalamum mentis præparat sponso, implens illud Psalmi : Quæ dicitis in cordibus vestris, in cubilibus vestris compungimini.
paras.en: [[4:2|Thy teeth as flocks of sheep, that are shorn, which come up from the washing|Dentes tui sicut greges tonsarum, quæ ascenderunt de lavacro]]. The rational soul, through intellect and will, can turn back upon its own acts and return to itself; therefore it ought to consider its own acts and examine whether they are truly virtuous and pure, and to judge itself. Such sifting, examination, discernment and judgment of one's own acts, inward and outward, and of oneself, are the teeth of a truly wise soul. They are compared to sheep that are shorn and washed and that go along in good order: for as from such sheep the wool and the dirt have been taken away, and their confused wandering and running about, so the sifting and considerations we have spoken of are cleansed of vices, and separate the faults mixed in with the soul's acts, and purge the soul itself, and set it in order within itself and in its acts. This is wholly wholesome, since the Apostle says: [[1 Cor 11:31|if we would judge ourselves, we should not be judged|Si nos ipsos dijudicaremus, non utique judicaremur]]. Hence the Lord commands through Aggeus: [[Agg 1:5|Set your hearts to consider your ways|Ponite corda vestra super vias vestras]] [literally, "set your hearts upon your ways"]. And in Proverbs we read: [[Prov 12:5|The thoughts of the just are judgments|Cogitationes justorum, judicia]]. This is what Moses too commands: [[Deut 4:9|Keep thyself|Custodi temetipsum]] [[Deut 4:9|and thy soul carefully|et animam tuam sollicite]]. How acceptable this is to God is clear from what the Lord himself declares to Jeremias: If [[Jer 15:19|thou wilt separate the precious from the vile, thou shalt be as my mouth|separaveris pretiosum a vili, quasi os meum eris]]. This holy Job did, who said: [[Job 13:15|I will reprove my ways in his sight|Vias meas in conspectu Dei arguam]] [Denis reads "in the sight of God"], [[Job 13:16|And he shall be my saviour|et ipse erit salvator meus]]. Indeed he who sifts himself in this way washes every night the bed of his soul from its faults[[Ps 6:7||]], and makes ready the chamber of his mind for the Bridegroom, fulfilling that word of the Psalm: [[Ps 4:5|the things you say in your hearts, be sorry for them upon your beds|Quæ dicitis in cordibus vestris, in cubilibus vestris compungimini]].

paras.t: Omnes gemellis fetibus, et sterilis non est inter eas : id est, prætactæ discretivæ examinationes sui ipsius, actuumque suorum, duplicem habent fecunditatem : quia in se sunt laudabiles, meritoriæ, et sapientiales ; et alios animæ actus spiritualiter circumcidunt, purificant et fecundant. Hinc per discretionem compendiosius proficit homo : prout sanctus pater noster gloriosus Antonius dixit, quod nulla virtus tam recto ac brevi tramite ducit hominem ad perfectionem, sicut discretio.
paras.en: [[4:2|all with twins, and there is none barren among them|Omnes gemellis fetibus, et sterilis non est inter eas]]: that is, the discerning examinations of oneself and of one's acts, touched on above, have a twofold fruitfulness: for in themselves they are praiseworthy, meritorious and wise; and they spiritually circumcise, purify and make fruitful the soul's other acts. Hence through discretion a man makes progress by a shorter way, as our holy father, the glorious Antony, said: that no virtue leads a man by so straight and short a path to perfection as discretion [Latin discretio: the discernment by which one weighs and orders one's acts; the saying of St Antony is told in Cassian's Conferences, II].

paras.t: Sicut vitta coccinea labia tua : quoniam sicut vitta talis constringit capillos ne defluant : sic anima amorosa, ne sponsum offendat in aliquo, timorate comprimit labia sua, ne ad inutilia aperiantur ; sicque verba inutilia, nociva, perversa, corde concepta, refrenat, ne effluant. Qui enim moderatur labia sua, prudentissimus est. Qui autem inconsideratus est ad loquendum, sentiet mala : patet siquidem jaculis hostium malignorum, dicente Scriptura : Sicut urbs patens et absque murorum ambitu, ita homo qui non potest in loquendo cohibere spiritum suum. Hæc labiorum repressio, est animæ contemplativæ necessaria valde, ne per inutilem superfluumque sermonem, incurrat distractionem et sponsi offensam, sicque amittat ipsius allocutionem internam. Nec solum claudenda sunt corporalia labia a locutione vocali inordinata ; sed et labia interiora, quibus verbum mentale profertur interius, sunt præservanda ab omni cogitatione non bona : quoniam cogitationes verba sunt coram Deo, qui loquitur per Michæam. Væ qui cogitatis inutile : atque per Jeremiam, Usquequo morabuntur in te cogitationes noxiæ ? et item per Isaiam, Auferte malum cogitationum vestrarum ab oculis meis. Et eloquium tuum dulce : quia interna locutione Deum intra te laudas, exoras, meditaris, ac contemplaris ; verba quoque tua vocalia ex caritate aliisque procedunt virtutibus ideo dulcia sunt. Virtus namque ex sua natura delectabilis est, et dulcis in actu suo ; sed quod laboriosa ac dura sentitur, ex nostra infectione contingit, sicut asserit Augustinus : Panis in fastidio est, delectat venenum.
paras.en: [[4:3|Thy lips are as a scarlet lace|Sicut vitta coccinea labia tua]]: for as such a band binds the hair so that it does not hang loose, so the loving soul, lest she offend the Bridegroom in anything, fearfully presses her lips together so that they are not opened to useless things; and so she reins in useless, harmful and perverse words conceived in the heart, so that they do not flow out. For [[Prov 10:19|he that refraineth his lips, is most wise|Qui enim moderatur labia sua, prudentissimus est]]. But [[Prov 13:3|he that hath no guard on his speech shall meet with evils|Qui autem inconsideratus est ad loquendum, sentiet mala]]: for he lies open to the darts of malicious enemies, as Scripture says: [[Prov 25:28|As a city that lieth open and is not compassed with walls, so is a man that cannot refrain his own spirit in speaking.|Sicut urbs patens et absque murorum ambitu, ita homo qui non potest in loquendo cohibere spiritum suum]] This restraint of the lips is very necessary for the contemplative soul, lest through useless and superfluous talk she fall into distraction and offend the Bridegroom, and so lose his inward speaking to her. And not only must the bodily lips be closed against disordered spoken words; the inward lips too, by which the word of the mind is uttered within, must be kept from every thought that is not good, since thoughts are words before God, who says through Micheas: [[Mich 2:1|Woe to you that devise that which is unprofitable|Væ qui cogitatis inutile]]; and through Jeremias: [[Jer 4:14|how long shall hurtful thoughts abide in thee?|Usquequo morabuntur in te cogitationes noxiæ]] and again through Isaias: [[Is 1:16|take away the evil of your devices from my eyes|Auferte malum cogitationum vestrarum ab oculis meis]]. [[4:3|and thy speech sweet|Et eloquium tuum dulce]]: because by inward speech thou praisest God within thee, prayest to him, meditatest and contemplatest; and thy spoken words also proceed from charity and the other virtues, and therefore they are sweet. For virtue by its nature is delightful, and sweet in its act; that it is felt to be laborious and hard comes from our infection, as Augustine says: Bread is loathsome, poison delights.

paras.t: Sicut fragmen mali punici, ita genæ tuæ. Genæ corporales, sunt quasi duo parietes, os et linguam inter se continentes. Spirituales vero genæ, sunt memoria præteritorum, ac providentia : inter quæ continetur intuitio præsentium. Porro malum punicum intus est candidum, ac forinsecus rubicundum. Intus etiam continet grana, et redolet extra. Dum itaque memoria recolit dominicam passionem, futurum judicium, et infernale supplicium, instar mali punici rubet foris ; dum vero providentia cogitat gaudia regni cœlestis, puritatemque cordis, ac veritatis splendorem, candet intus. Dum autem malum punicum frangitur, grana ejus mox elabuntur : ita dum anima veraciter virtuosa adversitatibus circumvallatur, virtutes quæ in ea sunt, declarantur, ac suaviter eos qui bene perpendunt, afficiunt. Tunc enim caritatem ostendit, patientiam exhibet, humilitatem declarat, mansuetudinemque diffundit, et orat pro inimico, imo et condolet ei, tanquam interficienti propriam animam.
paras.en: [[4:3|Thy cheeks are as a piece of a pomegranate|Sicut fragmen mali punici, ita genæ tuæ]]. The bodily cheeks are like two walls holding the mouth and tongue between them. The spiritual cheeks are the memory of things past and foresight, between which is held the beholding of things present. Now the pomegranate is white within and red without. It also holds seeds within, and gives off its fragrance outside. So when the memory recalls the Lord's passion, the judgment to come and the punishment of hell, it is red outside like the pomegranate; but when foresight thinks on the joys of the heavenly kingdom, on purity of heart and the splendour of truth, it is white within. And when the pomegranate is broken, its seeds at once fall out: so when a truly virtuous soul is hemmed in by adversities, the virtues that are in her are made known, and sweetly move those who weigh them well. For then she shows charity, displays patience, makes humility plain and spreads meekness abroad, and prays for her enemy, and even grieves for him, as for one who is killing his own soul.

paras.t: Sicut turris David collum tuum : id est, elevatio, qua elevas et conjungis te sponso tuo, recta et valida est. Et quamvis sit simplex in se, utpote actus fidei aut caritatis, vel sapientiæ aut latriæ ; tamen ceteris virtutibus constipatur, munitur, protegitur, sicut rex suo exercitu : siquidem virtutes et actus earum, se mutuo juvant ac roborant, opportunoque tempore una alteri cedit, prout rationabilis exigit causa. Hinc subditur : Quæ ædificata est cum propugnaculis. Mille clypei pendent ex ea : sic virtutes invicem sibi connexæ, concurrunt in anima, et ejus sunt arma.
paras.en: [[4:4|Thy neck, is as the tower of David|Sicut turris David collum tuum]]: that is, the lifting up by which thou raisest thyself and joinest thyself to thy Bridegroom is upright and strong. And though it is simple in itself, being an act of faith or of charity, or of wisdom or of latria [the worship due to God alone], yet it is thronged about, fortified and protected by the other virtues, as a king by his army: for the virtues and their acts help and strengthen one another, and at the fitting time one gives place to another, as reasonable cause requires. Hence it is added: [[4:4|which is built with bulwarks|Quæ ædificata est cum propugnaculis]]. [[4:4|a thousand bucklers hang upon it|Mille clypei pendent ex ea]]: so the virtues, linked to one another, come together in the soul and are her weapons.

paras.t: Duo ubera tua, sicut duo hinnuli capreæ gemelli. Duo ubera animæ virtuosæ, sunt virtus misericordiæ, et donum pietatis : ita quod per misericordiam condolet ac subvenit proximis propter Deum, quia sunt indigentes ac miseri ; per pietatem vero quæ donum est, in quantum sunt summæ Trinitatis imagine insigniti. Rursus, duo ubera animæ, sunt intellectus bene instructus, et voluntas caritate accensa : per quæ duo spiritualiter nutrit se ipsam et alios, implens quod summum hortatur Apostolus : Unusquisque sicut accepit gratiam, in alterutrum illam administrantes, sicut boni dispensatores multiformis gratiæ Dei. Exhibitio quoque corporalium operum misericordiæ, et exhibitio operum misericordiæ spiritualium, sunt fecunda, pulchra, atque instar hinnulorum capreæ agilia.
paras.en: [[4:5|Thy two breasts like two young roes that are twins|Duo ubera tua, sicut duo hinnuli capreæ gemelli]]. The two breasts of the virtuous soul are the virtue of mercy and the gift of piety: so that through mercy she grieves with her neighbours and helps them for God's sake, because they are needy and wretched; but through piety, which is a gift[[Is 11:2||]] [one of the seven gifts of the Holy Ghost; the Douay-Rheims has "godliness"], in so far as they are marked with the image of the most high Trinity. Again, the two breasts of the soul are a well-instructed intellect and a will kindled with charity: by these two she nourishes herself and others spiritually, fulfilling what the chief Apostle [that is, Peter] exhorts: [[1 Pet 4:10|As every man hath received grace, ministering the same one to another: as good stewards of the manifold grace of God.|Unusquisque sicut accepit gratiam, in alterutrum illam administrantes, sicut boni dispensatores multiformis gratiæ Dei]] The showing of the bodily works of mercy, and the showing of the spiritual works of mercy, are also fruitful, beautiful, and nimble like the young of the roe.

paras.t: Consequenter loquitur sponsus : Vadam ad montem myrrhæ, et ad collem thuris. Dum anima per pœnitentiam sua deplorat peccata, et carnem suam cum vitiis concupiscentiisque mortificat, et de proximorum miseriis pie amaricatur, ut sic sponso cœlesti pro se ac aliis miseris passo assimiletur ; tunc anima amorosa est mons myrrhæ : ad quem Christus vadit, dum animam sic afflictam consolatur, et gratiæ incrementa ei largitur, sicut ait Apostolus : Benedictus Deus, qui consolatur nos in omni tribulatione nostra. Et de Deo dicitur in Tobia : Post tempestatem tranquillum facis, et post fletum exsultationem infundis. De quo scriptum est et in Job : Mœrentes erigit sospitate. At vero dum anima Christi sponsa, suavissimis exercitiis orationum, meditationum, contemplationum inhæret, efficitur collis thuris : ad quem sponsus accedit, dum animam his intentam, confortare, perficere, et amplecti dignatur.
paras.en: Next the Bridegroom says: [[4:6|I will go to the mountain of myrrh, and to the hill of frankincense|Vadam ad montem myrrhæ, et ad collem thuris]]. When the soul through penance bewails her sins, and mortifies her flesh with its vices and concupiscences[[Gal 5:24||]], and is lovingly embittered over the miseries of her neighbours, so as to be made like the heavenly Bridegroom, who suffered for her and for the other wretched: then the loving soul is a mountain of myrrh. To it Christ goes when he consoles the soul thus afflicted and bestows on her increases of grace, as the Apostle says: [[2 Cor 1:3|Blessed be the God|Benedictus Deus]], [[2 Cor 1:4|Who comforteth us in all our tribulation|qui consolatur nos in omni tribulatione nostra]]. And of God it is said in Tobias: [[Tob 3:22|after a storm thou makest a calm|Post tempestatem tranquillum facis]], and after weeping [[Tob 3:22|thou pourest in joyfulness|exsultationem infundis]]. Of him it is written in Job too: He [[Job 5:11|comforteth with health those that mourn|Mœrentes erigit sospitate]]. But when the soul, the bride of Christ, cleaves to the most sweet exercises of prayer, meditation and contemplation, she becomes a hill of frankincense, to which the Bridegroom comes when he deigns to strengthen, perfect and embrace the soul intent on these things.

paras.t: Tota pulchra es, amica mea, et macula non est in te. Venialia enim peccata (ut dicitur) non ponunt proprie maculam in anima. Et quanto tu venialia mala tua gravius ponderas, cordialius defles, et propter ea turpiorem te arbitraris, eo minus reputantur a me : quia naturalem tuam fragilitatem ac instabilitatem perpendo, ideo prorsus ea tibi dimitto, non imputo ; imo caritatem et veram in te virtutum perfectionem augmento, atque ob id te totam perhibeo pulchram. Siquidem humilis tua recognitio, dolorosa confessio, verecunda deploratio, satisfactio quoque quotidiana, assidua cordis custodia, et fervor tui amoris ad me, consumunt ut stipulam omnia illa. Quod enim in ardenti camino est gutta aquæ, hoc in viro perfecto peccatum veniale.
paras.en: [[4:7|Thou art all fair, O my love, and there is not a spot in thee.|Tota pulchra es, amica mea, et macula non est in te.]] For venial sins (as is said) do not, properly speaking, leave a stain on the soul [in scholastic usage the stain, macula, is the loss of the soul's lustre that mortal sin brings]. And the more heavily thou weighest thy venial faults, the more heartily thou weepest for them and the fouler thou thinkest thyself on their account, the less are they counted against thee by me: for I weigh thy natural frailty and instability, and therefore I wholly forgive them thee and do not impute them; nay, I increase charity and the true perfection of the virtues in thee, and for that reason I declare thee all fair. For thy humble acknowledgment, sorrowful confession, shamefaced lamenting, and daily satisfaction too, the constant keeping of thy heart, and the fervour of thy love for me, burn all those things up like stubble[[Ps 82:14||]]. For what a drop of water is in a blazing furnace, that is a venial sin in a perfect man.

paras.t: Veni de Libano, sponsa mea, veni, id est de candore gratiæ ad lumen gloriæ, de nuptiis viæ ac imperfectionis, ad perfectas nuptias patriæ Beatorum. Beati enim, qui ad cœnam nuptiarum Agni vocati sunt. Sic vocantur animæ perfectorum virorum, qui evolant : Veni de carcere carnis, atque exsilio peregrinationis, ad palatium spirituum beatorum, et patriam claritatis æternæ. Audivi enim te sæpe dicentem : Heu mihi ! quia incolatus meus prolongatus est ; et iterum, Quando veniam et apparebo ante faciem Dei ? itemque, Educ de custodia animam meam ad confitendum nomini tuo.
paras.en: [[4:8|Come from Libanus, my spouse|Veni de Libano, sponsa mea]], come: that is, from the whiteness of grace to the light of glory [Libanus was taken to mean "whiteness"], from the nuptials of the way and of imperfection to the perfect nuptials of the fatherland of the Blessed. For [[Apoc 19:9|Blessed are they that are called to the marriage supper of the Lamb|Beati enim, qui ad cœnam nuptiarum Agni vocati sunt]]. So are the souls of perfect men called when they fly away: Come from the prison of the flesh and the exile of pilgrimage to the palace of the blessed spirits and the fatherland of eternal brightness. For I have often heard thee saying: [[Ps 119:5|Woe is me, that my sojourning is prolonged!|Heu mihi ! quia incolatus meus prolongatus est]]; and again: [[Ps 41:3|when shall I come and appear before the face of God?|Quando veniam et apparebo ante faciem Dei]] and also: [[Ps 141:8|Bring my soul out of prison, that I may praise thy name|Educ de custodia animam meam ad confitendum nomini tuo]] [the margin gives Ps. cxi, 8; the verse is Ps. cxli, 8].

paras.t: Coronaberis de capite Amana, de vertice Sanir et Hermon, id est pro eo quod legitime certando, vicisti spiritum inquietudinis mundialis ac turbulentiæ, iræ ac impatientiæ, qui per caput Amana designatur : quoniam Amana, inquietudo seu turbulentia interpretatur. Qui autem in omni eventu manet in pace pectoris tranquillus et constans in Domino, non contristans se inordinate, sed gratulans in adversis, caput Amana vincit, et de ejus triumpho coronari meretur. Sanir vero, interpretatur fœtor : sicque per verticem Sanir, spiritus gulæ atque luxuriæ designatur, quia in vitiis carnis est major ac evidentior fœtor ac turpitudo. Qui igitur his vitiis dominatur, nec infelici ac vili eorum servituti subjicitur, de vertice Sanir desuper gloriose inthronizatur. Porro Hermon dicitur anathema : idcirco qui nihil sibi usurpat de anathemate Jericho, id est, non conformat se huic sæculo, neque cum mundo in vanitatibus ejus communicat, sed renovatur spiritu mentis suæ, coronandus est de vertice Hermon.
paras.en: [[4:8|thou shalt be crowned from the top of Amana, from the top of Sanir and Hermon|Coronaberis de capite Amana, de vertice Sanir et Hermon]]: that is, because by striving lawfully thou hast overcome the spirit of worldly restlessness and turbulence, of anger and impatience, which is signified by the top of Amana; for Amana is interpreted "restlessness" or "turbulence". He who in every event remains tranquil in peace of heart and constant in the Lord, not grieving inordinately but rejoicing in adversities, overcomes the top of Amana and deserves to be crowned for his triumph over it. Sanir is interpreted "stench"; and so by the top of Sanir the spirit of gluttony and lust is signified, since in the vices of the flesh there is a greater and more evident stench and foulness. He therefore who rules over these vices, and is not subjected to their unhappy and vile servitude, is gloriously enthroned above the top of Sanir. Hermon, again, means "anathema" [that is, a thing devoted to destruction and accursed]: therefore he who takes nothing for himself of the anathema of Jericho[[Jos 7:1||]], that is, who is not conformed to this world[[Rom 12:2||]], nor shares with the world in its vanities, but is renewed in the spirit of his mind[[Eph 4:23||]], is to be crowned from the top of Hermon.

paras.t: De cubilibus quoque leonum, id est pro eo quod repausationes, torpores, dormitationes magnatum hujus sæculi (qui per leonem regem animalium figurantur) abhorruisti ac evitasti. De montibus pardorum, id est victoria habita de spiritibus crudelitatis, et simulationis, atque elationis. Itaque quot immundos spiritus dæmoniorum, quot genera vitiorum, imo quot vitia superaverit anima, tot coronas, tot præmia consequetur.
paras.en: And [[4:8|from the dens of the lions|De cubilibus quoque leonum]]: that is, because thou hast abhorred and shunned the idle repose, the torpor and the drowsing of the great men of this world (who are figured by the lion, the king of beasts). [[4:8|from the mountains of the leopards|De montibus pardorum]]: that is, for the victory won over the spirits of cruelty, of pretence and of pride. And so as many unclean spirits of the demons, as many kinds of vices, nay, as many vices as the soul has overcome, so many crowns, so many rewards will she obtain.

paras.t: Vulnerasti cor meum, soror mea, sponsa : quia amore tuæ salutis factus sum homo, et crucifixus ; et quamvis amarissimam pertuli corporis passionem, dolor tamen compassionis fuit intensior in corde animæ meæ. Sicque vulnerasti me in uno oculorum tuorum, id est in oculo tuo intellectuali : cujus illuminationem per fidem ac sapientiam, deinde per beatificam visionem, in tantum desideravi, quod discolorationem speciosissimi corporis mei, velationem, obscurationem, atque eversionem exteriorum oculorum meorum sidereorum, omni vino pulchriorum, sustinui ; et in uno crine colli tui, id est in naturali appetitu beatitudinis, formato per caritatem et gratiam, quam omnis rationalis creatura naturaliter appetit. Jam etenim dictum est, quod per capillos capitis, designantur cogitationes, appetitionesque cordis : inter quas ista præcipua est, et præcipue fuit sponsi attractiva, quod naturaliter cupit felicitatem. Denique interior oculus animæ, in quantum per fidem, discretionem, scientiam, ac sapientiam adornatur, potissime placet sponso. Similiter unus crinis colli ipsius sponsæ, est elevatio contemplationis, seu sursum actio sancti amoris, qua anima erigit se ad Deum.
paras.en: [[4:9|Thou hast wounded my heart, my sister, my spouse|Vulnerasti cor meum, soror mea, sponsa]]: because for love of thy salvation I was made man and crucified; and though I bore a most bitter passion of the body, yet the pain of compassion was more intense in the heart of my soul. And so [[4:9|thou hast wounded my heart with one of thy eyes|vulnerasti me in uno oculorum tuorum]] [Denis reads "thou hast wounded me"]: that is, in thy eye of the intellect, whose enlightening through faith and wisdom, and then through the beatific vision, I so desired that I endured the discolouring of my most beautiful body, and the veiling, darkening and overturning of my outward eyes, bright as stars and more beautiful than any wine[[Gen 49:12||]]. [[4:9|and with one hair of thy neck|et in uno crine colli tui]]: that is, in the natural appetite for beatitude, formed by charity and grace [that is, raised by them to a meritorious act], which every rational creature naturally desires. For it has already been said that by the hairs of the head are signified the thoughts and desires of the heart; and among these the chief, and the one that chiefly drew the Bridegroom, is that it naturally desires happiness. In short, the inner eye of the soul, in so far as it is adorned with faith, discretion, knowledge and wisdom, most of all pleases the Bridegroom. Likewise the one hair of the bride's neck is the lifting up of contemplation, or the upward movement of holy love, by which the soul raises herself to God.

paras.t: Quam pulchræ sunt mammæ tuæ ! id est dilectio, qua pro meo honore zelaris, et zelatio fraternæ salutis ; similiter pietas tuæ compassionis, qua meam amarissimam passionem recogitando, pie compateris, proximis quoque in omni eorum afflictione, transgressione, periculo condoles. Vel, ubera tua, id est spiritualis opulentia, ac liberalitas tua, quibus proximis tuis communicas quidquid gratiæ ac virtutum desuper accepisti. Rursus, ubera ista sunt sapientia et scientia. Unde subjungitur : Pulchriora sunt ubera tua vino : id est, sapientia et scientia quæ sunt dona Spiritus Sancti, habitusque infusi, similiter sapientia et scientia quæ sunt dona gratiæ gratis datæ, et notitia sacræ Scripturæ, præstantiores et pulchriores existunt omni naturali et philosophica eruditione ac theoria. Imo stultam fecit Deus sapientiam hujus mundi ; et prudentia carnis, mors est ; tonanteque cœlo, taceant ranæ.
paras.en: [[4:10|How beautiful are thy breasts|Quam pulchræ sunt mammæ tuæ]]! That is, the love with which thou art zealous for my honour, and thy zeal for thy brethren's salvation; likewise the tenderness of thy compassion, with which, recalling my most bitter passion, thou lovingly sufferest with me, and grievest too with thy neighbours in all their affliction, transgression and danger. Or, thy breasts: that is, thy spiritual wealth and liberality, with which thou sharest with thy neighbours whatever grace and virtues thou hast received from above. Again, these breasts are wisdom and knowledge. Hence it is added: [[4:10|thy breasts are more beautiful than wine|Pulchriora sunt ubera tua vino]]: that is, wisdom and knowledge which are gifts of the Holy Ghost and infused habits, and likewise wisdom and knowledge which are gifts of grace freely given [gratia gratis data: graces given for the good of others, as prophecy or the word of wisdom, rather than to sanctify the one who has them], and the knowledge of Holy Scripture, are more excellent and more beautiful than all natural and philosophical learning and speculation. Nay, [[1 Cor 1:20|God made foolish the wisdom of this world|stultam fecit Deus sapientiam hujus mundi]]; and [[Rom 8:6|the wisdom of the flesh is death|prudentia carnis, mors est]] [Latin prudentia, "prudence"; the Douay-Rheims has "wisdom"]; and when heaven thunders, let the frogs be still.

paras.t: Et odor unguentorum tuorum super omnia aromata : id est, virtutes tuæ infusæ cum meritoriis actibus suis, delectationibusque sinceris, multo sunt digniores ac salubriores virtutibus naturalibus acquisitis, earumque actibus et gaudiis, de quibus philosophi ac gentiles locuti sunt, et non mediocriter gloriati (quorum quidam reputati sunt inter eos viri heroici) ; et virtutes illas arbitrati sunt sibi sufficere ad salutem.
paras.en: [[4:10|and the sweet smell of thy ointments above all aromatical spices|Et odor unguentorum tuorum super omnia aromata]]: that is, thy infused virtues, with their meritorious acts and pure delights, are far worthier and more wholesome than the acquired natural virtues, with their acts and joys, of which the philosophers and the gentiles spoke and in which they gloried not a little (some of whom were reckoned heroic men among them); and they thought those virtues enough for their salvation.

paras.t: Favus distillans labia tua, sponsa : id est, verba vere sapientialia, salubria ac divina, melle et favo suaviora, pronuntias, dum in hymnis et psalmis ac canticis spiritualibus mecum assidue fabularis, dum mala tua accusas, et mea beneficia recommendas, dum te ipsam totis viribus vilipendis ac dejicis, et meam majestatem cum omni reverentia admiraris, extollis, prædicas, veneraris. Sicque, mel et lac sub lingua tua, id est sermo de mea deitate, atque loquutio de mea humanitate. Mel quoque, id est consolatio de futura beatissima et prorsus dulcissima refectione ; et lac, id est consolatio refovens ex præsentium munerum exhibitione et consideratione.
paras.en: [[4:11|Thy lips, my spouse, are as a dropping honeycomb|Favus distillans labia tua, sponsa]]: that is, thou utterest words truly wise, wholesome and divine, sweeter than honey and the honeycomb, when in hymns and psalms and spiritual canticles[[Col 3:16||]] thou talkest with me without ceasing, when thou accusest thy own faults and praisest my benefits, when thou belittlest and castest thyself down with all thy strength, and with all reverence marvellest at my majesty, extollest, proclaimest and venerest it. And so [[4:11|honey and milk are under thy tongue|mel et lac sub lingua tua]]: that is, speech about my Godhead, and talk about my manhood. Honey also: that is, consolation from the most blessed and wholly sweet refreshment to come; and milk: that is, the consolation that cherishes, from the showing and consideration of present gifts.

paras.t: Et odor vestimentorum tuorum, sicut odor thuris. Vestimenta animæ, quemadmodum patuit, sunt virtutes et dona cum actibus suis : quorum odor, est delectatio eis adjuncta. Verum, sicut cujuslibet virtutis sunt tres gradus : scilicet infimus, competens statui incipientium et spectans ad viam purgativam ; medius, pertinens ad statum proficientium et viam illuminativam ; et summus, qui ad statum perfectorum viamque unitivam est pertinens : sic ipsarum virtutum et actionum earum odor seu delectatio habet tres gradus, proportionatos gradibus actibusque virtutum. Quo enim virtutes fuerint in suo subjecto magis radicatæ ac prædominantes, eo promptius ac delectabilius operantur.
paras.en: [[4:11|and the smell of thy garments, as the smell of frankincense|Et odor vestimentorum tuorum, sicut odor thuris]]. The garments of the soul, as has been shown, are the virtues and gifts with their acts, and their smell is the delight joined to them. But as every virtue has three degrees: the lowest, befitting the state of beginners and belonging to the purgative way; the middle, belonging to the state of those making progress and to the illuminative way; and the highest, which belongs to the state of the perfect and to the unitive way: so the smell or delight of the virtues themselves and of their acts has three degrees, in proportion to the degrees and acts of the virtues. For the more deeply rooted and the more dominant the virtues are in their subject, the more readily and delightfully they work.

paras.t: Hortus conclusus, soror mea, sponsa, hortus conclusus : in quo sunt semina verbi cœlestis ; flores, id est floridæ dispositiones ad fructus virtutum. Et juxta præcedentis articuli expositionem, sicut Ecclesiæ, ita et animæ suo modo competit esse hortum, et hortum conclusum ac fontem signatum ; et ea quæ dicta sunt ibi de Ecclesia, possunt ad animam virtuosam facillime applicari. Idcirco prolixitas est vitanda. Præterea de Ecclesia emittuntur ac diffunduntur diversæ virtutes, et actus præclari ac eminentes personæ, quæ per mala punica et alia poma, per cypros ac nardum, crocum, fistulam, cinnamomum, myrrham et aloen, secundum præhabitam expositionem, intelliguntur : sic proportionabiliter virtutes et actus ac personæ hujusmodi, ab anima sapiente et amorosa, aliorum animas convertente, progrediuntur.
paras.en: [[4:12|My sister, my spouse, is a garden enclosed, a garden enclosed|Hortus conclusus, soror mea, sponsa, hortus conclusus]]: in which are the seeds of the heavenly word, and flowers, that is, flowering dispositions towards the fruits of the virtues. And following the exposition of the preceding article, as it befits the Church, so it befits the soul too in its own way to be a garden, and a garden enclosed, and a fountain sealed up; and what was said there of the Church can very easily be applied to the virtuous soul. Therefore length is to be avoided. Further, as from the Church there are sent out and spread abroad various virtues, and splendid acts, and eminent persons, who are understood, according to the exposition already given, by the pomegranates and other fruits, by the cypress and spikenard, saffron, sweet cane, cinnamon, myrrh and aloes: so, in proportion, virtues and acts and persons of this kind go forth from a wise and loving soul that converts the souls of others.

paras.t: Postremo, sicut universalem sponsam suam, ita et sponsam suam particularem, scilicet animam contemplativam heroicam, Christus diversimode visitat, nunc per prospera, nunc per adversa. Et ita quod subditur, Surge, Aquilo, et veni, Auster, etc., potest dupliciter exponi de hujusmodi anima, sicut præcedenti articulo expositum est de universali Ecclesia.
paras.en: Lastly, as Christ visits his universal bride in different ways, so he visits his particular bride too, that is, the heroic contemplative soul, now through prosperity, now through adversity. And so what follows, [[4:16|Arise, O north wind, and come, O south wind|Surge, Aquilo, et veni, Auster]], etc., can be expounded of such a soul in two ways, as it was expounded in the preceding article of the universal Church.

paras.t: Ecce quam ineffabiliter virtutes infusæ, et dona Spiritus Sancti, ac meritorii actus dignificant, ornant, ac beatificant animam : quæ propter illa, tam præstantissimis, affectuosissimis, atque dulcissimis appellationibus nominatur, exprimitur, collaudatur a sponso cœlesti, Unigenito Dei, Deo vero et homine in una persona : qui animam talem vocat sponsam, sororem, amicam, columbam, speciosam, formosam, pulchram, immaculatam, hortum conclusum, fontem signatum, puteum aquarum viventium : cui tot bona promittit, tot beneficia confert, tam familiariter, amorose, ac suavissime loquitur, ut ejus amore quasi insanire quodammodo videatur.
paras.en: See how unspeakably the infused virtues, the gifts of the Holy Ghost and meritorious acts dignify, adorn and make blessed the soul, who for their sake is named, described and praised by the heavenly Bridegroom, the Only-begotten of God, true God and man in one person, with such excellent, such affectionate and such sweet names. He calls such a soul spouse, sister, love [Latin amica, "friend"], dove, comely, fair, beautiful, undefiled, a garden enclosed, a fountain sealed up, a well of living waters; he promises her so many good things, confers on her so many benefits, speaks to her so familiarly, lovingly and sweetly, that he seems in a manner almost to have lost his senses for love of her.

paras.t: Nam et ejus amore se perhibet vulneratum, non solum in uno oculorum ipsius, sed item (quod quasi puerilius prima facie videtur sonare) in uno crine colli sui.
paras.en: For he even declares that he is wounded with love of her, not only in one of her eyes, but also (which at first sight seems to sound almost childish) in one hair of her neck[[4:9||]].

paras.t: Resistamus igitur vitiis usque ad sanguinem, et studeamus virtutibus indefesse usque in finem, proficere in eisdem conemur indesinenter ; vincamus nos ipsos, et passionum immoderantiis nullatenus succumbamus ; in puritate et caritate crescere non cessemus, Deum semper invocantes in adjutorem, et omnem nobis possibilem diligentiam apponentes, ac totam nostram fiduciam collocantes in sponso, et ejus vestigia ac doctrinas sequentes continue.
paras.en: Let us therefore resist vices even unto blood, and apply ourselves tirelessly to the virtues even to the end, and strive unceasingly to advance in them; let us conquer ourselves, and by no means give way to the excesses of the passions; let us not cease to grow in purity and charity, always calling on God for help, and applying all the diligence we can, and putting all our trust in the Bridegroom, and following his footsteps and teachings continually.

4.title: EXPLANATIO EJUSDEM CAPITULI QUARTI, DE CHRISTO ET SPONSA SINGULARI.
4.title_en: Explanation of the same fourth chapter: of Christ and the singular Bride

paras.t: EA quæ in hoc libro dicuntur de Ecclesia, quantum ad meliores et perfectiores in ea, certum est de nulla persona tam eminenter et convenienter posse exponi, sicut de Virgine gloriosa. Cui sponsus et Filius ait : Quam pulchra es, amica mea! quam pulchra es! Tanto plane pulchrior ceteris universis, quanto in omni gratia, virtute, dono, beatitudine, fructu perfectior, quanto purior, innocentior, et ab omni culpa immunior, quanto Fonti totius pulchritudinis ac decoris propinquior, utpote vera Mater illius : imo tam pulchra, quod Fons ille superpulcherrimus, concupivit decorem istius; tamque delectabilis et jucunda fuit in superspeciosissimo Unigenito Patris æterni, ad intuendum, ad convivendum, ad diligendum, quod in ea, et cum ea præ cunctis commorari et conversari elegit in terris. Et sicut ille speciosus forma præ filiis hominum ; sic ista est speciosa præ filiabus, ergo et præ filiis hominum, post unicum Filium suum. Cujus oculi columbarum, id est maxime columbini, pudicissimi, plenissime custoditi, nunquam inordinate aperti, nunquam in aliquem indecenter directi aut fixi; cujus intentio fuit inviolabiliter recta, simplex, purissima, nunquam ad proprium commodum aut honorem reflexa.
paras.en: The things said in this book of the Church, as regards the better and more perfect in her, can certainly be expounded of no person so eminently and so fittingly as of the glorious Virgin. To her, her Bridegroom and Son says: [[4:1|How beautiful art thou, my love, how beautiful art thou!|Quam pulchra es, amica mea! quam pulchra es!]] So much more beautiful, plainly, than all others, as she is more perfect in every grace, virtue, gift, beatitude and fruit; as she is purer, more innocent, and more free from all fault; as she is nearer to the Fount of all beauty and comeliness, being indeed His true Mother: nay, so beautiful that that Fount, beautiful beyond all beauty, desired her comeliness; and to the only-begotten Son of the eternal Father, fair beyond all fairness, she was so delightful and pleasing to look upon, to live with, to love, that He chose to dwell and converse on earth in her and with her above all others. And as He is [[Ps 44:3|beautiful above the sons of men|speciosus forma præ filiis hominum]], so she is beautiful above the daughters, and therefore above the sons of men too, after her only Son. Her [[4:1|eyes are doves' eyes|oculi columbarum]], that is, supremely dove-like: most chaste, most fully guarded, never opened inordinately, never directed or fixed on anyone unbecomingly; her intention was inviolably right, simple, most pure, never bent back towards her own advantage or honour.

paras.t: Absque eo quod intrinsecus latet. Incomprehensibilis etenim sponsus, munificentissimus, optimus, omnipotens Filius, incomprehensibiliter, secretissime, liberalissime operabatur, radiabat, communicabat se in Matre. O quis queat excogitare aut capere, qualiter Verbum illud æternum, quod suo claro intuitu angelos sanctos felicitat, mentem suæ dilectissimæ, capacissimæ, ac innocentissimæ Matris assidue visitavit; quam copiosissime omnia interiora ejus illuminavit, quam calidissime inflammavit ipsius affectum, quam mire et ineffabili modo fidelissimam et affectuosissimam suam Genitricem corroboravit, ornavit, perfecit, implevit, totaliterque possedit? Quidquid de perfectione raptus et ecstasis, quidquid de prælibatione et participatione futuræ beatitudinis fuit in aliis, multo eminentius in ea creditur exstitisse. Et si quidam Sanctorum creduntur Deum in hac vita vidisse per speciem, cur non potius atque limpidius, et forsan frequentius ac diuturnius ipsa? Nonne caritas communicat et ostendit se personæ, singulariter familiarissimeque dilectæ? Hoc ergo latuit in Virgine summa intrinsecus: quæ utique cum fervore, devotione, puritate, et stabilitate soli Deo et sibi nota [ei] vacavit, inhæsit, intenta immersaque fuit; cujus interior incomparanda sinceritas, tranquillitas, sapientia, virtuositas resplenduit in vultu ipsius, eamque gratissimam, venustissimam, et compositissimam fecit in omnibus.
paras.en: [[4:1|besides what is hid within|Absque eo quod intrinsecus latet]]. For the incomprehensible Bridegroom, the most bountiful, the best, the almighty Son, was working, shining and communicating Himself in His Mother incomprehensibly, most secretly, most liberally. O who could conceive or grasp how that eternal Word, who by His clear vision makes the holy angels blessed, constantly visited the mind of His most beloved, most capacious and most innocent Mother; how most abundantly He enlightened all her inner parts, how most warmly He inflamed her affection, in how wonderful and ineffable a way He strengthened, adorned, perfected, filled and wholly possessed His most faithful and most loving Mother? Whatever of the perfection of rapture and ecstasy, whatever of the foretaste and sharing of the beatitude to come there was in others, is believed to have been in her far more eminently. And if some of the Saints are believed to have seen God in this life by sight [per speciem, that is, as He is, and not only by faith], why not she rather, and more clearly, and perhaps more often and for longer? Does not charity communicate and show itself to a person singularly and most intimately loved? This, then, lay hid within the supreme Virgin: she who, with a fervour, devotion, purity and steadfastness known only to God and to herself, gave herself to Him, clung to Him, and was intent upon and immersed in Him; whose inward, incomparable sincerity, tranquillity, wisdom and virtue shone out in her face, and made her most gracious, most lovely, and most composed in all things.

paras.t: Capilli tui sicut greges caprarum. Universæ namque cogitationes, meditationes, contemplationes, affectionesque Virginis admirandæ, erant ordinatissimæ, decentissimæ, atque mundissimæ, totius caritatis fervore perfusæ, formatæ, splendifluæ, et cum omni promptitudine in Deum reductæ, recollectæ ac stabilitæ. Et testimonia Scripturarum ad Christum spectantia, intra se prudentissima Domina recolligit, conferens in corde suo, quidquid de prædilectissimo Filio suo audivit ab angelo, a pastoribus, ab Elisabeth, a Zacharia, a Simeone et Anna, a Joseph, a Magis : ita quod de monte Galaad, de acervo testimoniorum, a tumulo testis agnoscitur ascendisse.
paras.en: [[4:1|Thy hair is as flocks of goats|Capilli tui sicut greges caprarum]]. For all the thoughts, meditations, contemplations and affections of the wondrous Virgin were most well ordered, most seemly and most pure, steeped in and formed by the fervour of all charity, flowing with splendour, and with all readiness drawn back, gathered and made steadfast in God. And the most prudent Lady gathered within herself the testimonies of the Scriptures that concern Christ, pondering in her heart whatever she heard of her most dearly beloved Son from the angel, from the shepherds, from Elizabeth, from Zachary, from Simeon and Anna, from Joseph, from the Magi: so that she is known to have come up [[4:1|from mount Galaad|de monte Galaad]], from the heap of testimonies, from the mound of the witness [Galaad was taken to mean "heap of witness": see Gen 31:47–48].

paras.t: Dentes tui sicut greges tonsarum, quæ ascenderunt de lavacro. Spirituales dentes incomparabilis Dominæ, fuerunt subtilissimæ et acutissimæ considerationes animæ ejus, quibus intra se trivit, et aliis trita exposuit, ac optime masticata digessit mysteria Filii sui, omnemque gratiam sibi ab ipso concessam, ac beneficia Dei impensa generi humano per Christum. Hæ considerationes, discretiones ac masticationes illustrissimæ Virginis, instar tonsarum ovium puræ et innocentes fuerunt, ab omni errore admixtioneque culpæ penitus alienæ : utpote ascendentes de totius luminis fonte, de lavacro, id est de flumine sapientiæ Virginis sacræ, hoc est de exuberantissima habituali sapientia ei infusa. Nempe si verum est quod generaliter Christus disseruit, Qui credit in me, flumina de ventre ejus fluent aquæ vivæ : quanto magis de fidelissimæ et prorsus illuminatissimæ Virginis corde exuberanter fluxerunt flumina aquæ viventis? Et in ea tanquam in amœnissimo paradiso, fuit fons copiosus, clarus, perlucidus, diffundens ex se rivos limpidissimarum meditationum, sanctissimarumque affectionum.
paras.en: [[4:2|Thy teeth as flocks of sheep, that are shorn, which come up from the washing|Dentes tui sicut greges tonsarum, quæ ascenderunt de lavacro]]. The spiritual teeth of the incomparable Lady were the most subtle and most keen considerations of her soul, with which she ground within herself the mysteries of her Son, set them out ground for others, and digested them well chewed, and with them all the grace granted her by Him, and the benefits of God bestowed on mankind through Christ. These considerations, discernments and chewings of the most illustrious Virgin were, like shorn sheep, pure and innocent, wholly free of all error and of any admixture of fault: since they came up from the fount of all light, [[4:2|from the washing|de lavacro]], that is, from the river of the holy Virgin's wisdom, that is, from the most overflowing habitual wisdom infused into her [habitual, that is, given to her as an abiding disposition of the soul]. For if what Christ declared in general is true, [[John 7:38|He that believeth in me|Qui credit in me]], [[John 7:38|Out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water|flumina de ventre ejus fluent aquæ vivæ]]: how much more did rivers of living water flow in abundance from the heart of the most faithful and wholly enlightened Virgin? And in her, as in a most delightful paradise, there was an abundant fountain, clear and translucent, pouring forth from itself streams of most limpid meditations and most holy affections.

paras.t: Sicut fragmen mali punici, ita genæ tuæ. Genæ generosissimæ ac regiæ Virginis, intelliguntur vernantissima pudicitia, et virginalis formidolositas ejus, sanctam Virginem decens : quæ instar malogranati, rubore igniti amoris ac splendore sapientiæ præfulgebant ac redolebant. Nec dubium quin et genæ ejus corporeæ, ex optima complexione, convenienti colore, et frequenti deosculatione adorandi sui Filii, velut fragmen mali punici, temperate rubescebant, ac dulces erant. Præcedentis quoque articuli de his verbis expositio, ei recte aptatur, intelligendo per genas ejus interiores, memoriam præteritorum, quæ in ea ex assidua sui Filii passione, quasi sanguineo fuit rubore perfusa; atque providentiam futurorum, quæ ex consideratione fructus passionis ejusdem, quasi candens pollebat, et consolationis refloritionem produxit in mente ipsius.
paras.en: [[4:3|Thy cheeks are as a piece of a pomegranate|Sicut fragmen mali punici, ita genæ tuæ]]. By the cheeks of the most noble and royal Virgin are understood her most blooming modesty and her virginal shyness, becoming to the holy Virgin: which, like a pomegranate, shone forth and gave out fragrance with the redness of burning love and the splendour of wisdom. Nor is there any doubt that her bodily cheeks too, from her excellent complexion, their fitting colour, and her frequent kissing of her adorable Son, were gently red like a piece of a pomegranate, and were sweet. The exposition of these words given in the preceding article also fits her rightly, understanding by her inward cheeks the memory of things past, which in her, from the passion of her Son ever before her, was suffused as it were with a blood-red flush; and the foresight of things to come, which, from the consideration of the fruit of that same passion, was strong as it were with a shining whiteness, and brought forth in her mind a fresh flowering of consolation.

paras.t: Sicut turris David collum tuum. Per collum mentis, intelligi solet voluntas, quæ sua libertate in altum extenditur. Porro voluntas Virginis benedictæ vere fuit liberrima, id est subjectissima ac obedientissima Deo, cui servire, regnare est, id est vitiis, concupiscentiis, vanitatibus, dæmonibus prævalere, ac dominari. Hæc voluntas Reginæ ac Dominæ nostræ, per caritatem fuit altissima, imo summo universorum principio perfecte unita, ac directissime ad ipsum extensa, per profundissimam humilitatem et inæstimabilem pietatem ad miseros inclinata, cunctis donis ac virtutibus ad voluntatem spectantibus, scilicet caritate Dei ac proximi, spe, justitia, pietate, fortitudine quæ est donum, præclarissime ac victoriosissime decorata : in qua nihil mansit de proprio, nec de privato amore; sed abnegatissima fuit, et resignatissima Deo.
paras.en: [[4:4|Thy neck, is as the tower of David|Sicut turris David collum tuum]]. By the neck of the mind is usually understood the will, which by its freedom stretches upward. Now the will of the blessed Virgin was truly most free, that is, most subject and most obedient to God, whom to serve is to reign, that is, to prevail over and master vices, concupiscences, vanities and demons. This will of our Queen and Lady was, through charity, most high, nay perfectly united to the supreme principle of all things and stretched out most directly towards Him; bowed down towards the wretched by the deepest humility and inestimable pity; adorned most splendidly and most victoriously with all the gifts and virtues that belong to the will, namely charity towards God and neighbour, hope, justice, godliness, and fortitude which is a gift[[Is 11:2||]] [that is, fortitude as one of the gifts of the Holy Ghost, as distinct from the virtue of that name]: in which nothing of self remained, nor of private love; but it was utterly self-denying, and wholly resigned to God.

paras.t: Duo ubera tua, sicut duo hinnuli capreæ gemelli. De pretiosissimis optimæ Virginis uberibus dictum est supra, in expositione primi capituli. Breviter ergo tangendo, duo ubera ejus, quibus nutrit, lactat et refovet confugientes ad se, sunt caritas ejus materna et pietas maxima, per quas prona est omnibus misereri ac subvenire, ac velocissima instar hinnulorum, misericorditer intueri ac refovere. De qua nil durum austerumve legitur, imo omni affectui misericordiæ videtur tota esse conversa : propter quod Mater gratiæ, et Regina misericordiæ nuncupatur. Præterea, quam gloriose ac flagrantissime corporea ejus ubera, quibus Deum verum ex se natum lactavit, resplendeant, nemo valet concipere.
paras.en: [[4:5|Thy two breasts like two young roes that are twins|Duo ubera tua, sicut duo hinnuli capreæ gemelli]]. Of the most precious breasts of the excellent Virgin we have spoken above, in the exposition of the first chapter. To touch on it briefly, then: her two breasts, with which she nourishes, suckles and cherishes those who flee to her, are her motherly charity and her very great pity, through which she is inclined to have mercy on all and to help them, and is most swift, like young roes, to look on them with mercy and to cherish them. Nothing hard or harsh is read of her; nay, she seems wholly turned to every feeling of mercy: for which reason she is called the Mother of grace and the Queen of mercy. Moreover, how gloriously and how most radiantly her bodily breasts, with which she suckled the true God born of her, shine, no one can conceive.

paras.t: Vadam ad montem myrrhæ, et ad collem thuris. Unica Dei, passionem Filii sui jugiter in suo corde dolorose gestando, peccata mundi, præsertim Judæorum, deflendo, et plurimos a vitiorum putredine præservando, fuit mons myrrhæ : quem Christus incessabiliter, munificentissime et consolatorie visitavit. Fuitque collis thuris, orationum suarum thymiamata, meditationum suarum fragrantiam, caritatis suæ incensum, pietatis suæ dulcedinem, imo se totam Deo in holocaustum plenissime offerendo : quem etiam collem sponsus ipsius ubertim, gratiose et deliciose accessit, et in medio ejus demoratus est, ejus dulcedine delectatus. Sanctificavit enim tabernaculum hoc suum Altissimus, et in medio ejus non est commotus.
paras.en: [[4:6|I will go to the mountain of myrrh, and to the hill of frankincense|Vadam ad montem myrrhæ, et ad collem thuris]]. The only one of God, by carrying the passion of her Son constantly and sorrowfully in her heart, by weeping for the sins of the world, above all of the Jews, and by preserving very many from the rottenness of vice, was the mountain of myrrh [myrrh, bitter, and used to keep bodies from corruption]: which Christ visited unceasingly, most bountifully and with consolation. And she was the hill of frankincense, by offering most fully to God the incense of her prayers, the fragrance of her meditations, the burnt incense of her charity, the sweetness of her pity, nay her whole self as a holocaust: to which hill too her Bridegroom came abundantly, graciously and delightfully, and dwelt in the midst of it, delighted with its sweetness. For [[Ps 45:5|the most High hath sanctified his own tabernacle|Sanctificavit enim tabernaculum hoc suum Altissimus]] (this one), and [[Ps 45:6|in the midst thereof, it shall not be moved|in medio ejus non est commotus]] [Denis has "in the midst of it he was not moved"].

paras.t: Tota pulchra es, amica mea, et macula non est in te. Hoc de Virgine divinissima præ ceteris cunctis convenientissime explanatur : quæ antonomastice Christi amica asseritur, et ei in omni sanctitate et perfectione similior creditur; in qua cunctæ virtutes in termino præclaræ excellentiæ sunt inventæ. At vero de pulchro ac pulchritudine, divinus Dionysius tractat subtiliter ac profunde quarto capitulo de Divinis nominibus : Divina, inquiens, bonitas laudatur in Scripturis, ut pulchrum, et pulchritudo quæ effectiva est omnis pulchri. In creaturis autem dicitur pulchrum, quod participat pulchritudinem. Loquentes vero de Deo, dicimus quod ipse est supersubstantiale pulchrum et pulchritudo, quia pulchrificat exsistentia omnia secundum propriam singulorum proportionem, et causat universalem omnium harmoniam et claritatem, et juxta proprietatem solaris radii, immittit cum fulgore universitati rerum pulchrificas suæ fontanæ lucis distributiones. Juxta horum imitationem dicere possumus, quod sacratissima puerpera virgo Maria, est tota pulchra, ad intuendum delectabilissima : quæ suis meritis, precibus, virtutibus, fama, pulchrificat et decorat millia multa, imo totam Ecclesiam, et causat in ipsis fidelibus concordiam, lucem, et caritatis unitatem ; quam Fons totius pulchritudinis, natus ex ea, tanta pulchritudine venustavit, ut puræ creaturæ major communicari aut nequeat, aut non deceat.
paras.en: [[4:7|Thou art all fair, O my love, and there is not a spot in thee.|Tota pulchra es, amica mea, et macula non est in te.]] This is explained most fittingly of all, before all others, of the most divine Virgin: she who by antonomasia [that is, by way of pre-eminence] is called the friend of Christ [amica, the verse's word, rendered "my love"], and is believed to be more like Him in all holiness and perfection; in whom all the virtues have been found at the very limit of surpassing excellence. Now of the beautiful and of beauty the divine Dionysius treats subtly and profoundly in the fourth chapter of the Divine Names, saying: The divine goodness is praised in the Scriptures as the beautiful, and as the beauty which is productive of everything beautiful. In creatures, that is called beautiful which participates in beauty. But speaking of God, we say that He is the superessential beautiful and beauty, because He makes beautiful all things that exist, according to the proper proportion of each, and causes the universal harmony and brightness of all things, and, after the manner of the sun's ray, sends forth with brightness upon the whole universe of things the beautifying distributions of His fontal light. In imitation of this we can say that the most holy Mary, Virgin and Mother, is [[4:7|all fair|tota pulchra]], most delightful to look upon: who by her merits, prayers, virtues and fame beautifies and adorns many thousands, nay the whole Church, and causes in the faithful concord, light, and the unity of charity; whom the Fount of all beauty, born of her, graced with such beauty that a greater either cannot be communicated to a mere creature, or would not be fitting.

paras.t: Amplius, ut ait Philosophus, ad hoc quod homo sit corporaliter pulcher, tria requiruntur. Primum est, quod sit elegantis staturæ : ideo homines parvi, non dicuntur proprie pulchri, quamvis valeant dici formosi, aut speciosi. Secundum est, congrua membrorum comproportionatio et habitudo ad invicem. Tertium est, superficies vividi et congruentis coloris. Conformiter ad hoc quod aliqua persona sit spiritualiter pulchra, primo requiritur, quod ad eminentem quamdam virtutum proceritatem, altitudinemve pervenerit ; secundo, quod sit in ea virtutum quædam proportio, et congrua habitudo in actibus earumdem ; tertio, quod omnibus sit superfusa discretio, seu sapientialis directio, aut caritatis floritio. Ex quibus probatur electissima Virgo fuisse pulcherrima : quippe quæ ad tam præeminentem universarum perfectionem virtutum devenerat, et in qua virtutes sibi invicem tam comproportionatæ fuerunt, et præclarissima discretione jugiter regebantur, sapientissima directione fulgebant, ferventissimo formabantur amore divino, imo quotidie recentiori innovatione decorabantur.
paras.en: Further, as the Philosopher says [Aristotle, Ethics IV, 3], for a man to be beautiful in body three things are required. The first is that he be of graceful stature: hence small men are not properly called beautiful, though they can be called shapely or comely. The second is a fitting proportion and relation of the members to one another. The third is a surface of lively and fitting colour. In like manner, for a person to be beautiful in spirit, it is required first that he have reached a certain eminent tallness or height of the virtues; secondly, that there be in him a certain proportion of the virtues, and a fitting relation in their acts; thirdly, that discretion, or the direction of wisdom, or the flowering of charity, be spread over all. From which it is proved that the most chosen Virgin was most beautiful: for she had come to so pre-eminent a perfection of all the virtues, and in her the virtues were so proportioned to one another, and were constantly ruled by the most excellent discretion, shone with the wisest direction, were formed by the most fervent divine love, nay were adorned every day with a fresh renewal.

paras.t: Vulnerasti cor meum, soror mea, sponsa, vulnerasti cor meum. Quanto quis ad majorem beatitudinem est electus, tanto amplius videtur Christus pro ipso passus. Quum itaque ad excellentissimam felicitatem et gloriam dignissima Virgo electa sit ab æterno, nonne pro ipsa, pro ejus amore, pro ejus salute, specialissime crucifixus est Filius ejus, et ipsa verissime dicere potuit illud Apostoli, In fide vivo Filii Dei, qui dilexit me, et tradidit semetipsum pro me? Vulnerasti ergo cor meum, id est, vehementissime attraxisti me ad te, ita quod amore tuo quasi vulneratus videbar; in uno oculorum tuorum, id est per sincerissimam contemplationem, qua me reverentissime ac ferventissime inspexisti, totis tuis præcordiis me peroptans; et in uno crine colli tui, id est una affectione cordis tui purissimi, qua commune totius humani generis bonum præcordialissime concupisti. Imo tantum mihi complacuisti, tam amabilis facta es mihi, quod etiam una quacumque tua intuitione et affectione ad me, rapuisti me totum in te, et placuit mihi magnifice quidquid fuit in anima tua, et quidquid processit ex ea.
paras.en: [[4:9|Thou hast wounded my heart, my sister, my spouse, thou hast wounded my heart|Vulnerasti cor meum, soror mea, sponsa, vulnerasti cor meum]]. The greater the beatitude to which anyone is chosen, the more Christ seems to have suffered for him. Since, then, the most worthy Virgin was chosen from eternity to the most excellent happiness and glory, was not her Son crucified most specially for her, for love of her, for her salvation, and could she not most truly say that word of the Apostle, [[Gal 2:20|I live in the faith of the Son of God, who loved me and delivered himself for me|In fide vivo Filii Dei, qui dilexit me, et tradidit semetipsum pro me?]]? So: [[4:9|Thou hast wounded my heart|Vulnerasti ergo cor meum]], that is, thou hast most vehemently drawn me to thee, so that I seemed as it were wounded by love of thee; [[4:9|with one of thy eyes|in uno oculorum tuorum]], that is, by the most sincere contemplation with which thou didst gaze on me most reverently and most fervently, longing for me with all thy heart; [[4:9|and with one hair of thy neck|et in uno crine colli tui]], that is, by one affection of thy most pure heart, with which thou didst most heartily desire the common good of the whole human race. Nay, so greatly hast thou pleased me, so lovable hast thou become to me, that even by any one look and affection of thine towards me thou hast ravished the whole of me into thee, and whatever was in thy soul, and whatever proceeded from it, has pleased me magnificently.

paras.t: Quam pulchræ sunt mammæ tuæ, soror mea, sponsa! Speciosissimæ utique erant mammæ illæ internæ Virginis admirandæ : dilectio Dei, caritas proximorum ; item pietas quæ est cultus Dei, et zelus divini honoris atque fraternæ salutis; sapientia ejus atque scientia; gratia et affluentia; ac munificentia ejus, compassio miserorum : quæ omnia, vino rigoris legalis, et omni naturali scientia, omni corporali materia fuerunt ineffabiliter pulchriora. Corporea quoque spiritualissimæ Virginis ubera, quæ Regem gloriæ lactaverunt, Deo vero alimoniam præbuerunt, Fonti totius boni lac purissimum influxerunt, speciosissima, suavissima, honorabilissima, amabilissima facta sunt, et miro modo deificata, ipsisque angelicis mentibus honoranda.
paras.en: [[4:10|How beautiful are thy breasts, my sister, my spouse!|Quam pulchræ sunt mammæ tuæ, soror mea, sponsa!]] Most fair indeed were those inward breasts of the wondrous Virgin: love of God and charity towards her neighbours; likewise godliness, which is the worship of God, and zeal for the divine honour and for the salvation of her brethren; her wisdom and knowledge; grace and abundance; and her bountifulness and compassion for the wretched: all of which were ineffably more beautiful than the wine of the rigour of the Law, than all natural knowledge, than all bodily matter [Denis is glossing the rest of the verse: "thy breasts are more beautiful than wine"]. The bodily breasts too of the most spiritual Virgin, which suckled the King of glory, gave nourishment to the true God, and poured the purest milk into the Fount of all good, were made most fair, most sweet, most honourable, most lovable, and in a wonderful way deified, to be honoured even by the angelic minds themselves.

paras.t: Et odor unguentorum tuorum super omnia aromata. Tanta certissime est suavitas charismatum et meritorum, virtutum et actuum, unctionum et diffusionum serenissimæ Matris Dei, quod cuncta mundi odoramenta transcendit : imo et totam perfundit, adspergit, delectat triumphantem Ecclesiam inenarrabili modo. Creatoremque universi, ac totam supergloriosissimam Trinitatem, universi cives superni in Virgine Christifera medullitus laudant, extollunt, mirantur, amant, et amplectuntur : felicitati ac gloriæ Genitricis Domini Dei sui inæstimabiliter congratulantes, atque in ea gloriantes in Domino ; tam beatissimæ creaturæ pulchritudinem, post Creatoris pulchritudinem, maxime admirantes, ejus dulcedinem haurientes, ejus odoribus mirifice oblectati ; Deoque gratias incessabiliter referentes pro omni salute et excellentia, quas suæ præstantissimæ contulit Genitrici. Insuper universa Ecclesia militans, in fœtoribus hujus exsilii degens, odore, suavitate, adspersione, consolatione hujus Deiferæ Virginis, advocatæ ac dominæ suæ, non mediocriter recreatur, fovetur, juvatur, et exhilaratur.
paras.en: [[4:10|and the sweet smell of thy ointments above all aromatical spices|Et odor unguentorum tuorum super omnia aromata]]. So great, most certainly, is the sweetness of the charisms and merits, the virtues and acts, the anointings and outpourings of the most serene Mother of God, that it surpasses all the perfumes of the world: nay, it pervades, sprinkles and delights the whole Church triumphant in an unspeakable way. And all the citizens of heaven, in the Christ-bearing Virgin, praise from their inmost hearts the Creator of the universe and the whole supremely glorious Trinity, and extol, wonder at, love and embrace Him: rejoicing beyond all reckoning in the happiness and glory of the Mother of the Lord their God, and glorying in her in the Lord; wondering above all, after the beauty of the Creator, at the beauty of so most blessed a creature, drinking in her sweetness, wondrously delighted with her fragrance; and giving thanks to God unceasingly for all the salvation and excellence He has conferred on His most excellent Mother. Moreover the whole Church militant, dwelling amid the stenches of this exile, is not a little refreshed, cherished, helped and gladdened by the fragrance, sweetness, sprinkling and consolation of this God-bearing Virgin, her advocate and lady.

paras.t: Favus distillans labia tua, sponsa. Fons et causa universæ suavitatis, eam quam præelegit in matrem, tanta replevit suavitate, ut nec ratio capere, nec lingua queat exprimere. Itaque labia intellectualia Virginis sanctæ, quibus Deum suum intra cordis sui arcana assidue alloquebatur, laudavit, oravit, suavissima esse noscuntur, et suavissimum favum distillaverunt : quoniam actus internos Deo acceptissimos, jam præactos, produxerunt, imo incessanter producunt. Sub quibus sacratissimis labiis mel et lac continentur : mel utique ardentissimæ caritatis et suavitatis internæ, ex divina summi boni plenissima fruitione ; lac quoque refectionis salutiferæ, ex inspectione et dilectione humanæ Filii sui naturæ ex se sumptæ : sicque ingrediens, invenit pascua in deitate ; et egrediens, in Christi humanitate.
paras.en: [[4:11|Thy lips, my spouse, are as a dropping honeycomb|Favus distillans labia tua, sponsa]]. The Fount and cause of all sweetness filled her whom He chose beforehand as His mother with such sweetness that neither reason can grasp it nor tongue express it. And so the intellectual lips of the holy Virgin, with which she constantly spoke to her God within the secret places of her heart, praised Him and prayed, are known to be most sweet, and have dropped a most sweet honeycomb: since they brought forth inward acts most acceptable to God, already performed, nay bring them forth unceasingly. Under these most sacred lips are contained [[4:11|honey and milk|mel et lac]]: the honey of most ardent charity and of inward sweetness, from the divine and most full fruition of the supreme good; and the milk of saving refreshment, from looking upon and loving the human nature of her Son, taken from her: and so, going in, she found pasture in the Godhead, and going out, in the humanity of Christ [compare John 10:9: "he shall go in and go out, and shall find pastures"].

paras.t: Hortus conclusus, soror mea, sponsa, hortus conclusus, fons signatus. Deliciosissimus, vernantissimus, fructuosissimus hortus Dei est optima Domina ista : in qua omnium arborum spiritualium species sunt plantatæ; in qua lignum sapientiæ requievit, lignum scientiæ boni et mali, id est summa discretio immarcescibiliter floret; in qua universæ virtutes sunt consitæ, cuncta divina charismata floruerunt, Sol sapientiæ plenissime radiavit, nulli venti, pluviæ, flumina vitiorum unquam potuerunt locum habere : quæ peperit eum qui Creator est omnium, totiusque mundi genuit Salvatorem; quæ inviolabilis virginitatis signaculo indesinenter clausa et signata permansit; quæ fons est gratiæ, et post Deum origo, mater, largitrix universorum quæ nobis conferuntur charismatum : ei namque regnum misericordiæ est commissum, et per manus ipsius dat nobis et dare disposuit Deus, quidquid gratiæ tribuit nobis.
paras.en: [[4:12|My sister, my spouse, is a garden enclosed, a garden enclosed, a fountain sealed up|Hortus conclusus, soror mea, sponsa, hortus conclusus, fons signatus]]. This excellent Lady is God's most delightful, most blooming, most fruitful garden: in which every kind of spiritual tree has been planted; in which the tree of wisdom has rested, and the tree of knowledge of good and evil, that is, the highest discretion, blooms unfading; in which all the virtues have been planted, all the divine charisms have flowered, the Sun of wisdom has shone most fully, and no winds, rains or floods of vice could ever find place: she who bore Him who is the Creator of all, and brought forth the Saviour of the whole world; who remained ceaselessly closed and sealed with the seal of inviolable virginity; who is the fountain of grace and, after God, the origin, mother and bestower of all the charisms conferred on us: for to her the kingdom of mercy is committed, and through her hands God gives us, and has disposed to give us, whatever grace He grants us.

paras.t: Emissiones tuæ paradisus malorum punicorum. Quidquid a dulcissima, ditissima, liberalissima, misericordissima Domina nostra, sponsa ac virgine ista, emittitur et procedit, dulce et pium est. Verba et opera ejus, Deo cunctisque Beatis ac omnibus bene dispositis mirabiliter placent, dulcescunt, et grata sunt : caritatem namque et misericordiam excellentissime redolent, et gratiosa sunt nimis. Omnes demum virtutes, et virtuosæ personæ, clarissimique effectus, per mala punica pomaque alia, per nardum, crocum, fistulam, cinnamomum, myrrham, thus, aloen, ac cetera in textu expressa, gloriose ac eminenter emissa sunt et prodierunt ex ea, juxta expositionem præhabitam.
paras.en: [[4:13|Thy plants are a paradise of pomegranates|Emissiones tuæ paradisus malorum punicorum]] [emissiones, literally "what is sent forth", which Denis takes of all that proceeds from her]. Whatever is sent forth and proceeds from this most sweet, most rich, most liberal, most merciful Lady of ours, this bride and virgin, is sweet and loving. Her words and works wonderfully please God and all the Blessed and all who are well disposed; they are sweet and welcome to them: for they breathe most excellently of charity and mercy, and are exceedingly gracious. Finally, all the virtues and virtuous persons, and the most illustrious effects, signified by the pomegranates and other fruits, by the spikenard, saffron, sweet cane, cinnamon, myrrh, frankincense, aloes, and the rest set down in the text, have gloriously and eminently been sent forth and have come forth from her, according to the exposition given before.

paras.t: Surge, Aquilo; et veni, Auster. Sponsus ille sapientissimus, Deus et homo, Christus Jesus, dilectissimam Matrem suam permisit in sæculo isto multipliciter contristari, affligi, et compati de excessibus hominum, de ipsius Filii sui et aliorum Sanctorum amarissimis martyriis ac tormentis : præsertim in triduo mortis sepulturæque Christi, durissimus ventus Aquilo flavit in eam, penitusque replevit. Verum in hora resurrectionis et apparitionis Filii sui, dulcissimus Auster successit, et lætificavit eam dulciflue, ita quod ejus aromata diffuderunt se undique.
paras.en: [[4:16|Arise, O north wind, and come, O south wind|Surge, Aquilo; et veni, Auster]]. That most wise Bridegroom, God and man, Christ Jesus, allowed His most beloved Mother to be saddened in many ways in this world, to be afflicted, and to suffer with others over the excesses of men, over the most bitter martyrdoms and torments of her Son Himself and of the other Saints: above all in the three days of Christ's death and burial the harshest north wind blew upon her and filled her wholly.
