paras.t: O quam mira et ingens est vis sancti amoris! cujus aculeus mentem amantis medullitus penetrat, affectum transverberat; penetralia sic inflammat, et ebullire atque erumpere facit, ita ut desideriorum suorum intimarumque commotionum gestus, effectus, atque indicia nequeat cohibere, nec dissimulare : pectus concutitur, et interiora omnia alterantur, oculi madent, corpus debilitatur, ardet affectio, cor æstuat profundissime ingemiscens, ac longa suspiria trahens. Hæc languidæ vulneratæque animæ certa censentur indicia, facies pallens, vultus tabescens, fastidium mundi, inadvertentia omnis terreni negotii, vilipensio totius carnalis affectus, et frequens ascensio caritatis cum profectu ejusdem. Cetera patent.
paras.en: O how wondrous and how great is the power of holy love! Its sting pierces the lover's mind to the marrow and transfixes the affection; it so inflames the inmost parts and makes them boil up and break out that the lover cannot hold back or hide the bearing, the effects and the signs of his desires and of his inmost stirrings: the breast is shaken, all within is changed, the eyes are wet, the body grows weak, the affection burns, the heart is on fire, groaning most deeply and drawing long sighs. These are held to be the sure signs of a soul languishing and wounded with love: a pale face, a wasting look, loathing of the world, inattention to all earthly business, contempt of all carnal affection, and a frequent rising up of charity with its increase. The rest is plain.

6.title: ELUCIDATIO CAPITULI SEXTI : QUO ABIIT DILECTUS TUUS, O PULCHERRIMA MULIERUM ? DE CHRISTO ET ECCLESIA.
6.title_en: Elucidation of the sixth chapter: Whither is thy beloved gone, O thou most beautiful among women? Of Christ and the Church

paras.t: Capitulo præcedenti locuta est sponsa adolescentulis : Adjuro vos, filiæ Jerusalem, si inveneritis dilectum meum, ut annuntietis ei quia amore langueo. Ex quibus verbis adolescentulæ ad duas motæ sunt quæstiones. Prima fuit : Qualis est dilectus tuus? Ad quam præinducto respondit sponsa capitulo. Secunda est, quæ modo proponitur : Quo abiit dilectus tuus sponsus, Dei Filius? quem in præcedentibus dixisti te quærere nec invenisse : unde elicimus, quod aliquo modo recessit a te (juxta præcedentis elucidationem articuli) ; o pulcherrima mulierum. Quo declinavit dilectus tuus? et quæremus eum tecum, id est, adjuvabimus te in quærendo, et simili intentione quæremus eum, qua et tu, orabimusque ut eum simul inveniamus.
paras.en: In the preceding chapter the bride said to the young maidens: [[Cant 5:8|I adjure you, O daughters of Jerusalem, if you find my beloved, that you tell him that I languish with love|Adjuro vos, filiæ Jerusalem, si inveneritis dilectum meum, ut annuntietis ei quia amore langueo]]. From these words the young maidens were moved to two questions. The first was: [[Cant 5:9|What manner of one is thy beloved|Qualis est dilectus tuus]]? To this the bride answered in the preceding chapter. The second is the one now put: [[Cant 5:17|Whither is thy beloved gone|Quo abiit dilectus tuus]], thy spouse, the Son of God, whom in what went before thou saidst thou wast seeking and hadst not found[[Cant 5:6||]]? From which we gather that he has in some way withdrawn from thee (according to the explanation in the preceding article), [[Cant 5:17|O thou most beautiful among women? whither is thy beloved turned aside, and we will seek him with thee?|o pulcherrima mulierum. Quo declinavit dilectus tuus? et quæremus eum tecum]] that is, we will help thee in seeking, and we will seek him with the same intention as thou, and we will pray that we may find him together.

paras.t: Ad hæc sponsa mater Ecclesia respondet : Dilectus meus descendit in hortum suum, id est, pie et gratiose a regalibus sedibus venit in mundum, introivit corda credentium, et me suam visitavit Ecclesiam : quia non sic recessit aut declinavit a me, quin jugiter maneat in me, id est in multis electis et sanctis ac virtuosis hominibus. Cur autem Ecclesia et quælibet anima virtuosa dicatur hortus, in expositione præcedentium patuit. Ad areolam aromatum, id est ad parvam aream, in qua aromaticæ herbæ arboresque nascuntur : hoc est ad pusillum gregem valde electorum et virtuosorum fidelium, in quibus specialiter et gratiosissime demoratur, sicut in Evangelio contestatur : Nolite timere, pusillus grex, quia complacuit Patri dare vobis regnum. Sicque per areolam aromatum, accipi possunt viri contemplativi, et veri religiosi : qui virtutum suavitate et mentis tranquillitate, bonæ quoque famæ fragrant odore, aliisque medentur in anima; ideo dici queunt aromata. De spirituali tamen significatione areolæ aromatum, dictum est plenius in præcedentibus. Ut pascatur in hortis, id est, virtuosis actibus Ecclesiæ ac congregationum fidelium delectetur, et cœnet cum eis, cooperando eisdem, ac invicem se constringant et deosculentur; et lilia colligat, id est, personas virtutum candore fulgentes, præcipue continentes ac mente puras, in suorum computet numero electorum, ac secernat a reprobis, ac demum in cœlesti collocet throno. Unde et sacratissimus dixit Joannes Baptista : Cujus ventilabrum in manu ejus, et permundabit aream suam; et triticum colliget in horrea sua, paleas autem comburet igne inextinguibili. Hinc sancto regi Josiæ dixit : Jam colligam te ad patres tuos.
paras.en: To this the bride, Mother Church, answers: [[6:1|My beloved is gone down into his garden|Dilectus meus descendit in hortum suum]]: that is, in his loving-kindness and grace he came into the world from his royal throne[[Wis 18:15||]], entered the hearts of believers, and visited me, his Church: for he has not so withdrawn or turned aside from me as not to abide in me continually, that is, in many chosen, holy and virtuous men. Why the Church, and every virtuous soul, is called a garden was made plain in the exposition of what went before[[Cant 4:12||]]. [[6:1|to the bed of aromatical spices|Ad areolam aromatum]], that is, to a little plot in which aromatic herbs and trees grow: that is, to the little flock of the truly chosen and virtuous faithful, in whom he dwells in a special way and most graciously, as he testifies in the Gospel: [[Luke 12:32|Fear not, little flock, for it hath pleased your Father to give you a kingdom|Nolite timere, pusillus grex, quia complacuit Patri dare vobis regnum]]. And so by the bed of aromatical spices may be understood contemplative men and true religious, who are fragrant with the sweetness of virtues and tranquillity of mind, and also with the odour of a good name, and heal others in soul; and so they may be called spices. Of the spiritual meaning of the bed of aromatical spices, however, more has been said above[[Cant 5:13||]]. [[6:1|to feed in the gardens|Ut pascatur in hortis]], that is, that he may take delight in the virtuous acts of the Church and of the congregations of the faithful, and sup with them[[Apoc 3:20||]], working together with them, and that they may embrace and kiss one another; [[6:1|and to gather lilies|et lilia colligat]], that is, that he may count among the number of his elect the persons who shine with the whiteness of virtues, chiefly the continent and the pure in mind, and set them apart from the reprobate, and at last place them on a heavenly throne. Whence the most holy John the Baptist also said: [[Matt 3:12|Whose fan is in his hand, and he will thoroughly cleanse his floor and gather his wheat into the barn; but the chaff he will burn with unquenchable fire|Cujus ventilabrum in manu ejus, et permundabit aream suam; et triticum colliget in horrea sua, paleas autem comburet igne inextinguibili]]. Hence he said to the holy king Josias: [[2 Par 34:28|now I will gather thee to thy fathers|Jam colligam te ad patres tuos]].

paras.t: Quum ergo hæc ita se habeant, certa sum de caritate sponsi ad me et de familiaritate ac communione ipsius, ideo fiducialiter dico : Ego dilecto meo, et dilectus meus mihi. Cui verbo simile est illud : Dilectus meus mihi, et ego illi. Unde ex dictis ibidem, patet hujus intelligentia dicti. Itaque, Ego dilecto meo, et dilectus meus mihi : id est, ego illi intenta sum, illi adhæreo, illi sum placita, ei familiariter juncta sum; ab ipso amplector, fecundor, deosculor. Quis me separabit a caritate ipsius? Ipse quoque ad me habet se dulciter, familiariter, amorose, liberaliter valde. Qui pascitur inter lilia : id est, in animabus puris suaviter redolentibus et in Ecclesiis particularibus reformatis, claustris, congregationibusque devotis delectatur, reficitur, conquiescit. Tales etenim implent desiderium sponsi, nostram salutem esurientis, et nostrum sitientis profectum.
paras.en: Since, then, these things are so, I am certain of the spouse's love towards me and of his familiarity and fellowship with me, and so I say with confidence: [[6:2|I to my beloved, and my beloved to me|Ego dilecto meo, et dilectus meus mihi]]. Like this saying is that other: [[Cant 2:16|My beloved to me, and I to him|Dilectus meus mihi, et ego illi]]; so the meaning of this saying is plain from what was said there. Thus, [[6:2|I to my beloved, and my beloved to me|Ego dilecto meo, et dilectus meus mihi]]: that is, I am intent on him, I cleave to him, I am pleasing to him, I am joined to him in familiar friendship; by him I am embraced, made fruitful, kissed. Who shall separate me from his love[[Rom 8:35||]]? He too bears himself towards me sweetly, familiarly, lovingly, and most generously. [[6:2|who feedeth among the lilies|Qui pascitur inter lilia]]: that is, he takes delight, is refreshed and finds rest in pure and sweetly fragrant souls, and in reformed particular churches, cloisters and devout congregations. For such fulfil the desire of the spouse, who hungers for our salvation and thirsts for our progress.

paras.t: Pulchra es, amica mea, suavis, et decora sicut Jerusalem : id est, tu, universalis Ecclesia mihi carissima, pulchra es intus omni ornatu virtutum, donorum, et fructuum, excellentiis meritorum ; suavis per delectationem spiritualem, ac pectoris tranquillitatem, et optimam famam ; pulcherrime quoque ordinata, et ordinate disposita per gradus et status atque officia, per ordines sacros et dignitates, ac potestates prælaticas, et copiosissimam abundantiam ministrorum ; sicut Jerusalem, id est instar Ecclesiæ triumphantis, sicut in Apocalypsi asseritur : Vidi civitatem sanctam Jerusalem novam, descendentem de cœlo : prout hoc supra clarius est inductum. Propter quod magnus Dionysius contestatur, Ecclesiam militantem se medio modo habere inter Synagogam et triumphantem Ecclesiam : quod consonat verbis Apostoli ad Hebræos : Umbram habens lex futurorum bonorum, non ipsam imaginem rerum. Vel, Sicut Jerusalem, id est instar Ecclesiæ primitivæ, quæ in urbe Jerusalem cœpit, et Spiritum Sanctum recepit, atque in omni sanctitate et justitia Domino ministravit, ac ordinatissima fuit : ex qua tota Ecclesia est exorta, et illius primitivæ Ecclesiæ vestigia, ordinem et doctrinam secuta. Vel, Sicut Jerusalem : quoniam sicut urbs illa tempore legis Mosaicæ fuit præ ceteris urbibus Terræ sanctæ ad cultum et sacrificia Dei electa, atque ad studium legis et ad sedem regni ac pontificatus assumpta ; ita Ecclesia præ cunctis gentibus ad Omnipotentis obsequium, sacrificia, regnum, et sacerdotium, electa esse cognoscitur.
paras.en: [[6:3|Thou art beautiful, O my love, sweet and comely as Jerusalem|Pulchra es, amica mea, suavis, et decora sicut Jerusalem]]: that is, thou, the universal Church, most dear to me, art beautiful within with every adornment of virtues, gifts and fruits, and with excellences of merit; sweet through spiritual delight, peace of heart, and the best of good names; most beautifully ordered too, and set out in order through degrees and states and offices, through sacred orders and dignities and the powers of prelates, and a most copious abundance of ministers; [[6:3|as Jerusalem|sicut Jerusalem]], that is, like the Church triumphant, as is said in the Apocalypse: I [[Apoc 21:2|saw the holy city, the new Jerusalem, coming down out of heaven|Vidi civitatem sanctam Jerusalem novam, descendentem de cœlo]]: as was set out more clearly above. For this reason the great Dionysius [that is, Dionysius the Areopagite, in the *Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*] declares that the Church militant stands midway between the Synagogue and the Church triumphant: which agrees with the words of the Apostle to the Hebrews: [[Heb 10:1|the law, having a shadow of the good things to come, not the very image of the things|Umbram habens lex futurorum bonorum, non ipsam imaginem rerum]]. Or, [[6:3|as Jerusalem|Sicut Jerusalem]], that is, like the primitive Church, which began in the city of Jerusalem, and received the Holy Ghost, and served the Lord in all holiness and justice, and was most perfectly ordered: from which the whole Church has sprung, and which it has followed in its footsteps, its order and its doctrine. Or, [[6:3|as Jerusalem|Sicut Jerusalem]]: because as that city, in the time of the law of Moses, was chosen above the other cities of the Holy Land for the worship and sacrifices of God, and taken up for the study of the law and to be the seat of the kingdom and the high priesthood; so the Church is known to be chosen above all nations for the service of the Almighty, for sacrifices, kingdom and priesthood.

paras.t: Terribilis ut castrorum acies ordinata. Ecclesia Christi, spirituali et sæculari potestate multiplici coordinata, miro modo vallata est ; et summi Pontificis sui auctoritas præclara est nimis, supernaturalis ac deiformis, super omnes extenta, potens excommunicare, damnare, ligare, solvere, tradere Satanæ, et reconciliare. Sub hac potestate sunt ecclesiasticæ potestates spirituales multæ ac variæ, efficaciam gloriosam habentes. Deinde sequuntur potestates sæculares, imperialis, regalis, ducalis, et comitalis. Insuper sancta Ecclesia circummunita atque vallata et cincta est sui auxilio, præsentia protectioneque Salvatoris, tanquam muro et antemurali, angelorum quoque custodia, et prælatorum suorum diligentia pastorali. Roborata quoque est per dona gratiæ gratificantis ac gratiæ gratis datæ, per sapientiam et virtutes, per signa atque miracula, et toto orbe terrarum diffusa, meritis ac multitudine personarum ineffabiliter firmata. Verissime ergo terribilis est adversariis et rebellibus, spiritibusque malignis, sicut castrorum acies ordinata : intelligendo per castra, multitudinem fortalitiorum ad invicem bene dispositam : quam intueri, formidinem incutit potissime hostibus. Vel intelligendo per castrorum aciem ordinatam, grandem et fortem exercitum pugnatorum ac militum, convenienter coordinatum ac prudenter dispositum, non nimis constrictum, nec nimis patentem, ita ut ab adversariis penetrari, seu ab invicem separari non valeat : imo invicem bene concordem ac mutuo se stipantem, per quod exercitus talis, est hostibus suis maxime metuendus. Si autem inter se discors sit aut divisus, ac inordinate et imprudenter dispositus, non est nisi victima ac ridiculum adversariæ potestatis. Sic plane universitas Christianorum, per fidem, spem, caritatem concordans, sapienter disposita, et se invicem juvans, fortissima terribilisque consistit. Porro si per hæreses et schismata dividatur, seu per discordiam contra se invicem prælietur ; jam mox gaudent de ea adversarii ejus, cernentes eam sic debilitari et impugnabilem fieri.
paras.en: [[6:3|terrible as an army set in array|Terribilis ut castrorum acies ordinata]]. The Church of Christ, ordered together by manifold power, spiritual and secular, is wonderfully fortified; and the authority of her supreme Pontiff is exceeding glorious, supernatural and godlike, extending over all, with power to excommunicate, condemn, bind, loose, deliver to Satan, and reconcile. Under this power are many and various spiritual powers of the Church, which have a glorious efficacy. Then follow the secular powers: imperial, royal, ducal and comital. Moreover holy Church is fortified, walled and girded about by the help, presence and protection of her Saviour, as by [[Is 26:1|a wall and a bulwark|muro et antemurali]], and also by the guard of the angels and the pastoral diligence of her prelates. She is strengthened too by the gifts of sanctifying grace and of grace freely given [that is, the grace that makes the soul pleasing to God, and the gifts, such as prophecy or miracles, given for the good of others], by wisdom and virtues, by signs and miracles; and, spread over the whole world, she is made unspeakably firm by the merits and the multitude of her members. Most truly, then, she is terrible to her adversaries and rebels and to the evil spirits, [[6:3|as an army set in array|sicut castrorum acies ordinata]]: understanding by *castra* [camps] a number of fortresses well placed in relation to one another, the sight of which strikes fear above all into enemies. Or understanding by the army set in array [*castrorum acies*, literally "the battle line of the camps"] a great and strong army of fighting men and soldiers, fittingly ordered together and prudently disposed, neither too closely packed nor too open, so that it cannot be broken through by its adversaries or parted within itself, but is well united and closely massed together: by which such an army is most to be feared by its enemies. But if it is at strife within or divided, and disposed without order or prudence, it is nothing but a victim and a laughing-stock to the opposing power. So plainly the whole body of Christians, agreeing in faith, hope and charity, wisely ordered and helping one another, stands most strong and terrible. But if it is divided by heresies and schisms, or wars against itself through discord, at once its adversaries rejoice over it, seeing it so weakened and laid open to attack [the text has *impugnabilem*, which would normally mean "unassailable"; the sense requires "assailable"].

paras.t: Averte oculos tuos a me, quia ipsi me avolare fecerunt. In his verbis ad inflammandum cor sponsæ, videtur sponsus loqui per modum fervidissimi amatoris, ita devicti amore suæ dilectæ, ut eam non audeat intueri, ne ex illius inspectione lædatur ex vehementia prædominantis amoris : quam quanto diligentius ac diuturnius intuetur, tanto plus amore illius accenditur et torquetur. Itaque ait sponsus cœlestis carissimæ suæ Ecclesiæ : Averte oculos tuos a me, id est, tam intense te diligo, ut ardorem hujus amoris plenius exprimere nequeam, nisi te quasi hortando, ut cesses ad tempus me intueri orando, meditando, psallendo, et contemplando : quia oculi tui pudicissimi, columbini, fecerunt me avolare, id est, ad tempus subtrahere me tibi, quantum ad dulcem consolatoriamque præsentiam, ut fructuosius quæras me ; fecerunt me quoque avolare, id est, de cœlo ad terram pro tua salute descendere. Potest et ita exponi : Averte oculos tuos interiores a me, id est, non coneris me comprehendere velle, nec contemplando sis perscrutatrix curiosa majestatis meæ immensæ : quia ipsi me avolare fecerunt, id est, quoties me taliter vis videre, causa es quod capacitatem tuam me transcendere pando, et incomprehensibilem me esse tibi ostendo. Ideo dixit Psalmista : Mirabilis facta est scientia tua ex me : confortata est, et non potero ad eam. Et alibi scriptum est : Dixi, Sapiens efficiar ; et ipsa longius recessit a me. Quidam exponunt sic : Averte oculos tuos a me, id est, oculos cupiditatis, erroris, et carnalis amoris, quos aliquando habuisti, de cetero omnino abjicias, et a meo tollas adspectu : quia ipsi me avolare fecerunt, id est, propter eos recessi ab habentibus oculos tales, vel eos penitus relinquendo, aut ad tempus, quousque hujuscemodi oculi cruerentur ab eis.
paras.en: [[6:4|Turn away thy eyes from me, for they have made me flee away|Averte oculos tuos a me, quia ipsi me avolare fecerunt]]. In these words, to inflame the heart of the bride, the spouse seems to speak in the manner of a most ardent lover, so overcome by love of his beloved that he dare not look upon her, lest the sight of her wound him through the vehemence of the love that masters him: for the more attentively and the longer he looks on her, the more he is kindled and tormented with love of her. And so the heavenly spouse says to his dearest Church: [[6:4|Turn away thy eyes from me|Averte oculos tuos a me]], that is, I love thee so intensely that I cannot express the ardour of this love more fully than by, as it were, urging thee to cease for a time to gaze on me in prayer, meditation, psalmody and contemplation: for thy most chaste, dove-like eyes have made me flee away, that is, withdraw myself from thee for a time as to my sweet and consoling presence, so that thou mayest seek me more fruitfully; they have made me flee away also, that is, come down from heaven to earth for thy salvation. It may also be expounded thus: [[6:4|Turn away thy eyes|Averte oculos tuos]], thy inner eyes, from me, that is, do not try to comprehend me, nor be in contemplation a curious searcher of my boundless majesty[[Prov 25:27||]]: [[6:4|for they have made me flee away|quia ipsi me avolare fecerunt]], that is, whenever thou wouldst see me in such a way, thou art the cause that I reveal that I pass beyond thy capacity, and show myself incomprehensible to thee. Therefore the Psalmist said: [[Ps 138:6|Thy knowledge is become wonderful to me: it is high, and I cannot reach to it|Mirabilis facta est scientia tua ex me : confortata est, et non potero ad eam]]. And elsewhere it is written: [[Eccles 7:24|I have said: I will be wise: and it departed farther from me|Dixi, Sapiens efficiar ; et ipsa longius recessit a me]]. Some expound it thus: [[6:4|Turn away thy eyes from me|Averte oculos tuos a me]], that is, the eyes of covetousness, error and carnal love which thou hadst once, cast them away altogether henceforth and take them from my sight: [[6:4|for they have made me flee away|quia ipsi me avolare fecerunt]], that is, because of them I withdrew from those who have such eyes, either leaving them altogether, or for a time, until eyes of this kind should be plucked out of them.

paras.t: Capilli tui sicut grex caprarum, quæ apparuerunt de Galaad. Dentes tui sicut greges ovium, quæ ascenderunt de lavacro, omnes gemellis fetibus, et sterilis non est in eis. Ista quarto capitulo scripta sunt atque exposita. Porro quod subditur, Sicut cortex mali punici, ita genæ tuæ absque occultis tuis, coincidit cum eo quod scriptum est, Sicut fragmen mali punici, ita genæ tuæ, absque eo quod intrinsecus latet : nisi quod hic dicitur, Sicut cortex, ibi, Sicut fragmen. Cortex autem malogranati forinsecus durus est, asper, deformis ; intus vero albescens, continet grana alba : sic genæ Ecclesiæ arduam vitam gerentis, quæ foris adversitatibus exercetur : fructum habet internum pulchrum ac dulcem, imo et aliorum fecundativum, dum acceptam gratiam in proximos administrat.
paras.en: [[6:4|Thy hair is as a flock of goats, that appear from Galaad|Capilli tui sicut grex caprarum, quæ apparuerunt de Galaad]]. [[6:5|Thy teeth as a flock of sheep, which come up from the washing, all with twins, and there is none barren among them|Dentes tui sicut greges ovium, quæ ascenderunt de lavacro, omnes gemellis fetibus, et sterilis non est in eis]]. These things were written and expounded in the fourth chapter[[Cant 4:1||]][[Cant 4:2||]]. Further, what follows, [[6:6|Thy cheeks are as the bark of a pomegranate, beside what is hidden within thee|Sicut cortex mali punici, ita genæ tuæ absque occultis tuis]], coincides with what is written there, [[Cant 4:3|Thy cheeks are as a piece of a pomegranate, besides that which lieth hid within|Sicut fragmen mali punici, ita genæ tuæ, absque eo quod intrinsecus latet]]: except that here it says [[6:6|as the bark|Sicut cortex]], there, [[Cant 4:3|as a piece|Sicut fragmen]]. Now the rind of the pomegranate is hard outside, rough and unsightly, but whitish within, and holds white seeds: so the cheeks of the Church, which leads a hard life and is exercised outwardly by adversities, have a fruit within that is beautiful and sweet, and indeed makes others fruitful too, while she ministers to her neighbours the grace she has received.

paras.t: Sexaginta sunt reginæ, et octoginta concubinæ, et adolescentularum non est numerus. Quamvis sapientissimus Salomon in senio suo extreme infatuatus, multas valde habuerit uxores regales et concubinas et adolescentulas ; istud tamen de ipso ad litteram non potest intelligi, quum in libro Regum scriptum sit : Fuerunt ei uxores quasi reginæ, septingentæ, et concubinæ trecentæ. Hoc quoque probat Augustinus, affirmans Salomonem scripsisse hunc librum suæ tempore juventutis. Per mulieres autem sic depravatus est tempore senectutis. De hoc loquitur Augustinus, disputans contra Faustum Manichæorum episcopum. Intelligendum est ergo de Christo et credentium animabus. Quidam autem per sexaginta reginas, intelligunt animas hominum perfectorum, non propter numeri quantitatem, sed propter mysterii significationem. Sexagenarius namque consurgit ex senario atque denario in se ductis. Denarius vero impletionem signat Decalogi. Senarius, qui dicitur primus numerus perfectus, denotat perfectionem meritoriæ actionis, non tantum quantum ad observantiam præceptorum, sed etiam consiliorum, et quantum ad opera supererogationis. Per octoginta demum concubinas, intelligunt animas proficientium : quæ non pertingunt ad principales atque præcipuos illos sponsi amplexus, ad quos perductæ sunt animæ perfectorum, sed adspirant ad eos ; nec ita legitimum proferunt fructum virtutum, ut illæ. Octonarius namque, secundum Augustinum, est numerus diminutus et imperfectus : quoniam partes ipsius simul sumptæ, minus efficiunt, quam suum totum. Per adolescentulas autem innumeras, accipiunt animas incipientium, quæ multæ sunt nimis. Similiter per reginas, possunt intelligi animæ virginum devotarum ; per concubinas, animæ viduarum ; per adolescentulas, animæ conjugatorum. At vero Gregorius per reginas intelligit animas sanctorum, qui se laudabiliter regunt, et carnem rationi omnino subjiciunt ; per concubinas, quæ non prolem legitimam, sed voluptatem exquirunt, falsos prædicatores, qui nec Christi honorem, nec audientium salutem, sed propriam quærunt laudem et commoda sua ; per adolescentulas vero, animas vanitatibus atque lasciviis deditas, quarum numerus ignoratur.
paras.en: [[6:7|There are threescore queens, and fourscore concubines, and young maidens without number|Sexaginta sunt reginæ, et octoginta concubinæ, et adolescentularum non est numerus]]. Although the most wise Solomon, utterly besotted in his old age, had very many royal wives and concubines and young maidens, yet this cannot be understood of him literally, since it is written in the book of Kings: [[3 Kings 11:3|he had seven hundred wives as queens, and three hundred concubines|Fuerunt ei uxores quasi reginæ, septingentæ, et concubinæ trecentæ]]. Augustine also proves this, affirming that Solomon wrote this book in the time of his youth; it was in the time of his old age that he was so corrupted by women. Augustine speaks of this in his disputation against Faustus, bishop of the Manichees. It is to be understood, then, of Christ and the souls of believers. Now some understand by the threescore queens the souls of perfect men, not because of the size of the number but because of the meaning of the mystery. For sixty arises from six and ten multiplied together. Ten signifies the fulfilment of the Decalogue. Six, which is called the first perfect number [that is, a number equal to the sum of its parts: 1 + 2 + 3 = 6], denotes the perfection of meritorious action, not only as regards the keeping of the commandments but also of the counsels, and as regards works of supererogation. By the fourscore concubines, again, they understand the souls of those making progress, which do not attain to those chief and principal embraces of the spouse to which the souls of the perfect have been brought, but aspire to them; nor do they bring forth so lawful a fruit of virtues as those. For eight, according to Augustine [the margin gives *De Genesi ad litteram*, c. ii], is a deficient and imperfect number, because its parts taken together make less than their whole [1 + 2 + 4 = 7]. By the young maidens without number they take the souls of beginners, who are very many. Likewise by the queens may be understood the souls of devout virgins; by the concubines, the souls of widows; by the young maidens, the souls of the married. But Gregory understands by the queens the souls of the saints, who rule themselves in praiseworthy fashion and subject the flesh wholly to reason; by the concubines, who seek not lawful offspring but pleasure, false preachers, who seek neither the honour of Christ nor the salvation of their hearers, but their own praise and advantage; and by the young maidens, souls given over to vanities and wantonness, whose number is not known.

paras.t: Una est columba mea, perfecta mea : id est, quamvis diversæ sint animæ seu personæ fideles, magis aut minus virtuosæ, quæ deficere possunt ac cadere et spiritualiter constuprari ; una est tamen sponsa mea jugiter sancta, a columbina simplicitate nunquam deficiens, et sanctitatem in se ac perfectionem inviolabiliter continens ; quæ errare non valet, nec tota deficere, quia a Spiritu Sancto gubernatur ac conservatur, utpote universalis Ecclesia militans: quæ una est unitate fidei, spei, et caritatis, unione veræ concordiæ, et per eadem media ad eamdem finem salvificum tendens. De qua ait Apostolus: Elegit sibi gloriosam Ecclesiam, non habentem maculam neque rugam. Quod quamvis pro statu futuro magis convenire Ecclesiæ, secundum Hieronymum super Jeremiam, et secundum Bernardum in sermone; tamen et pro statu præsenti aliqualiter competit ei: quoniam quantum ad membra sua viva, caret mortalium vitiorum et pravarum intentionum ruga ac macula, et semper habet in se aliquas sanctas personas. Totum autem a suis partibus denominationem sortitur, imo denominationes diversas et quasi contrarias, sicut hæc ipsa Ecclesia dicitur sancta et deformata, virgo et meretrix, secundum expositores nonnullos super illud Isaiæ: Quomodo facta est meretrix urbs fidelis? quoniam quidam in Ecclesia Deo pura mente adhærent, plures vero mente, imo et corpore fornicantur ab eo, prout in Moralibus super Job diffuse tractat Gregorius.
paras.en: [[6:8|One is my dove, my perfect one|Una est columba mea, perfecta mea]]: that is, although the faithful souls or persons are diverse, more or less virtuous, and can fail and fall and be spiritually defiled, yet my bride is one, ever holy, never falling away from the simplicity of the dove, and keeping holiness and perfection within her inviolably; who cannot err nor wholly fail, because she is governed and preserved by the Holy Ghost, being the universal Church militant: which is one by unity of faith, hope and charity, by the union of true concord, and tends by the same means to the same saving end. Of her the Apostle says: He chose for himself [[Eph 5:27|a glorious church, not having spot or wrinkle|gloriosam Ecclesiam, non habentem maculam neque rugam]] [the Apostle's word is "present" (*exhiberet*), Denis has "chose" (*elegit*)]. And although this befits the Church rather in her future state, according to Jerome on Jeremias and to Bernard in a sermon, yet it belongs to her in some measure in her present state too: since, as regards her living members, she is without the wrinkle and spot of mortal sins and wicked intentions, and always has some holy persons in her. Now a whole takes its name from its parts, and indeed diverse and as it were contrary names, as this same Church is called holy and deformed, virgin and harlot, according to some expositors on that saying of Isaias: [[Is 1:21|How is the faithful city, that was full of judgment, become a harlot?|Quomodo facta est meretrix urbs fidelis?]] because some in the Church cleave to God with a pure mind, but more commit fornication away from him in mind, and indeed in body too, as Gregory treats at length in the *Morals on Job*.

paras.t: Una est matri suæ, electa genitrici suæ : id est, hæc ipsa venerabilis Ecclesia, subsistit et est ad laudem et gloriam pietatis et gratiæ Dei, seu increatæ sapientiæ ejus: quæ pietas, gratia, sapientia, mater totius Ecclesiæ appellatur, quia per dona gratiæ justificantis eam regenerat, fovet, maternaliterque custodit. Et potest per matrem, gratia baptismalis intelligi, quæ originaliter regenerat animas, tanquam janua sacramentorum. Mater quoque totius Ecclesiæ, potest vocari primitiva illa Ecclesia, sub Apostolorum regimine in Jerusalem inchoata, a qua tota Ecclesia est exorta, juxta illud in Isaia: De Sion exibit lex, et verbum Domini de Jerusalem. Juxta illius primitivæ Ecclesiæ institutionem, regulam, ac doctrinam, subsistit et conversatur universalis Ecclesia: quod etiam ad primitivæ Ecclesiæ magnum cedit præconium et honorem, et ad gloriæ ejus augmentum. Rursus, per matrem et genitricem Ecclesiæ militantis, intelligitur triumphans Ecclesia, quæ militantem meritis suis præcibusque tuetur. Nam et gaudium est angelis Dei super uno peccatore pœnitentiam agente.
paras.en: [[6:8|she is the only one of her mother, the chosen of her that bore her|Una est matri suæ, electa genitrici suæ]]: that is, this same venerable Church subsists and exists to the praise and glory of the loving-kindness and grace of God, or of his uncreated wisdom: which loving-kindness, grace and wisdom is called the mother of the whole Church, because by the gifts of justifying grace it regenerates her, cherishes her, and guards her like a mother. And by the mother may be understood baptismal grace, which first regenerates souls, as the door of the sacraments. The mother of the whole Church may also be called that primitive Church begun in Jerusalem under the rule of the Apostles, from which the whole Church has sprung, according to that saying in Isaias: [[Is 2:3|the law shall come forth from Sion, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem|De Sion exibit lex, et verbum Domini de Jerusalem]]. It is according to the institution, rule and doctrine of that primitive Church that the universal Church subsists and lives: which also redounds to the great praise and honour of the primitive Church and to the increase of her glory. Again, by the mother and her that bore the Church militant is understood the Church triumphant, which protects the Church militant by her merits and prayers. For there is [[Luke 15:10|joy before the angels of God upon one sinner doing penance|gaudium est angelis Dei super uno peccatore pœnitentiam agente]].

paras.t: Viderunt eam filiæ Sion, id est præfatæ adolescentulæ seu animæ de novo conversæ: quæ sunt filiæ Sion, id est filiæ speculationis per fidem; quæ vident per speculum in ænigmate, et virtutes sanctæ matris Ecclesiæ intuendo, mirantur et laudant eam; et beatissimam prædicaverunt reginæ, de quibus jam dictum est: id est, animæ perfectorum acutius considerando dona et privilegia almæ matri Ecclesiæ præstita, fassæ sunt eam beatissimam esse in spe, inchoatione, merito ac prælibatione. Nempe quo Ecclesia sanctior gratiosiorque consistit, eo hoc modo beatior perhibetur. Et concubinæ laudaverunt eam, tanquam omni alia congregatione et plebe præclariorem.
paras.en: [[6:8|The daughters saw her|Viderunt eam filiæ]] [Denis's text reads "the daughters of Sion"], that is, the young maidens spoken of before, or souls newly converted: who are daughters of Sion, that is, daughters of watching, through faith [*speculatio*, "watching" or "looking out", the usual meaning given for the name Sion; Denis plays on it with *speculum*, "glass", just after]; who see [[1 Cor 13:12|through a glass in a dark manner|per speculum in ænigmate]], and, looking on the virtues of holy Mother Church, wonder at her and praise her; [[6:8|and declared her most blessed: the queens|et beatissimam prædicaverunt reginæ]], of whom we have already spoken: that is, the souls of the perfect, considering more keenly the gifts and privileges granted to our kindly mother the Church, have confessed her to be most blessed in hope, in beginning, in merit and in foretaste. For the holier and more full of grace the Church is, the more blessed she is said to be in this way. [[6:8|and concubines, and they praised her|Et concubinæ laudaverunt eam]], as more glorious than every other congregation and people.

paras.t: Quæ est ista quæ progreditur? id est, quam venusta, commendabilis et præclara, est universalis Ecclesia! pergens de via hujus exilii ad æternæ patriam claritatis, non quiescens per torporem, quamdiu in hujus vitæ versatur curriculo; quasi aurora consurgens, id est, de imperfecto ad perfectiora jugiter properans, a tenebris ignorantiæ ad lucem sapientiæ scandens, a via purgativa per illuminativam ad unitivam ascendens; pulchra ut luna: quoniam a Sole justitiæ omnem, quam habet, accipit lucem et claritatem, sapientiam et virtutem. Et sicut luna illuminat noctem, ac inter nocturna sidera lucet splendidius; ita Ecclesia illustrat, docet, et dirigit sedentes in tenebris et umbra mortis hujus sæculi. Et cunctis in hoc mundo sapientior invenitur, determinans quid de necessitate salutis oporteat credere, agere, et tenere. Electa ut sol: quoniam sponsa est Solis æterni, et ei in perfectione similior, ad eamdem beatitudinem prædestinata atque ventura, ad quam ille secundum assumptam naturam electus est ac pervenit; terribilis ut castrorum acies ordinata : quod præcedenti capitulo expositum est.
paras.en: [[6:9|Who is she that cometh forth|Quæ est ista quæ progreditur]]? that is, how lovely, how commendable and how glorious is the universal Church! going on from the way of this exile to the fatherland of eternal brightness, not resting in sloth as long as she is passing along the course of this life; [[6:9|as the morning rising|quasi aurora consurgens]], that is, hastening ever from the imperfect to the more perfect, climbing from the darkness of ignorance to the light of wisdom, ascending from the purgative way through the illuminative to the unitive; [[6:9|fair as the moon|pulchra ut luna]]: because from the Sun of justice she receives all the light and brightness, wisdom and virtue that she has. And as the moon lights up the night, and shines more brightly among the stars of night, so the Church enlightens, teaches and directs [[Luke 1:79|them that sit in darkness and in the shadow of death|sedentes in tenebris et umbra mortis]] of this world. And she is found wiser than all in this world, determining what must be believed, done and held as necessary for salvation. [[6:9|bright as the sun|Electa ut sol]] [*electa*, literally "chosen"]: because she is the bride of the eternal Sun, and more like him in perfection, predestined to the same beatitude, and on her way to it, to which he, according to the nature he assumed, was chosen and came; [[6:9|terrible as an army set in array|terribilis ut castrorum acies ordinata]]: which was explained in the preceding chapter [in fact it was explained above, at v. 3].

paras.t: Descendi in hortum nucum. Istud tam de Christo quam de universali Ecclesia potest exponi. Christus ergo per suæ pietatis condescensionem et opem, descendit in hortum nucum, id est ad congregationem fidelium atque constantium personarum, quæ arduam ducunt vitam, et instar nucum contemptibiles foris videntur. Imo per soliditatem virtutum fortiter sunt contra suæ salutis hostes muniti, sicut nux forti ac ligneo tegitur tegumento; intus vero dulcem continet fructum, devotionem internam, mentis tranquillitatem, conscientiæ puritatem, contemplationisque gratiam, ac divini fervorem amoris, sicut nux nucleum. Et sicut ex nucleo extrahitur oleum, sic ex illorum virtutibus compassio, pietas ac vera devotio. Et sicut nux in exordio corticem habet humidum, mollem ac viridem, qui veniente maturitate aret ac decidit : sic perfecti in suæ conversionis initio vallati erant et cooperti propriæ carnis et sensualitatis mollitie, fervore, atque humore; sed virtutum adveniente maturitate, caro et sensualitas aruerunt, edomitæ ac repressæ.
paras.en: [[6:10|I went down into the garden of nuts|Descendi in hortum nucum]]. This may be expounded both of Christ and of the universal Church. Christ, then, by the condescension and help of his loving-kindness, went down into the garden of nuts, that is, to the congregation of faithful and steadfast persons, who lead a hard life and, like nuts, seem contemptible outwardly. Yet by the solidity of their virtues they are strongly armed against the enemies of their salvation, as a nut is covered by a strong, woody shell; but within it holds a sweet fruit, interior devotion, tranquillity of mind, purity of conscience, the grace of contemplation and the fervour of divine love, as the nut holds its kernel. And as oil is drawn from the kernel, so from their virtues come compassion, loving-kindness and true devotion. And as the nut at first has a husk that is moist, soft and green, which dries and falls off when ripeness comes, so the perfect, at the beginning of their conversion, were hemmed in and covered by the softness, heat and moisture of their own flesh and sensuality; but when the ripeness of the virtues came, the flesh and sensuality dried up, tamed and kept down.

paras.t: Ut viderem poma convallium, id est, minus perfectos attenderem ac juvarem, imo et in humilitatis imo positos approbarem. Tamen per poma possunt et nuces intelligi, quoniam omnis arborum fructus comestibilis, communi nomine pomum vocatur : sicut in Evangelio fertur de ficu, quam Christus accessit, quod non erat tempus pomi illius. Denique, per superiores et perfectiores Christus visitat, dirigit, et adjuvat minus perfectos : quos tamen interius tangit multoties per se ipsum. Et inspicerem, si floruissent vineæ, id est, an particulares Ecclesiæ seu congregationes, claustra, collegia, ad fructum spiritualis vini essent dispositæ, et floribus salubrium meditationum piarumque affectionum ornatæ ac fecundatæ; et germinassent mala punica, id est, an fructuosi essent, qui in statu contemplationis et igneæ caritatis sunt positi, et quorum est dominicam passionem jugiter ferre in corde, ac prælati quorum præcipue est ad sanguinis effusionem pro fide ac justitia esse paratos (ut instar malorum punicorum rubeant intus), et [qui] contemplationis ac dilectionis, bonæque famæ odore ac suavitate ornantur ac fragrant, et alios attrahunt. Christus itaque tanquam pastor bonus, visitat suam Ecclesiam in singulis gradibus ac statibus ejus, et ab unoquoque requirit, ut secundum exigentiam suæ vocationis fructificet. Insuper ipsa Ecclesia synodaliter congregata, seu ejus prælati et ipsa per suos prælatos, considerat, visitat, et reformare conatur particulares Ecclesias, et singulos gradus ac ordines.
paras.en: [[6:10|to see the fruits of the valleys|Ut viderem poma convallium]], that is, that I might attend to and help the less perfect, and indeed approve those set in the lowest place of humility. Yet by *fruits* the nuts too may be understood, since every edible fruit of trees is called by the common name *pomum* [fruit; the word used here for the fruits of the valleys], as is said in the Gospel of the fig tree to which Christ came, that it was not the season of its fruit[[Mark 11:13||]]. Further, Christ visits, directs and helps the less perfect through their superiors and those more perfect; yet he often touches them inwardly by himself. [[6:10|and to look if the vineyard had flourished|Et inspicerem, si floruissent vineæ]] [Denis reads *vineæ*, "the vineyards"], that is, whether the particular churches or congregations, cloisters and colleges, were disposed to the fruit of spiritual wine, and adorned and made fruitful with the flowers of wholesome meditations and devout affections; [[6:10|and the pomegranates budded|et germinassent mala punica]], that is, whether they were fruitful who are placed in the state of contemplation and of fiery charity, and whose part it is to bear the Lord's passion continually in their heart; and the prelates, whose part above all it is to be ready to shed their blood for the faith and for justice (so as to be red within like pomegranates); and those who are adorned and fragrant with the odour and sweetness of contemplation and love and of a good name, and draw others. Christ, then, like a good shepherd[[John 10:11||]][[John 10:14||]], visits his Church in each of her degrees and states, and requires of each one that he bear fruit as his calling demands. Moreover the Church herself, gathered in synod, or her prelates, and she herself through her prelates, considers, visits and strives to reform the particular churches, and each degree and order.

paras.t: Subditur in persona Synagogæ, in fine sæculi convertendæ : Nescivi, id est, dignitatem, sanctitatem, et gratiam Ecclesiæ Christi non consideravi, nec novi. Cujus annectitur ratio : Anima mea, id est voluntas seu ratio male disposita, seu animalis affectio, conturbavit, id est, inquietavit et a veritatis consideratione impedivit me propter quadrigas Aminadab, id est, ex consideratione potestatis et magnificentiæ, virtutis et gratiæ regni Juda : quod designatur per Aminadab, de cujus stirpe reges regni Juda progeniti sunt; et per quadrigas illius, fortitudo et excellentia regni illius insinuantur. Atque (ut dicitur) Aminadab cum tribu Juda primo post Moysen ingrediendo fundum maris Rubri siccatum, promeruit regium sceptrum, ceteris tribubus Moysen sequi timentibus. Judæi autem usque in præsens, considerando quam mirabiliter et præclare lex vetus per Moysen data fuit et confirmata et inclyte conservata, præcipue a populo tribus Juda, atque ibidem per Prophetas et signa præconizata, renuunt credere legem illam per legem evangelicam esse evacuatam, et Jesum, legis Mosaicæ exterminatorem, esse divinitus missum.
paras.en: There follows, in the person of the Synagogue, which is to be converted at the end of the world: [[6:11|I knew not|Nescivi]], that is, I did not consider nor know the dignity, holiness and grace of the Church of Christ. The reason is added: [[6:11|my soul|Anima mea]], that is, my will or reason ill disposed, or my animal affection, [[6:11|troubled me|conturbavit]], that is, disquieted me and kept me from considering the truth, [[6:11|for the chariots of Aminadab|propter quadrigas Aminadab]], that is, from considering the power [the margin gives a variant, *pietatis*, "loving-kindness"] and magnificence, the might and grace of the kingdom of Juda: which is signified by Aminadab, from whose stock the kings of the kingdom of Juda were born; and by his chariots [*quadrigæ*, chariots drawn by four horses] the strength and excellence of that kingdom are suggested. And (as is said) Aminadab, with the tribe of Juda, by being the first after Moses to go down into the dried-up bed of the Red Sea[[Ex 14:22||]], earned the royal sceptre, while the other tribes were afraid to follow Moses. But the Jews to this day, considering how wonderfully and gloriously the old law was given through Moses[[John 1:17||]], and confirmed, and nobly preserved, chiefly by the people of the tribe of Juda, and foretold there by the Prophets and by signs, refuse to believe that that law has been made void by the law of the Gospel, and that Jesus, the destroyer of the law of Moses, was sent by God.

paras.t: Expositores vero communiter per quadrigas Aminadab, intelligunt quatuor Evangelia Christi, et primos eorumdem prædicatores, sanctos Apostolos, qui evangelizando tanquam quadrigæ discurrerunt per mundum, circumferentes Jesum et Evangelium ejus ubique terrarum. Aminadab quippe interpretatur, spontaneus populi mei : sicque per Aminadab accipitur Christus, qui Patre volente, spontaneus pro salute populi sui venit ad passionem, sicut testatur : Nemo tollit animam meam a me, sed ego pono eam. De quo Isaias prædixit : Oblatus est, quia voluit. Qui Christus etiam in Psalmo fatetur : In capite libri scriptum est de me, ut facerem voluntatem tuam : Deus meus, volui, et legem tuam in medio cordis mei. Conturbata est igitur Synagoga propter quadrigas Aminadab, id est ex prædicatione Evangelii Christi, quoniam interim perturbatur propria incredulitate, et ad contradicendum movetur propter diversa motiva, tamen irrationabilia et insufficientia ac faciliter solubilia. In fine autem concutietur ad credendum Evangelio Salvatoris, prædicantibus Elia et Enoch.
paras.en: But the expositors commonly understand by the chariots of Aminadab the four Gospels of Christ, and their first preachers, the holy Apostles, who in preaching the gospel ran through the world like chariots[[Mark 16:15||]][[Rom 15:19||]], carrying Jesus and his Gospel about everywhere on earth. For Aminadab is interpreted "the willing one of my people": and so by Aminadab is taken Christ, who, by the Father's will, came willingly to his passion for the salvation of his people, as he testifies: [[John 10:18|No man taketh it away from me: but I lay it down|Nemo tollit animam meam a me, sed ego pono eam]]. Of him Isaias foretold: [[Is 53:7|He was offered because it was his own will|Oblatus est, quia voluit]]. And Christ also confesses in the Psalm: [[Ps 39:8|In the head of the book it is written of me|In capite libri scriptum est de me]], [[Ps 39:9|That I should do thy will: O my God, I have desired it, and thy law in the midst of my heart|ut facerem voluntatem tuam : Deus meus, volui, et legem tuam in medio cordis mei]]. The Synagogue, then, was troubled for the chariots of Aminadab, that is, by the preaching of the Gospel of Christ, since for the present she is disturbed by her own unbelief, and moved to contradict for various reasons, which are yet unreasonable and insufficient and easily answered. But at the end she will be stirred to believe the Gospel of the Saviour, when Elias and Enoch preach.

paras.t: Denique, ut aliqui dicunt, Aminadab non est hic nomen proprium, nec una dictio secundum Hebræos; sed nomen commune, seu potius duo nomina appellativa, significantia populum principantem : quod ad prætactam potest expositionem reduci.
paras.en: Lastly, as some say, Aminadab is not here a proper name, nor one word according to the Hebrews, but a common noun, or rather two common nouns, meaning a ruling people [in Hebrew *ammi nadib*, "my people, a prince"]: which can be brought back to the exposition touched on above.

paras.t: Consequenter Ecclesia hortatur Synagogam ad conversionem. Revertere, revertere, Sunamitis : revertere, revertere, ut intueamur te : id est, tu, plebs Israelitica, redi ad verum Messiam Jesum, crede in eum, revertere ad fidem patrum sanctorum : sicut Malachias prædixit, quod Elias convertet cor filiorum ad patres eorum.
paras.en: Then the Church exhorts the Synagogue to conversion: [[6:12|Return, return, O Sulamitess: return, return that we may behold thee|Revertere, revertere, Sunamitis : revertere, revertere, ut intueamur te]] [Denis reads *Sunamitis*, "Sunamitess", where the Douay-Rheims has Sulamitess]: that is, thou, people of Israel, come back to the true Messias, Jesus, believe in him, return to the faith of the holy fathers: as Malachias foretold that Elias[[Mal 4:5||]] shall turn [[Mal 4:6|the heart of the children to their fathers|cor filiorum ad patres eorum]].

paras.t: Revertere ad pœnitentiam, ad obedientiam, perseverantiamque finalem. Revertere a quatuor plagis terræ, ab hac extrema captivitate, ab indurata excæcatione, ad credendum, ad obediendum omnibus quæ in quatuor Evangeliis credi seu impleri jubentur. Recte demum per Sunamitem, intelligitur plebs Hebræa, nunc captivata et aspernata : quoniam Sunamitis, captiva seu despecta interpretatur; et quoniam Suna civitas erat terræ promissionis, de qua pulcherrima illa Abisag, ultima David regis conjux, fuit, ut patet tertio Regum : quæ et frequenter Sunamitis vocata est.
paras.en: Return to penance, to obedience, and to final perseverance. Return from the four quarters of the earth, from this last captivity, from hardened blindness, to believing and to obeying all that the four Gospels command to be believed or fulfilled. Rightly, lastly, is the Hebrew people, now taken captive and despised, understood by the Sunamitess: for *Sunamitis* is interpreted "captive" or "despised"; and because Suna was a city of the land of promise[[Jos 19:18||]] [the Douay-Rheims has Sunem], from which came that most beautiful Abisag, the last wife of King David, as is plain in the third book of Kings[[3 Kings 1:3||]]: who is also often called the Sunamitess.

paras.t: Postremo huic caritativæ ac piæ petitioni Ecclesiæ Deus cito adsistens ac favens, respondet Ecclesiæ : Quid videbis in Sunamite, nisi choros castrorum? tanquam dicat : O Ecclesia, fiet quod exhortaris, in tantum quod Synagoga in fine convertenda, erit tam fortis in fide, tam roborata in spe, et accensa in caritate, ac omni sapientia et virtute munita, angelicis spiritibus circumvallata, ac multis agminibus credentium copiosa, quod non videbis in ea nisi choros castrorum, id est societates militantium Deo, quia pro Deo ac fide mori erunt parati. Choros quoque castrorum, id est acies et connexiones gratiarum, virtutum, donorum ac aliorum charismatum divinorum : ita quod quæ diu jam ante contra fidem pugnavit, de cetero tecum pro fidei defensione, contra Antichristum seu alios perfidos, dimicabit. Dicit autem Methodius martyr ac præsul in suo libello, quod centum quadraginta quatuor millia Judæorum tunc crediturorum, occidentur ab Antichristo.
paras.en: Finally God, quickly assisting and favouring this charitable and devout petition of the Church, answers the Church: [[Cant 7:1|What shalt thou see in the Sulamitess but the companies of camps?|Quid videbis in Sunamite, nisi choros castrorum?]] as if to say: O Church, what thou urgest shall come to pass, so far that the Synagogue, which is to be converted at the end, will be so strong in faith, so strengthened in hope, so kindled in charity, so armed with all wisdom and virtue, so walled about by angelic spirits, and so abounding in many hosts of believers, that thou shalt see in her nothing but companies of camps, that is, fellowships of those who fight for God, because they will be ready to die for God and the faith. Companies of camps also, that is, ranks and joinings of graces, virtues, gifts and other divine charisms: so that she who for so long before fought against the faith will henceforth fight with thee in defence of the faith, against Antichrist or other faithless men. And Methodius, martyr and bishop, says in his little book that a hundred and forty-four thousand of the Jews who will then believe will be slain by Antichrist.
